-1750: Erlitou on the middle Yellow River is one of East Asia's first Bronze Age capitals, and most scholars link it with the Xia of later texts. No writing survives from it, so the areas on the map are only the rough spread of archaeological cultures. Around it are the Dongyi, the forerunners of the Shang, and other bronze cultures of the north and the Yangtze.
-1500: Around 1600 BC Tang of Shang overthrew the Xia. The Shang capital now stands near modern Zhengzhou (the Erligang culture), and its bronzes reach as far as Panlongcheng on the middle Yangtze. Sanxingdui in the Sichuan basin and the Dongyi in the east lie beyond Shang power.
-1250: King Wu Ding rules from Yin (modern Anyang). The oracle bones begin in his reign, the earliest systematic Chinese writing; they record campaigns against the Guifang and the Qiang, some led by his consort Fu Hao. The Zhou in the west are still a minor people.
-1000: Around 1046 BC King Wu of Zhou destroyed the Shang at Muye. By the reigns of Cheng and Kang the Duke of Zhou's eastern campaign is over, and the royal house has planted kinsmen and allies across the land as lords of Qi, Lu, Yan, Jin and other states. The kings rule from Haojing in Guanzhong, with Luoyi to watch the east. 'Zhou states' on the map is the sum of these fiefs.
-800: King Xuan reigns. After the revolt of 841 BC drove out King Li, the Gonghe regency governed for a time; exact Chinese chronology begins that year. Xuan campaigns against the Xianyun, the Huai Yi and Chu in the south, and his reign is remembered as a revival, but within thirty years King You is killed and the Western Zhou ends.
-700: In 770 BC King Ping moved east to Luoyi; from then on the Zhou king is overlord in name only. The most active ruler of the past decades was Duke Zhuang of Zheng, whose army beat the king's at Xuge in 707 BC; he died last year. Qi, Jin, Qin and Chu are growing on the four sides, and Rong and Di peoples still live among the Zhou states.
-650: Duke Huan of Qi, with Guan Zhong as minister, rallies the states to 'honour the king and repel the barbarians': he rescues Yan, restores Xing and Wey, leads the lords against Chu in 656 BC and presides at Kuiqiu in 651 BC as the first hegemon. Chu presses north, Jin under the late Duke Xian has swallowed its small neighbours, and Duke Mu of Qin begins to look east.
-600: The contest between Jin and Chu is at its height. Duke Wen of Jin beat Chu at Chengpu in 632 BC and became hegemon. Now King Zhuang of Chu has paraded his army at Luoyi and asked the weight of the royal tripods (606 BC), and in 597 BC he will rout Jin at Bi. Zheng, Song and the other states between them change sides as each power advances.
-500: Wu rises in the south-east: in 506 BC King Helü, with Wu Zixu and Sun Wu, takes the Chu capital Ying. Yue then rises behind Wu, and their struggle lasts over thirty years until Yue destroys Wu in 473 BC. In the central states power is passing to the great ministerial houses, the six ministers in Jin and the Three Huan in Lu, where Confucius now holds office.
-453: In this year the houses of Han, Zhao and Wei destroy the Zhi clan beneath the walls of Jinyang and divide Jin among themselves, setting the pattern of the Warring States; the Zhou king recognises them as lords in 403 BC. In Qi the Tian clan already holds real power. Yue, having destroyed Wu, has moved north to Langya; Chu expands eastward and Qin is still a western outlier.
-350: Wei, the first state to reform, under Marquis Wen, is still the leading power, though Qi checked it at Guiling in 353 BC. In Qin, Duke Xiao has put Shang Yang in charge of reform: after the laws of 356 BC a second round comes this year, with the capital moved to Xianyang, counties across the land and rewards for farming and fighting. Qin's rise begins here.
-300: Qin annexed Ba and Shu in 316 BC and beat Chu at Danyang and Lantian, becoming the threat every other state must reckon with. Persuaders in the mould of Zhang Yi travel from court to court, urging 'vertical' alliances against Qin or 'horizontal' ones with it. King Wuling of Zhao adopts nomad dress and mounted archery in 307 BC and pushes north; Qi in the east is at its peak.
-260: In this year the Qin general Bai Qi crushes Zhao at Changping; the Shiji says 400,000 men who had surrendered were buried alive. No eastern state can now face Qin alone. Chu lost its capital Ying to Bai Qi in 278 BC and moved east, and Qi never recovered from the five-state invasion of 284 BC. Four years from now Qin will end the Zhou royal house.
-221: Within ten years King Zheng of Qin has destroyed Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi; this year the realm is one and he takes the title First Emperor. Fiefs give way to commanderies and counties, and script, weights and measures and axle widths are made uniform. The Xiongnu in the north and the Baiyue in the south still lie outside; Qin armies take the Ordos and enter Lingnan a few years later.
-200: The early Han and the Xiongnu

Qin fell under its second emperor, and after the war between Chu and Han, Liu Bang founded the Han in 202 BC. This year he marches against the Xiongnu and is trapped for seven days at Baideng by the chanyu Modu; afterwards the Han buys peace with marriage alliances. Modu has beaten the Donghu, driven back the Yuezhi and united the steppe. In the south Zhao Tuo holds Lingnan as king of Nanyue.
-100: Emperor Wu has reigned for forty years. Wei Qing and Huo Qubing have driven the Xiongnu north of the Gobi, the Han holds the Hexi corridor with four commanderies, and Zhang Qian's missions have opened the road to Central Asia. Nanyue, Minyue, Korea and the south-western peoples are now commanderies. Li Guangli's expedition to Dayuan succeeded in 101 BC, but the endless wars have drained the treasury.
-1: The last years of Western Han

The Xiongnu split in the mid-first century BC; the chanyu Huhanye submitted to the Han, Wang Zhaojun went north as his bride in 33 BC, and the frontier has been quiet for decades. Since 60 BC a Protector-General has overseen the oasis states on both sides of the Tianshan. This year Emperor Ai dies and Wang Mang returns to power; nine years on he will take the throne and found the Xin dynasty.
100: The Eastern Han at its height

Liu Xiu, Emperor Guangwu, restored the Han in AD 25 with his capital at Luoyang. Under Emperor He, Ban Chao has spent nearly thirty years in the Western Regions, where he re-established the Protectorate and three years ago sent Gan Ying towards Rome as far as the Persian Gulf. Dou Xian broke the Northern Xiongnu in 89–91, and the Xianbei have taken over the Mongolian steppe. The Southern Xiongnu live along the frontier as Han dependants.
200: Since the Yellow Turban rising of 184 the Eastern Han has been an empire in name, its provinces held by governors and generals. This year Cao Cao defeats the much larger army of Yuan Shao at Guandu and goes on to unite the north. Sun Ce has just died, leaving the lower Yangtze to Sun Quan; Liu Bei is still a guest in other men's camps. Emperor Xian is in Cao Cao's hands, a figurehead.
262: The Three Kingdoms near their end

Wei, Shu and Wu have stood side by side for forty years. In Wei real power belongs to the Sima family; Shu Han, since Zhuge Liang's death, has worn itself out in Jiang Wei's northern campaigns. Next year Wei armies invade, Deng Ai slips through the Yinping trail and Shu falls; two years after that Sima Yan replaces Wei with the Jin dynasty.
280: This year six Jin armies invade Wu; Wang Jun's fleet sails down the Yangtze into Jianye and Sun Hao surrenders, ending nearly a century of division since the Yellow Turbans. Unity is brief. Emperor Wu hands out princedoms to his kinsmen, who will fight the War of the Eight Princes after his death, and Xiongnu, Jie, Di, Qiang and Xianbei settlers already fill the north. The Western Jin falls some thirty-five years from now.
320: The Xiongnu state of Han Zhao sacked Luoyang in 311 and took Chang'an in 316, ending the Western Jin. In 317 Sima Rui, Prince of Langya, revived the dynasty at Jiankang as the Eastern Jin, and northern gentry families streamed south. In the north Liu Yao's Han Zhao faces Shi Le's Later Zhao, while the Zhang family in Liangzhou, the Murong Xianbei in Liaodong and Cheng Han in Sichuan each hold their own.
360: Later Zhao collapsed around 350, and Ran Min's Wei lasted little more than two years. The Murong Xianbei state of Former Yan has moved into the central plain with its capital at Ye, and the Di house of Fu has founded Former Qin in Guanzhong, where Fu Jian took the throne three years ago and Wang Meng is putting the government in order. For the Eastern Jin, Huan Wen destroyed Cheng Han in 347 and has twice marched north, recovering Luoyang in 356.
383: The battle of the Fei River

Fu Jian destroyed Former Yan in 370 and Former Liang and Dai in 376, uniting the north. This year he leads a vast army south and is beaten at the Fei River by the Eastern Jin's Northern Headquarters troops under Xie Xuan. Former Qin falls apart at once: Murong Chui, Yao Chang, Tuoba Gui and others set up states of their own, and the north is divided again.
400: Seventeen years after the Fei River the north is again a field of rivals. The Qiang house of Yao rules Guanzhong as Later Qin; Tuoba Gui's Northern Wei crushed Later Yan at Canhe Slope in 395 and took Hebei, leaving the Yan state split in two; several 'Liang' states share the Hexi corridor. On the steppe the Rouran are rising. In the Eastern Jin, Sun En's rebellion rages and Huan Xuan is gathering power.
420: Liu Yu, a soldier of the Northern Headquarters army, put down Huan Xuan and the rebels Sun En and Lu Xun, then marched north to destroy Southern Yan and Later Qin and for a time held Chang'an. This year he deposes the last Jin emperor and founds the Song, the first of the Southern Dynasties. In the north only Northern Wei and a few smaller states remain, among them Helian Bobo's Xia, Northern Liang, Northern Yan and Western Qin; over the next twenty years Wei will absorb most of them.
439: Emperor Taiwu of Northern Wei took the Xia capital Tongwan in 427 (Xia ended in 431) and destroyed Northern Yan in 436; this year he takes Guzang and ends Northern Liang. The age of the Sixteen Kingdoms is over, and north and south now face each other. Beyond Wei's northern frontier are the Rouran, whom Taiwu attacks again and again; to the south the Liu Song enjoys the Yuanjia era. Eleven years on the two will fight a great war.
500: Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei moved his capital from Pingcheng to Luoyang in 494 and had his Xianbei nobles take Chinese surnames, dress and speech; he died last year. In the south the Song gave way to Xiao Daocheng's Qi in 479. Its ruler now is the Marquis of Donghun, whom Xiao Yan will replace in two years, founding the Liang. The Rouran still rule the steppe.
540: After the revolt of the Six Garrisons the Northern Wei split: Gao Huan set up Eastern Wei at Ye in 534 and Yuwen Tai Western Wei at Chang'an the next year, each with a puppet emperor, and the two fight year after year along the Yellow River. In the south Emperor Wu of Liang, Xiao Yan, has reigned almost forty years, a devout Buddhist over a realm that seems secure. Eight years from now the defector Hou Jing will rebel and lay the south waste.
560: The Gao family replaced Eastern Wei with Northern Qi in 550, and the Yuwen replaced Western Wei with Northern Zhou in 557. The Liang collapsed after Hou Jing's rebellion, and in that same year Chen Baxian founded the Chen, which holds little beyond the lands south of the Yangtze. The steppe has new masters: the Türks overthrew the Rouran in 552 and within a few years built a khaganate from Manchuria to Central Asia, courted by both Zhou and Qi.
580: Emperor Wu of Northern Zhou destroyed Northern Qi in 577 and united the north, then died the next year on his way to fight the Türks. His heir Emperor Xuan ruled badly and died young; this year Yang Jian, father of the empress, takes charge as regent and crushes the resistance of Yuchi Jiong and others. Next year he will replace the Zhou with his own Sui dynasty. The Chen holds only the lands south of the Yangtze.
589: This year Sui armies cross the Yangtze and enter Jiankang; the last Chen ruler is taken, and more than 270 years of division since the fall of the Western Jin are over. Emperor Wen governs through the Three Departments and Six Ministries, keeps the equal-field system and abolishes the Nine Ranks system of appointment. The Türks split into eastern and western khaganates around 583, and the eastern one acknowledges Sui overlordship. Koguryo in the north-east is the next opponent.
700: The Tang destroyed the Eastern Türks in 630, the Western Türks in 657 and Koguryo in 668, reaching its greatest extent. Wu Zetian has now been emperor in her own right for ten years, her dynasty called Zhou and her capital Luoyang. Tibet contests the Western Regions and Qinghai, and the Tang recovered the Four Garrisons of Anxi in 692; the Türks restored their khaganate in 682 and hold the steppe again; and in the north-east Dae Joyeong founded Balhae two years ago.
742: The Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong was the Tang's golden age; this year the reign title changes to Tianbao. Tang power reaches the Pamirs, and Chang'an is one of the largest cities in the world. To the north the Türk khaganate will fall to the Uyghurs in two years; in the south-west Tibet contests the Western Regions, and Nanzhao has just united the Erhai basin. The An Lushan rebellion is 13 years away.
800: The An Lushan rebellion (755–763) broke the Tang's strength: the governors of Hebei rule as they please, and the court lives on the taxes of the south. Tibet seized Hexi and Longyou and briefly entered Chang'an in 763. The Tang garrisons of the Western Regions have been cut off for years; Beiting fell in 790, and the region is now fought over by Tibet and the Uyghurs. The Uyghur khaganate, which helped put down the rebellion, dominates the steppe; Nanzhao, after siding with Tibet, returned to the Tang alliance in 794.
900: After Huang Chao's rebellion (875–884) the Tang court controls little beyond Chang'an, while Zhu Wen, Li Keyong and other governors fight each other; in seven years Zhu Wen will end the dynasty. The neighbouring empires have fallen apart too: the Kyrgyz destroyed the Uyghur khaganate in 840, its remnants moving west to Ganzhou and Qocho, and the Tibetan empire broke up after 842. In the north-east the Khitan leader Abaoji is on the rise.
910: In 907 Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor and founded the Later Liang at Kaifeng, opening the age of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. In Hedong Li Cunxu, who succeeded his father Li Keyong as Prince of Jin in 908, fights on against Liang; Wu, Wuyue, Chu, Min and Southern Han in the south and Former Shu in Sichuan are states of their own. Also in 907, Abaoji became khagan of the Khitans. In Korea, Silla has declined and the Later Three Kingdoms have begun.
926: Li Cunxu destroyed the Later Liang in 923 and founded the Later Tang, then took Former Shu in 925, giving the largest realm of the Five Dynasties. This year he is killed in a mutiny and Li Siyuan succeeds him. In the same year the Khitan ruler Abaoji conquers Balhae and dies soon after. Korea is divided between Wang Geon's Goryeo, Gyeon Hwon's Later Baekje and what is left of Silla.
938: In 936 Shi Jingtang destroyed the Later Tang with Khitan troops and founded the Later Jin, at the price of becoming the Khitan emperor's vassal and calling him father; this year he formally cedes the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun. The central plain loses the line of the Great Wall and will not regain it for more than four centuries. In Sichuan Meng Zhixiang has founded Later Shu, on the Yangtze Xu Zhigao has replaced Wu with the state soon to be called Southern Tang, and in Yunnan Duan Siping founded Dali in 937.
950: The last year of Later Han

In early 947 the Khitans entered Kaifeng and ended the Later Jin; their ruler Yelü Deguang named his state Liao but soon withdrew north. Liu Zhiyuan seized the moment to found the Later Han, which lasts only four years: at the end of this year the general Guo Wei rebels, and next year he founds the Later Zhou while a branch of the Liu family holds out at Taiyuan as Northern Han. In the south, Southern Tang is the strongest state, having destroyed Min; next year it takes Chu.
958: Chai Rong, Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou, is the ablest ruler of the Five Dynasties. He has reformed the army and the finances, beaten Northern Han and Liao at Gaoping in 954 and campaigned three times against Southern Tang, which this year cedes its fourteen prefectures north of the Yangtze and gives up the imperial title to become a Zhou vassal. Next year he will march on Liao and retake three passes, fall ill on campaign and die; half a year later Zhao Kuangyin is acclaimed emperor at Chenqiao.
970: Zhao Kuangyin founded the Song in 960 and is taking the separate states one at a time, south before north: Jingnan and Hunan in 963, Later Shu in 965. Southern Han, Southern Tang, Wuyue and Northern Han still stand; Southern Han falls next year, Southern Tang in 975 and Northern Han in 979. Taizu has also talked his generals into giving up their commands over a cup of wine.
1000: The Song has united the central plain and the south, but Emperor Taizong's two northern campaigns were beaten by the Liao, which still holds the Sixteen Prefectures. Liao armies raid south year after year; in 1004 Emperor Shengzong and Empress Dowager Xiao invade in force, Emperor Zhenzong goes to the front at Chanzhou, and the Treaty of Chanyuan gives over a century of peace. In the north-west the Tangut leader Li Jiqian is breaking away from the Song.
1100: Song, Liao and Western Xia have long shared the land between them. The Northern Song is at its height in wealth and culture, with over a million people in Kaifeng, though the court has been split between reformers and conservatives ever since Wang Anshi's New Policies; this year Emperor Zhezong dies and Huizong succeeds him. The Jurchens of the north-east are still Liao subjects. In fifteen years Aguda will found the Jin, which destroys the Liao and then the Northern Song within twelve.
1142: In 1127 Jin armies took Kaifeng and carried off Emperors Huizong and Qinzong, ending the Northern Song; Gaozong rebuilt the dynasty in the south with his capital at Lin'an. Yue Fei's counter-offensive came close to Kaifeng, but Gaozong and Qin Hui were set on peace and had him put to death as the treaty was concluded. Under the Shaoxing peace, in force this year, the Song pays tribute as Jin's vassal and the border runs along the Huai River and the Dasan Pass. Far to the west the Liao prince Yelü Dashi has founded the Western Liao.
1279: Chinggis Khan united the Mongols in 1206; he and his heirs destroyed Western Xia (1227), Jin (1234) and Dali (1253). Khubilai named his dynasty Yuan in 1271 and took Lin'an in 1276. This year the last Song fleet is destroyed at Yamen, Lu Xiufu leaps into the sea with the boy emperor on his back, and the Southern Song is no more. The Yuan rules all China, but the Mongol empire itself has split into the Yuan and several khanates.
1400: Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming in 1368 and drove the last Yuan emperor back to the steppe, where the Northern Yuan still confronts the Ming. After his death the Jianwen emperor moved against the princes, and the Prince of Yan, Zhu Di, has now been in revolt for a year. In two years he will take Nanjing and reign as the Yongle emperor, later moving the capital to Beijing and sending Zheng He's fleets overseas. In Korea the Joseon dynasty replaced Goryeo in 1392.
1500: The Ming is a hundred and thirty years old and steady under the Hongzhi emperor. Since the Tumu disaster of 1449 it has stood on the defensive against the Mongols and begun the great rebuilding of the Wall; Dayan Khan is reuniting the Mongol tribes, and the Ordos is in Mongol hands. In the west Turfan disputes Hami with the Ming. At sea the Portuguese reached India round the Cape two years ago.
1600: The Wanli emperor has reigned for nearly thirty years. From 1592 to 1598 Ming armies helped Korea beat off Toyotomi Hideyoshi's invasion, at great cost. In Liaodong the Jurchen chief Nurhaci has united the Jianzhou tribes and is now absorbing the Haixi Jurchens; in sixteen years he will found the Later Jin. The Mongol tribes are divided, and the heirs of Altan Khan trade peacefully with the Ming. Next year Matteo Ricci reaches Beijing with Western astronomy and maps.
1650: In 1644 Li Zicheng took Beijing, the Chongzhen emperor hanged himself, and Wu Sangui let the Qing army through the Wall; the Qing made Beijing its capital. It now holds most of China. The regent Dorgon dies at the end of this year, and the Shunzhi emperor then begins to rule in person. The Southern Ming court of the Yongli emperor has fallen back to the south-west, Zheng Chenggong holds Xiamen and Jinmen, and the Dutch have a base in south-west Taiwan. In the west two Oirat peoples, the Dzungars and the Khoshuts, have khanates of their own.
1715: The Kangxi emperor is in the fifty-fourth year of his reign. He has put down the Three Feudatories (1681), taken Taiwan (1683), driven the Russians from Albazin and signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689), and led three campaigns that broke Galdan of the Dzungars and brought the Khalkha Mongols under the Qing. The Dzungar khanate still holds both sides of the Tianshan and remains the Qing's great rival in the north-west; their wars have forty years still to run.
1800: In the 1750s the Qianlong emperor destroyed the Dzungars and subdued the Muslim south of Xinjiang, taking the Qing to its greatest extent: west to Lake Balkhash and the Pamirs, north to the Stanovoy range. He died last year, and the Jiaqing emperor at once put the favourite Heshen to death. The population has passed three hundred million, and the White Lotus rebellion is spreading through Sichuan and Hubei. In 1793 the British envoy Macartney asked for wider trade and was refused.
1900: After two Opium Wars, the Taiping war and defeat by Japan, the Qing has lost Hong Kong, Outer Manchuria and Taiwan, and the powers have carved leases and spheres of influence along the coast. This year the Boxers enter Beijing, the Eight-Nation Alliance takes the capital, and the Empress Dowager Cixi flees to Xi'an with the Guangxu emperor, while Russia occupies Manchuria. The Boxer Protocol follows next year; eleven years from now the 1911 Revolution breaks out and the dynasty falls.

presets.-600--500: From hegemons to Wu and Yue
presets.200-262: From Han to the Three Kingdoms
presets.500-589: The Sui reunite north and south
presets.950-1000: From the Five Dynasties to the Song

names.Western Regions oasis states: Oasis states of the Western Regions

xia-founded: By the traditional reckoning, Yu's son Qi succeeds him and the throne passes from father to son: the Xia. All that is told of the Xia comes from later texts; no Xia writing has been found.
erlitou: At Erlitou in the Luoyang basin rise palace compounds, a grid of roads and bronze foundries, the largest settlement in East Asia at the time; many take it for the late Xia capital.
tang-conquers-xia: Tang of Shang defeats Jie of Xia at Mingtiao and founds the Shang. The walled city at Yanshi, about 6 km from Erlitou, is thought to have been built by the Shang after the conquest.
zhengzhou-shang-city: A great early Shang city, its inner wall nearly 7 km round, with bronze, pottery and bone workshops outside; many take it for Bo, the capital of Tang.
panlongcheng: The Shang build Panlongcheng near the Yangtze (Huangpi, Wuhan); its bronzes match Zhengzhou's, and it is widely seen as an outpost for southern copper.
pangeng-moves-to-yin: King Pan Geng moves the capital to Yin (Anyang, Henan), where it stays until the fall of the Shang; hence the Shang are also called the Yin.
wu-ding: King Wu Ding reigns over fifty years and campaigns against the Guifang, Qiang, Tufang and others; his consort Fu Hao leads armies herself. Most of the Anyang oracle bones date from his reign.
zhou-moves-to-qi: The Zhou move to Mount Qi
Pressed by the Rong and Di, Gugong Danfu leads the Zhou from Bin to Zhouyuan, the plain below Mount Qi, where they build a town and begin to rise.
sanxingdui: At Sanxingdui (Guanghan, Sichuan) bronze masks, bronze trees, a gold staff and elephant tusks are buried; their style is unlike anything in the Central Plains, the mark of a separate bronze civilisation on the upper Yangtze.
muye: King Wu of Zhou and his western allies defeat the Shang army at Muye, south of Zhaoge; King Zhou of Shang burns himself to death and the Shang falls. The Li gui bronze records that the battle was fought on the morning of a jiazi day.
duke-of-zhou-east: The Duke of Zhou goes east

After King Wu's death his brothers Guan and Cai rise with Wu Geng, son of the last Shang king, and the states of the east. The regent, the Duke of Zhou, spends three years crushing them, then enfeoffs lords across the east.
chengzhou: The Duke of Zhou builds Luoyi (Chengzhou) on the Luo River as the base for ruling the east. The He zun bronze, which speaks of dwelling in 'this central land' (zhongguo), is the earliest known use of the word.
king-zhao-dies: King Zhao leads his armies against Chu and is lost with them on the Han River; the Zhou advance to the south stalls.
guoren-uprising: The people of Haojing rise against King Li, who had seized the realm's resources and silenced his critics; he flees to Zhi. This year, the first of the Gonghe regency, begins China's exact year-by-year chronology.
king-xuan: King Xuan comes to the throne; Yin Jifu drives back the Xianyun in the north and Duke Mu of Shao subdues the Huai Yi. The court briefly recovers.
fall-of-haojing: The Lord of Shen, with Zeng and the Quanrong, takes Haojing; King You is killed below Mount Li and the Western Zhou ends.
ping-moves-east: Escorted by Jin, Zheng and Qin, King Ping moves the court to Luoyi: the Eastern Zhou, and the Spring and Autumn period, begin.
qin-first-counties: Qin conquers the Gui and Ji Rong and rules their lands as counties.
guan-zhong: Duke Huan of Qi takes the throne and makes Guan Zhong his chief minister.
zhaoling: Duke Huan leads the states against Chu and makes peace with it at Shaoling.
kuiqiu: Duke Huan of Qi, the first hegemon, presides over a meeting of the states at Kuiqiu.
chonger-returns: After nineteen years in exile Chong'er comes home with Qin's help as Duke Wen.
chengpu: Duke Wen of Jin pulls back three days' march, then defeats Chu and becomes hegemon.
xiao: Jin ambushes and destroys a Qin army returning from a failed raid on Zheng.
wen-ding: King Zhuang of Chu, camped on the Luo, asks the weight of the Zhou cauldrons.
yellow-river-602: In its first recorded change of course, the Yellow River breaks out at Suxukou and turns east.
battle-of-bi: King Zhuang of Chu defeats Jin near the Yellow River and becomes hegemon of the central states.
yanling: Jin defeats Chu at Yanling, where King Gong of Chu is shot in the eye.
confucius: Confucius is born in Lu; his sayings, gathered by his disciples in the Analects, will shape Chinese thought.
mibing: Jin, Chu and their allies agree at the Song capital to stop fighting; peace holds for decades.
zichan-code: Zichan of Zheng casts the penal code on bronze vessels, traditionally seen as the first written law made public in China.
baiju: King Helü of Wu, served by Wu Zixu (and, Sima Qian says, Sun Wu), routs Chu and takes its capital Ying.
confucius-travels: Confucius leaves Lu and travels among the states with his disciples for fourteen years.
jin-civil-war: Zhao Yang fights the Fan and Zhonghang clans from Jinyang and drives them from Jin.
hangou: King Fuchai of Wu links the Yangtze and the Huai, the oldest section of the future Grand Canal.
huangchi: Fuchai of Wu contests the lead with Jin at Huangchi while Yue raids his capital.
tian-chang: The minister Tian Chang kills Duke Jian of Qi; his clan now rules Qi.
goujian-conquers-wu: After years of tasting gall to steel himself, King Goujian of Yue destroys Wu.
battle-of-jinyang: Han, Zhao and Wei turn on the besieging Zhi clan and divide its lands.
wei-wen-reforms: Reforms of Marquis Wen of Wei
Marquis Wen comes to power and, with Li Kui and Wu Qi, makes Wei the leading state.
partition-of-jin: The Zhou king recognises the Han, Zhao and Wei families as lords; Sima Guang's chronicle starts here.
tian-qi: The Zhou king recognises Tian He as lord of Qi, replacing the old ruling house.
shang-yang: Lord Shang's laws reward farming and war and make Qin ever richer and stronger.
guiling: To relieve Handan, Qi threatens Wei's capital, and Sun Bin ambushes the Wei army hurrying home.
maling: Sun Bin lures the Wei army into an ambush of Qi crossbowmen; Pang Juan dies.
jixia: King Xuan of Qi pays scholars of every school to teach and debate at Linzi.
qin-takes-shu: On Sima Cuo's advice Qin conquers Shu and Ba, gaining a rich granary.
hufu-qishe: King Wuling of Zhao has his army adopt the dress and horseback archery of the northern nomads.
qi-annexes-song: King Min of Qi conquers Song, and the alarmed states unite against him.
yue-yi-attacks-qi: Led by Yue Yi of Yan, five states crush Qi and take Linzi and over seventy cities.
tian-dan: Breaking out of Jimo with burning oxen, Tian Dan routs Yan and recovers Qi.
qu-yuan: The poet of the Chu Ci is said to have drowned himself in the Miluo River this year; the Dragon Boat Festival remembers him.
ying-falls: The Qin general Bai Qi captures the Chu capital, and the Chu court moves east to Chen.
changping: Bai Qi destroys the Zhao army, and the surrendered soldiers, said to number 400,000, are buried alive.
handan-siege: Lord Xinling seizes a Wei army with a stolen tally and, with Chu, saves Handan.
dujiangyan: Li Bing, Qin governor of Shu, builds irrigation works that still water the Chengdu plain.
zhou-ends: Qin annexes the last royal domain at Luoyang, ending a dynasty of nearly eight centuries.
zhengguo-canal: An engineer from Han, sent to exhaust Qin, digs a canal that instead enriches the Guanzhong plain.
qin-takes-han: Qin captures King An of Han and annexes his state, the first of the six to fall.
qin-conquers-zhao: Wang Jian takes Handan and its king; a Zhao prince holds Dai until 222 BC.
jing-ke: Jing Ke's attempt on the King of Qin
An assassin sent by Crown Prince Dan of Yan fails to kill the future First Emperor.
qin-conquers-wei: Wang Ben floods Daliang from the Yellow River until its walls collapse.
qin-conquers-chu: Wang Jian's army of 600,000 overcomes the largest of Qin's rivals.
qin-conquers-yan: Wang Ben captures the king of Yan in Liaodong, then ends Zhao's remnant in Dai.
qin-unification: With the fall of Qi, King Zheng rules all the states and takes the title First Emperor.
great-wall-qin: Meng Tian drives the Xiongnu from the Ordos, and Qin joins older walls into one Great Wall.
qin-lingnan: Supplied by the new Lingqu canal, Qin armies conquer the Yue lands and set up three commanderies.
burning-books: On Li Si's advice, the First Emperor orders the classics and histories burned, except official copies.
dazexiang: Conscripts led by Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rise against Qin, and revolt spreads across the empire.
modu-chanyu: Modu kills his father and takes power, then unites the Xiongnu into a great steppe empire.
julu: Xiang Yu sinks his boats and smashes his cooking pots, then crushes the main Qin army.
qin-falls: Ziying surrenders to Liu Bang outside Xianyang; Liu then escapes Xiang Yu at the Feast at Hong Gate.
gaixia: Surrounded, and hearing Chu songs on all sides, Xiang Yu is defeated; Liu Bang founds the Han.
baideng: Modu traps Emperor Gaozu near Pingcheng; Han turns to marriage alliances and gifts.
zhang-qian: Emperor Wu sends Zhang Qian to seek allies against the Xiongnu; his journeys open the Silk Road.
dong-zhongshu: Emperor Wu adopts Dong Zhongshu's proposal to honour Confucian learning above all other schools.
huzi: The river bursts its dykes and floods sixteen commanderies; the breach is closed only in 109 BC.
hexi: Huo Qubing takes the Hexi Corridor
Victories over the Xiongnu open the corridor, where Han later founds Wuwei, Zhangye, Jiuquan and Dunhuang.
mobei: Wei Qing and Huo Qubing strike north of the Gobi; Huo holds a victory sacrifice at Mount Langjuxu.
nanyue-conquered: Han takes Panyu and ends Zhao Tuo's kingdom; its lands, down to northern Vietnam, become commanderies.
gojoseon: Emperor Wu destroys Wiman Joseon and sets up four commanderies, among them Lelang.
dayuan: Li Guangli marches on Dayuan in Ferghana; on a second campaign he brings back its famed horses.
shiji: Sima Qian completes the Shiji, a history from the Yellow Emperor to his own day.
western-regions-protectorate: After a Xiongnu king submits, Han sets up a protector-general at Wulei to oversee the oasis states.
zhizhi: Chen Tang and Gan Yanshou storm the fortress of the rebel chanyu Zhizhi on the Talas.
wang-zhaojun: The court lady Wang Zhaojun is married to the Xiongnu chanyu Huhanye, sealing peace on the frontier.
wang-mang: The regent Wang Mang takes the Han throne and launches sweeping reforms of land and money.
eastern-han: After his victory at Kunyang and Wang Mang's fall, Liu Xiu proclaims himself emperor and settles at Luoyang.
trung-sisters: The Trung sisters lead a revolt in Jiaozhi; the Han general Ma Yuan crushes it in 43.
xiongnu-split: Bi, ruler of eight southern tribes, takes the title of chanyu and submits to Han; the Xiongnu divide in two.
na-gold-seal: Gold seal for the king of Na
Emperor Guangwu gives a gold seal to an envoy from Wa; it is found near Fukuoka in 1784.
white-horse-temple: White Horse Temple, traditionally China's first Buddhist temple, is built at Luoyang for two Indian monks who brought scriptures.
ban-chao: Ban Chao in the Western Regions
Sent west with 36 men, Ban Chao wins over Shanshan and spends three decades restoring Han authority.
yanran: Dou Xian crushes the Northern Xiongnu; Ban Gu's victory inscription on Mount Yanran is rediscovered in 2017.
cai-lun-paper: The court official Cai Lun presents paper made from bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets.
zhang-heng: The astronomer Zhang Heng builds an instrument that signals the direction of distant earthquakes.
yellow-turbans: Zhang Jue's Way of Great Peace rises across eastern China, and the Han begins to fall apart.
dong-zhuo: Facing a coalition of eastern warlords, Dong Zhuo burns Luoyang and moves the emperor to Chang'an.
guandu: Cao Cao burns Yuan Shao's supplies at Wuchao and wins mastery of northern China.
red-cliffs: Sun Quan and Liu Bei burn Cao Cao's fleet on the Yangtze, and China settles into three kingdoms.
jian-an-plague: A great epidemic sweeps the north, killing four of the Seven Scholars of Jian'an.
cao-pi: Emperor Xian abdicates to Cao Pi, who founds Wei; Liu Bei and Sun Quan later claim thrones too.
yiling: Lu Xun of Wu burns Liu Bei's line of camps; Liu dies at Baidi the next year.
wuzhangyuan: Zhuge Liang dies at Wuzhang Plains
The Shu chancellor dies in camp during his last northern campaign against Wei.
wei-conquers-shu: Deng Ai crosses the mountains by Yinping, and Liu Shan surrenders at Chengdu.
western-jin: Sima Yan, whose grandfather Sima Yi seized power in Wei, makes its last emperor abdicate.
jin-conquers-wu: Jin fleets sail down the Yangtze from Shu; Sun Hao surrenders at Jianye and China is reunited.
eight-princes: Empress Jia's coup sets the Jin princes fighting over the court until 306.
liu-yuan: During the War of the Eight Princes, the Xiongnu noble Liu Yuan proclaims a Han state at Lishi.
yongjia: Han-Zhao forces sack Luoyang and capture Emperor Huai; northern families flee south in great numbers.
western-jin-falls: Liu Yao starves out Chang'an, and Emperor Min's surrender ends the Western Jin.
eastern-jin: After Chang'an falls to Han-Zhao, Sima Rui rebuilds the Jin court at Jiankang.
later-zhao-founded: Shi Le founds the Later Zhao
The Jie leader Shi Le breaks with Liu Yao and becomes King of Zhao.
huan-wen-shu: The Jin general Huan Wen takes Chengdu, and the last Cheng Han ruler surrenders.
ran-min: Ran Min kills the Later Zhao emperor at Ye and proclaims his own state of Wei.
former-yan-emperor: Former Yan takes the Central Plain
Having crushed Ran Min and taken Ye, Murong Jun proclaims himself emperor at Ji.
lanting: At a gathering of poets near Kuaiji, Wang Xizhi writes the most celebrated work of Chinese calligraphy.
mogao: A Tang stele records that the monk Lezun cut the first cave at Dunhuang; carving went on for a thousand years.
qin-unites-north: Fu Jian's Qin absorbs the Former Liang and Dai, six years after conquering the Former Yan.
fei-river: Eastern Jin routs Fu Jian's far larger Former Qin army, and the north breaks apart again.
northern-wei-founded: Tuoba Gui restores his grandfather's state of Dai and soon renames it Wei.
canhebei: Tuoba Gui routs the Later Yan army and has tens of thousands of prisoners killed.
kumarajiva: The Kuchean monk reaches the Later Qin capital, where he translates many of the main Buddhist scriptures.
liu-yu-later-qin: Liu Yu conquers the Later Qin
Liu Yu's general Wang Zhen'e sails up the Wei and takes Chang'an; Yao Hong surrenders.
helian-changan: The Xia ruler drives out the Jin garrison and proclaims himself emperor outside Chang'an.
liu-song: The general Liu Yu takes the Jin throne, and the Southern Dynasties begin.
tongwan-falls: Emperor Taiwu storms the Xia capital; the last Xia ruler is captured in 431.
wei-unites-north: Emperor Taiwu takes Guzang from the Northern Liang, ending the Sixteen Kingdoms.
taiwu-persecution: Northern Wei orders temples destroyed and monks killed, the first of China's great persecutions of Buddhism.
yuanjia-campaign: A Song offensive stalls at Huatai, and Emperor Taiwu's counter-attack reaches the Yangtze.
yungang: The monk Tanyao begins five colossal Buddhas in the cliffs near Pingcheng, the Northern Wei capital.
zu-chongzhi: The mathematician who reckoned pi to seven decimal places presents his Daming calendar.
wei-takes-qingxu: The Wei exploits a Song civil war to seize Shandong and the north of the Huai.
southern-qi-founded: The general Xiao Daocheng takes the Song throne and founds the Qi at Jiankang.
xiaowen-luoyang: Emperor Xiaowen moves his capital south and orders the Xianbei to adopt Chinese dress, speech and surnames.
liang-founded: Xiao Yan takes Jiankang and founds the Liang, which he rules for almost fifty years.
zhongli: Liang fire ships burn the Wei pontoon bridges and break the siege of Zhongli.
six-garrisons: Frontier soldiers rise against Northern Wei, which soon splits into Eastern and Western Wei.
heyin: Erzhu Rong drowns the dowager and the child emperor and slaughters the Wei court.
wei-splits: Emperor Xiaowu flees to Yuwen Tai, and Gao Huan sets up a rival court at Ye.
buddhism-japan: The king of Baekje sends a Buddha image and sutras to the Yamato court (552 in the Nihon Shoki).
hou-jing: The turncoat general takes Jiankang; Emperor Wu of Liang dies a captive and the south is laid waste.
northern-qi-founded: Gao Yang deposes the Eastern Wei emperor and founds the Northern Qi at Ye.
turkic-khaganate: Bumin overthrows the Rouran and founds a Turkic empire that soon rules the whole steppe.
jiangling-554: Emperor Yuan of Liang burns his library and surrenders; over 100,000 captives go north.
chen-founded: The general Chen Baxian takes the Liang throne and founds the last southern dynasty.
northern-zhou-founded: Yuwen Jue takes the Western Wei throne at Chang'an and founds the Zhou.
chen-takes-huainan: Wu Mingche takes Shouyang from the Northern Qi and wins back the Huai lands.
zhou-conquers-qi: Emperor Wu of Zhou takes Ye and reunites northern China.
sui-founded: Yang Jian takes the Northern Zhou throne and becomes Emperor Wen of Sui.
sui-conquers-chen: Sui armies take Jiankang, reuniting China after nearly three centuries of division.
grand-canal: Emperor Yang begins the Tongji Canal; within six years waterways link Yuhang, Luoyang and the far north.
imperial-exams: Sui creates the jinshi degree (605 or 607); officials will be chosen by written examination until 1905.
salsu: Invading Goguryeo, a Sui army is destroyed by Eulji Mundeok as it retreats across the Salsu River.
tang-founded: After Emperor Yang is killed at Jiangdu, Li Yuan takes the throne in Chang'an.
xuanwu-gate: Li Shimin kills his two brothers at a palace gate and soon succeeds his father as Emperor Taizong.
eastern-turks: Li Jing routs the Eastern Turks, Illig Qaghan is captured, and the steppe chiefs hail Taizong as 'Heavenly Qaghan'.
alopen: The missionary Alopen brings the Church of the East to Tang, as a stele of 781 records.
wencheng: A Tang princess is married to Songtsen Gampo, king of the rising Tibetan Empire.
xuanzang: After years of study in India, the monk brings 657 Buddhist texts back to Chang'an and begins translating.
islam-arrives: The caliph sends envoys to Tang, the conventional date for the arrival of Islam in China.
baekgang: Tang and Silla fleets destroy a Japanese force sent to restore the kingdom of Baekje.
goguryeo-falls: Tang and Silla take Pyongyang, and Tang sets up a protectorate-general to rule the conquered land.
wu-zetian: The empress dowager proclaims her own Zhou dynasty, the only woman to rule China as emperor.
anxi-four-garrisons: Wang Xiaojie drives the Tibetans from the Tarim oases, and Tang keeps a standing army at Kucha.
balhae: Dae Joyeong founds a kingdom of Mohe and former Goguryeo people in eastern Manchuria.
kaiyuan: Xuanzong begins the Kaiyuan era, and with able ministers leads the Tang to its height.
nanzhao: With Tang support, Piluoge unites the six zhao around Erhai Lake into one kingdom.
li-bai-du-fu: The two greatest Tang poets meet at Luoyang and travel together.
talas: The Abbasids defeat Gao Xianzhi's Tang army near the Talas River.
jianzhen: On his sixth attempt, the monk crosses to Japan, where he later founds Toshodai-ji in Nara.
an-lushan-rebellion: The frontier general rises at Fanyang; eight years of war break the power of the Tang.
mawei: As Emperor Xuanzong flees Chang'an, his guards kill Yang Guozhong and force the death of Yang Guifei.
tibetans-take-changan: As the rebellion ends, a Tibetan army seizes the Tang capital and holds it for fifteen days.
two-tax-law: Chancellor Yang Yan replaces the old taxes with two payments a year, assessed on property.
tang-tibet-treaty: Tang and Tibet swear peace in Chang'an and Lhasa; the text still stands on a pillar in Lhasa.
uyghur-khaganate-falls: The Kyrgyz sack Ordu-Baliq; the Uyghurs scatter, many settling around Turfan and in the Hexi Corridor.
huichang-persecution: Emperor Wuzong destroys over 4,600 monasteries and returns some 260,000 monks and nuns to lay life.
diamond-sutra: The oldest surviving dated printed book is made; it is found in a Dunhuang cave in 1900.
huang-chao: Rebels led by Wang Xianzhi and then Huang Chao sweep across China and take Chang'an.
tang-ends: Zhu Wen deposes the last Tang emperor and founds the Later Liang; the Five Dynasties begin.
baixiang: Li Cunxu routs the Later Liang army, and Hebei goes over to Jin.
liao-founded: Yelü Abaoji proclaims himself emperor; in 926 he conquers Balhae, and the state later takes the name Liao.
later-liang-falls: Later Tang conquers the Later Liang
Li Cunxu dashes on Kaifeng, and the last Liang emperor has himself killed.
former-shu-falls: Later Tang conquers the Former Shu
Seventy days after the invasion begins, Wang Yan surrenders Chengdu.
sixteen-prefectures: Shi Jingtang wins Khitan help to found the Later Jin by ceding the lands around Youzhou and Yunzhou.
southern-tang-founded: Xu Zhigao takes the Wu throne at Jinling; his state is later renamed Tang.
bach-dang-938: Ngo Quyen traps the Southern Han fleet on iron-tipped stakes, and Vietnamese independence begins.
min-falls: The Southern Tang takes Jianzhou, and Fujian is soon split three ways.
later-jin-falls: Yelü Deguang takes Kaifeng, carries off the Jin emperor and proclaims the Liao.
gaoping: Shizong of the Later Zhou routs the Northern Han and their Liao allies.
huainan-campaign: Later Zhou takes the Huai lands
Shizong forces the Southern Tang to cede everything north of the Yangtze.
chenqiao: Troops drape the yellow robe on Zhao Kuangyin, who returns to Kaifeng and founds the Song.
later-shu-falls: Wang Quanbin's army reaches Chengdu, and Meng Chang surrenders.
southern-han-falls: Pan Mei takes Guangzhou, and Liu Chang, the last Southern Han ruler, surrenders.
southern-tang-falls: Crossing the Yangtze on a pontoon bridge, the Song take Jinling; Li Yu surrenders.
wuyue-submits: Qian Chu hands his thirteen prefectures to the Song without a fight.
northern-han-falls: Taizong takes Taiyuan, ending the last of the Ten Kingdoms.
chanyuan: Song agrees to pay Liao silver and silk every year, and peace holds for over a century.
jiaozi: The Song government begins issuing jiaozi notes in Sichuan, the first paper money issued by a state.
western-xia: The Tangut leader Li Yuanhao proclaims the Great Xia, which has its own script.
bi-sheng: In the Qingli years (1041–48) the commoner Bi Sheng prints with movable type made of baked clay, as Shen Kuo later records.
qingli-peace: Yuanhao accepts nominal Song overlordship in return for yearly silver, silk and tea.
wujing-zongyao: The military manual Wujing Zongyao gives the earliest known gunpowder recipes and a magnetic 'south-pointing fish'.
shanghu-1048: The river bursts its dykes near Puyang and turns north, reaching the sea near present-day Tianjin.
wang-anshi: Emperor Shenzong backs Wang Anshi's New Policies on state loans, taxes and local militia.
zizhi-tongjian: Sima Guang finishes his chronicle of 1,362 years, from 403 BC to the eve of the Song.
jin-founded: Wanyan Aguda rebels against the Liao and proclaims the Jin dynasty.
liao-falls: The Jin capture Emperor Tianzuo; Yelü Dashi leads Khitans west to found the Qara Khitai (Western Liao).
jingkang: Jin troops take Kaifeng and carry off Emperors Huizong and Qinzong, and the Northern Song ends.
southern-song: Prince Zhao Gou takes the throne at Yingtian; his court later settles at Lin'an.
du-chong-breach: Yellow River breached against the Jin
To halt the Jin, Song general Du Chong breaks the dykes, and the river turns south into the Huai.
yancheng: Yue Fei defeats Wuzhu's Jin cavalry and advances towards Kaifeng.
shaoxing-peace: Song accepts the Huai as its border and pays tribute to Jin; Yue Fei is put to death.
ehu: Zhu Xi and the Lu brothers debate how the Way is known, a landmark of Neo-Confucian thought.
genghis-khan: An assembly at the source of the Onon proclaims Temujin Genghis Khan of all the Mongols.
zhongdu-falls: After the Jin court flees south to Kaifeng, the Mongols capture and sack its northern capital.
otrar: After his envoys and merchants are killed at Otrar, Genghis Khan marches on the Khwarazmian empire.
qiu-chuji: The master of the Quanzhen school of Daoism travels to the Khan's camp in the Hindu Kush.
xia-falls: The Mongols destroy the Tangut state; Genghis Khan dies during the campaign.
caizhou: Mongol and Song armies take Caizhou; the last Jin emperor kills himself and the dynasty ends.
liangzhou-1247: Sakya Pandita, head of the Sakya school, meets the Mongol prince Köden and accepts Mongol overlordship for Tibet.
dali-conquered: Kublai leads an army through the mountains of the southwest and takes the kingdom of Dali.
diaoyucheng: Möngke Khan dies before the Song stronghold, and the Mongol armies withdraw to settle the succession.
kublai-khan: Kublai is proclaimed Great Khan at Kaiping and fights his brother Ariq Böke for the title.
xiangyang: The Mongols besiege the twin Song fortresses for nearly five years; Xiangyang falls in 1273.
yuan-founded: Kublai adopts the Chinese dynastic name Yuan and makes Dadu his capital.
mongol-invasion-japan: Yuan and Korean forces land at Hakata Bay; this attack and a larger one in 1281 both fail.
marco-polo: The Venetian reaches Kublai's summer capital and, by his own account, serves the khan for seventeen years.
linan-1276: The Song court surrenders its capital to Bayan; the child emperor is taken north.
yamen: The last Song fleet is destroyed; the minister Lu Xiufu leaps into the sea with the boy emperor.
shoushi-calendar: Guo Shoujing and Wang Xun complete a calendar that fixes the year at 365.2425 days.
wen-tianxiang: The captured Song chancellor refuses to serve the Yuan and is executed in Dadu.
bach-dang-1288: Tran Hung Dao repeats the stake trap and destroys the Yuan fleet, ending the invasions of Dai Viet.
tonghui-canal: Guo Shoujing's Tonghui River lets grain barges from the south sail into the capital itself.
hongdong-earthquake: A great earthquake in Shanxi destroys towns around Pingyang and Taiyuan and kills a great many people.
baimao-breach: Years of floods follow in Shandong and Henan; repairing the river in 1351 takes 150,000 labourers.
red-turbans: Liu Futong rises at Yingzhou among the river workers, and revolt spreads across the Yuan realm.
poyang: Zhu Yuanzhang defeats Chen Youliang's larger fleet in one of the largest naval battles in history.
ming-founded: Zhu Yuanzhang proclaims the Ming at Yingtian; his armies take Dadu and the Yuan court flees north.
buir-lake: Lan Yu surprises the Northern Yuan camp; the fleeing khan is later murdered.
jingnan: Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, rebels at Beiping against his nephew and takes the throne in 1402.
zheng-he: The admiral's treasure fleet leaves Liujiagang on the first of seven voyages, which reach East Africa.
yongle-dadian: Over two thousand scholars complete an encyclopedia of 22,877 chapters, the largest the world has yet seen.
ganden: The reformer Tsongkhapa founds Ganden Monastery near Lhasa, the seat of the Gelug school.
beijing-capital: With the Forbidden City complete, the Yongle Emperor moves the capital from Nanjing.
le-loi: Le Loi drives out the Ming
After ten years of revolt the Ming withdraws, and Le Loi founds the Later Le dynasty.
hangul: King Sejong of Joseon publishes a new alphabet for writing Korean.
tumu: The Oirat leader Esen captures the Zhengtong Emperor; Yu Qian then defends Beijing.
wang-yangming: In exile at Longchang in Guizhou, the philosopher concludes that principle is found in the mind.
jiajing-earthquake: The deadliest earthquake on record strikes Shaanxi; reports of the time count over 830,000 dead.
macau: Portuguese traders gain leave from local Ming officials to live and trade at Macau.
qi-jiguang: Qi Jiguang's army wins nine battles in a row against pirates around Taizhou in Zhejiang.
longqing-opening: The Ming lets private merchants sail from Yuegang in Fujian, and American silver pours in.
altan-peace: After decades of raids, the Ming names Altan Khan Prince Shunyi and opens markets on the border.
bencao-gangmu: Li Shizhen completes his great pharmacopoeia, describing nearly 1,900 drugs.
dalai-lama-title: Altan Khan meets the Gelug lama Sonam Gyatso by Qinghai Lake and gives him the title Dalai Lama.
single-whip: Zhang Juzheng extends empire-wide the merging of taxes and labour service into one silver payment.
imjin-war: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's armies land at Busan; the Ming sends troops to help Joseon, and war lasts until 1598.
matteo-ricci: The Jesuit is allowed to live in the capital, bringing Western maps, clocks and mathematics.
nurhaci: The Jurchen leader proclaims himself khan at Hetu Ala.
sarhu: Nurhaci defeats a Ming army advancing in four columns, and the Ming goes on the defensive in Liaodong.
ningyuan: Yuan Chonghuan's Western cannon repel Nurhaci, who dies months later.
qing-proclaimed: Hong Taiji, who has renamed his people Manchu, proclaims the Great Qing at Mukden.
tiangong-kaiwu: Song Yingxing's illustrated book describes China's farming and crafts, from rice and silk to iron and paper.
kaifeng-flood-1642: During Li Zicheng's siege the Yellow River dykes are broken and the city is drowned.
li-zicheng-beijing: Rebels enter the capital; the Chongzhen Emperor hangs himself on Coal Hill and the Ming falls.
shanhai-pass: Wu Sangui lets the Manchus through the pass; together they rout Li Zicheng, and the Qing takes Beijing.
jiangyin-1645: Defying the order to shave their heads, Jiangyin's people hold out for 81 days.
yangzhou-1645: Qing troops storm the city defended by Shi Kefa and massacre its people for ten days.
guangzhou-1650: Shang Kexi and Geng Jimao take Guangzhou from the Southern Ming after a ten-month siege.
koxinga-taiwan: Zheng Chenggong crosses with his fleet, and in 1662 the Dutch surrender Fort Zeelandia.
southern-ming-ends: Wu Sangui brings the Yongli Emperor back from Burma and has him put to death in Kunming.
three-feudatories: Wu Sangui rises in Yunnan, joined by the lords of Fujian and Guangdong; Kangxi wins after eight years.
penghu-1683: Shi Lang destroys the Zheng fleet; the Zheng regime surrenders and Taiwan comes under Qing rule.
albazin: Qing forces besiege the Russian fort on the Amur, in 1685 and again in 1686.
nerchinsk: China's first treaty with a European power sets the Russian border along the Argun and the Stanovoy Mountains.
lhasa-1720: A Qing army drives out the Dzungars who had seized Lhasa and installs the Seventh Dalai Lama.
christianity-banned: After the Rites controversy, the Yongzheng Emperor bans Christianity and expels provincial missionaries to Canton, and later to Macau.
gaitu-guiliu: On Ortai's advice, the Qing begins replacing hereditary chieftains in the southwest with appointed officials.
kyakhta: Qing and Russia fix the border of Mongolia and open trade at Kyakhta.
dzungar-conquest: Qianlong's armies take Ili; by 1759 the Dzungar state is destroyed and the Tarim Basin conquered.
canton-system: Qianlong limits European trade to Guangzhou, where it must pass through licensed merchants.
siku-quanshu: Qianlong orders a vast collection of all important books; many others are censored or destroyed.
honglou-meng: Dream of the Red Chamber printed
Cao Xueqin's novel is first printed in 120 chapters, edited by Cheng Weiyuan and Gao E.
golden-urn: A Qing ordinance for Tibet requires leading reincarnations to be chosen by drawing lots from a golden urn.
macartney: Britain's envoy meets Qianlong at Rehe, but his requests for trade and a resident ambassador are refused.
white-lotus: Sectarian risings in Hubei, Sichuan and Shaanxi drain the Qing treasury for nine years.
humen: Commissioner Lin Zexu destroys over a thousand tonnes of opium surrendered by foreign merchants.
opium-war-1840: A British expedition blockades the Pearl River and seizes Dinghai on Zhoushan.
treaty-of-nanjing: China cedes Hong Kong Island, pays an indemnity and opens five ports, the first of the unequal treaties.
taiping-rebellion: Hong Xiuquan, who calls himself the younger brother of Jesus, proclaims the Heavenly Kingdom at Jintian.
tianjing: Renamed Tianjing, the city is the Taiping capital until Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army takes it in 1864.
tongwaxiang: The river breaks out at Tongwaxiang and leaves its southern bed for a course to the Bohai Sea.
second-opium-war: After the Arrow incident, Britain, joined by France, attacks Guangzhou; the Treaties of Tianjin follow in 1858.
treaty-of-aigun: Russia gains the land north of the Amur; in 1860 it adds the coast east of the Ussuri.
old-summer-palace: Burning of the Old Summer Palace
Anglo-French forces take Beijing and burn the Yuanmingyuan; the Convention of Peking follows.
jiangnan-arsenal: Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang found China's largest modern arsenal, flagship of the Self-Strengthening Movement.
dingwu-famine: Three years of drought starve about ten million people in Shanxi, Henan and neighbouring provinces.
xinjiang-1876: Qing armies take Urumqi and by 1878 overthrow Yakub Beg; Xinjiang becomes a province in 1884.
ryukyu-annexed: Japan deposes the king of Ryukyu, a Qing tributary, and makes the islands Okinawa Prefecture.
battle-of-fuzhou: In the Sino-French War, the French fleet destroys the Fujian Fleet at Mawei in under an hour.
first-sino-japanese-war: Japan drives Qing forces out of Korea and defeats the Beiyang Fleet off the mouth of the Yalu.
treaty-of-shimonoseki: China recognises Korea's independence, cedes Taiwan, Penghu and, briefly, Liaodong, and pays 200 million taels.
hundred-days-reform: The Guangxu Emperor decrees sweeping reforms; Empress Dowager Cixi ends them after 103 days.
boxer-rebellion: Boxers besiege the foreign legations in Beijing; an Eight-Nation Alliance takes the capital and the court flees.
boxer-protocol: China agrees to pay 450 million taels and to let foreign troops guard the legations and the railway.
russo-japanese-war: Japan attacks Port Arthur; the war, fought on Chinese soil, leaves Japan dominant in southern Manchuria.
exams-abolished: The Qing ends the civil service examinations after some thirteen centuries.
tongmenghui: Sun Yat-sen unites revolutionary groups in Tokyo in a league to overthrow the Qing.
beijing-zhangjiakou-railway: Zhan Tianyou completes the first trunk line built by Chinese engineers, climbing past Badaling.
korea-annexed: The Korean Empire becomes a colony of Japan.
manchurian-plague: Pneumonic plague kills about 60,000 people; Wu Lien-teh contains it with masks and quarantine.
mongolia-1911: Mongol princes enthrone the Jebtsundamba Khutughtu as Bogd Khan in Urga.
wuchang-uprising: Revolutionary soldiers rise on 10 October, and the provinces declare independence one after another.
qing-abdication: The boy emperor Puyi abdicates, ending two thousand years of imperial rule; Yuan Shikai becomes president.
roc-founded: Sun Yat-sen takes office in Nanjing on 1 January as provisional president.

xia-shang-zhou.title: Xia, Shang and Western Zhou
xia-shang-zhou.lede: From the Xia of tradition and the Shang of the oracle bones to the Western Zhou, who parcelled out the land: in these thirteen centuries the pattern of the Central Plains dynasties took shape. The further back, the more the story rests on archaeology; dates before 841 BC are estimates and borders only approximate.
steps: The Xia and Erlitou

Sima Qian and the Bamboo Annals tell how Yu tamed the floods and how his son Qi inherited the throne, founding the Xia, the first dynasty to pass from father to son: seventeen kings in about 470 years. The Xia left no writing of its own, so its existence and extent are inferred from archaeology. On the map of 1750 BC the Xia is drawn as the Erlitou culture in western Henan and southern Shanxi; the Proto-Shang, Dongyi, Ancient Shu, Qijia and Lower Xiajiadian around it are archaeological cultures of the same age.

p: The Xia appear in later texts such as the Book of Documents and Sima Qian's Records. Yu, who tamed the floods, was chosen by Shun to succeed him; Yu meant his minister Yi to follow him in turn, but the throne went to his son Qi, and rule passed from merit to descent. The last king, Jie, was a tyrant overthrown by Tang of Shang. A mid-Western Zhou bronze, the Sui Gong xu, already tells how Yu 'spread out the land, followed the hills and dredged the rivers', so the flood story was told by then at the latest. But no Xia writing has been found, and whether the Xia was a real dynasty, and how large, rests on archaeology. The Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project dates it to about 2070–1600 BC, a framework not all scholars accept.

Erlitou, in the Luoyang basin at Yanshi, Henan, flourished from about 1750 to 1530 BC and covered some 3 square kilometres. It has the earliest known palace enclosure in China, a grid of main roads, bronze foundries, the first bronze ritual vessels, such as the jue wine cup, and a dragon made of over two thousand pieces of turquoise. Its place and date fit Zhenxun, the late Xia capital of the texts, and many Chinese scholars hold that it was the Xia capital; others say that without writing to name it, who built Erlitou remains an open question.

Erlitou had many contemporaries. The Xiaqiyuan culture of southern Hebei and northern Henan is taken for the ancestors of the Shang, the Yueshi culture of Shandong for the Dongyi; the Qijia culture of Gansu and Qinghai already worked copper, the Lower Xiajiadian culture built stone-walled villages either side of the Yan Mountains, and the Chengdu plain was home to what became the Sanxingdui civilisation. The Central Plains were one bright star among many, and only later the centre.
facts: mid-Western Zhou bronze naming Yu's flood work

steps: The Shang Replace the Xia

Around 1600 BC Tang of Shang defeated Jie of Xia at Mingtiao and founded the Shang, who then spread fast; archaeologists call this the Erligang culture. On the map of 1500 BC the early Shang reaches eastern Guanzhong in the west, central Hebei in the north and western Shandong in the east, and south as far as Panlongcheng on the Yangtze, far beyond the Erlitou culture; the Dongyi hold eastern Shandong, and the Lower Xiajiadian culture the Yan Mountains.

p: The Shang began as a people of the lower Yellow River; tradition says their ancestor Xie was granted Shang for helping Yu with the floods. Tang made Bo his capital, took Yi Yin as his minister, destroyed the Xia's allies Wei, Gu and Kunwu, and then met the Xia at Mingtiao; Jie fled to Nanchao and died there. In the ground, Erlitou is followed by walled Shang cities at Yanshi and Zhengzhou. Yanshi lies only about 6 km from Erlitou and is generally seen as a stronghold for watching the conquered Xia, and Erlitou's palaces fell out of use at about this time.

Zhengzhou was the greatest city of the early Shang: its inner wall ran nearly 7 km on footings over 20 m wide, with bronze, pottery and bone workshops outside. Most scholars take it for Bo, Tang's capital. Its Duling square cauldron, about a metre tall, is among the largest early Shang bronzes. The Shang capital moved often: tradition counts eight moves before Tang and five after, by way of Ao, Xiang, Xing and Yan, until Pan Geng settled at Yin.

The Erligang culture spread far beyond Erlitou. The Shang built strongholds at Yuanqu and Dongxiafeng in southern Shanxi and in eastern Guanzhong, and south across the Tongbai and Dabie hills they raised a walled town at Panlongcheng near the Yangtze (Huangpi, Wuhan), whose elite tombs and bronzes are just like Zhengzhou's. The usual explanation is copper and tin: the ores of the middle Yangtze were the lifeblood of bronze vessels and weapons.
facts: inner wall nearly 7 km; usually taken for Bo
Huangpi, Wuhan: a Shang outpost on the Yangtze

steps: Yin and the Oracle Bones

Around 1300 BC King Pan Geng moved the capital to Yin (Anyang, Henan), where it stayed until the end of the dynasty. The oracle bones found at Yin are the earliest full writing system known in China. The map of 1250 BC shows the reign of Wu Ding: the Shang have withdrawn from Guanzhong and the Yangtze and are centred on northern Henan, southern Hebei and western Shandong, ringed by peoples the oracle bones often name: the Guifang to the north-west, the Qiang and the Zhou to the west, the Yi to the east.

p: The oracle bones are records of royal divination: turtle shells and ox shoulder blades were drilled and heated until they cracked, the cracks were read for good or ill, and the question, sometimes with the outcome, was carved beside them. Wang Yirong recognised the writing in 1899; in 1917 Wang Guowei pieced the Shang king list together from the bones and showed that Sima Qian's was largely right; from 1928 the Academia Sinica dug at Anyang, finding the Shang palaces at Xiaotun and the royal tombs across the Huan River at Houjiazhuang. About 150,000 pieces have been found, with some 4,500 different characters, of which about 1,500 have been read.

Wu Ding was the ablest of the later Shang kings; the Book of Documents gives him a reign of fifty-nine years. He fought on every side: 'Gaozong attacked the Guifang and took three years to defeat them,' says the Book of Changes. His consort Fu Hao led rites and armies; one inscription has her raising 13,000 men against the Qiang. Her tomb, found intact in 1976, held nearly 2,000 objects, over 460 of them bronzes. The Houmuwu cauldron from Yin weighs 832.84 kg, the heaviest ancient Chinese bronze vessel known.

The Shang were devoted to spirits and sacrifice; the oracle bones often record Qiang captives offered as victims, and rows of sacrificial pits surround the royal tombs. The Shang was no state with clear borders: beyond the royal domain lay polities large and small that submitted and rebelled by turns. One of them, in the Wei valley to the west, was the Zhou, already named in the oracle bones.

steps: The Rise of the Zhou

The Zhou traced their line to Hou Ji, lord of millet, and long lived among the Rong and Di on the Jing and Wei rivers. When Gugong Danfu led them to the plain below Mount Qi, they began to grow; by King Wen they held, in Confucius's words, two-thirds of the realm. In the same age the people of Sanxingdui, on the Chengdu plain, buried hoards of bronze idols and gold. The map is still that of 1250 BC: the Zhou west of the Shang, Ancient Shu to the south-west.

p: In the Book of Songs and Sima Qian, the Zhou ancestor Hou Ji was a master farmer, and his descendant Gong Liu moved the people to Bin (around today's Binzhou, Shaanxi). Pressed by the Rong and Di, Gugong Danfu led them over the Liang hills to Zhouyuan, the plain below Mount Qi, where they built a walled town and changed their ways. Zhouyuan has yielded palace foundations and inscribed oracle bones, and it remained a centre of the Zhou. Danfu's son Jili fought the north-western Rong for the Shang with much success and, the Bamboo Annals say, was put to death by the Shang king Wen Ding.

Jili's son Ji Chang, King Wen, was made Lord of the West by the Shang and for a time imprisoned by King Zhou at Youli. Freed, he won a name for virtue, settled a quarrel between the states of Yu and Rui, conquered neighbours such as Li and Chong, and moved his capital from Qi to Feng, on the west bank of the Feng River south-west of today's Xi'an. The Zhou had grown from a western dependency of the Shang into its rival. After Wen died his son Ji Fa took his place: King Wu.

On the upper Yangtze, the Ancient Shu of Sanxingdui went their own way. Two sacrificial pits found in 1986, and six more opened since 2019, held a mask with protruding eyes 1.38 m wide, a bronze tree nearly 4 m tall, a life-size bronze standing figure, a gold staff and gold masks, but no writing. The latest dates put the pits at about 1200–1000 BC, the age of Yin. Sanxingdui had dealings with the Shang, but its world of gods was utterly unlike that of the Central Plains.
facts: King Wen's capital, south-west of today's Xi'an

steps: King Wu Conquers the Shang

In 1046 BC (the Chronology Project's date) King Wu of Zhou, with the Yong, Shu, Qiang and other peoples of the west and south, met the Shang army at Muye. The Shang ranks turned on their own side, King Zhou burned himself to death, and the Shang, rulers of the Central Plains for over five centuries, fell. The map is still that of 1250 BC, with the Zhou in the west; the next, of 1000 BC, shows the realm the Zhou parcelled out.

p: Later ages painted King Zhou (Di Xin) as a monster, with his pool of wine and forest of meat, his burning pillar and his cutting out of Bi Gan's heart; much of this is embroidered. More certain is that the late Shang fought the eastern Yi year after year and wore itself out. King Wu first gathered his allies at the Meng ford, where eight hundred lords are said to have come unbidden, but judged the time not yet ripe and withdrew; two years later he marched.

The Book of Documents preserves the speech King Wu made to his army at Muye. The Zhou were far outnumbered, but the Shang front ranks, tradition says, 'turned their spears', the Zhou entered Zhaoge, and King Zhou climbed the Deer Terrace and burned himself to death. The Li gui, a bronze found at Lintong, Shaanxi, in 1976, says that King Wu attacked the Shang 'on the morning of jiazi', just as the Documents does; it is the oldest record of the battle. From it and the heavens the Chronology Project dated the battle to 1046 BC.

Victory did not bring the east under Zhou control at once. King Wu left the Shang domain to Wu Geng, son of the last king, to rule the Yin people, and posted his brothers Guan, Cai and Huo nearby to watch him: the 'Three Overseers' (some early sources count Wu Geng, not Huo, among the three). The Zhou called themselves 'little Zhou' beside 'great Shang', and how to rule the populous, cultured east was the great question of the new dynasty. King Wu died soon after the conquest.
facts: 1046 BC (Chronology Project), morning of a jiazi day
found at Lintong in 1976; records the conquest
usually Guan, Cai and Huo (in one tradition, Wu Geng)

steps: The Duke of Zhou and the Fiefs

After King Wu died, the Duke of Zhou ruled for the boy King Cheng, crushed the revolt of the Three Overseers and Wu Geng, built an eastern capital at Luoyi, and gave lands across the realm to Zhou kinsmen, allies and the heirs of earlier dynasties. On the map of 1000 BC the royal domain runs from Zongzhou in Guanzhong to Chengzhou at Luoyi; the fiefs of Qi, Lu, Wey, Song, Jin and Yan are in the Zhou's paler shade, while Chu in the south, Wu and Yue in the south-east and Ba and Shu in the south-west stand at the edge of the Zhou order.

p: Guan and Cai suspected the Duke of Zhou of wanting the throne and rose with Wu Geng and eastern states such as Shangyan and Pugu. The Duke spent three years in the east, killed Wu Geng and Guan, banished Cai and destroyed the rebel states. To hold the east he built Chengzhou on the Luo River and moved the Yin nobles there. The He zun, a bronze found at Baoji in 1963, quotes King Wu's wish to 'dwell in this central land' (zhongguo), the earliest known use of the word that became the name of China.

Fiefs were how the Zhou held their new realm. The Duke of Zhou's son Boqin received Lu (at Qufu); Grand Duke Wang, Qi (at Yingqiu); King Wu's brother Kangshu, Wey, with seven clans of Yin people to rule; Weizi Qi, an elder half-brother of the last Shang king, Song (at Shangqiu), to keep up the Shang sacrifices; King Cheng's brother Shu Yu, Tang, later called Jin; and the son of the Duke of Shao, Yan (at Liulihe, in today's Beijing). Xunzi says the early Zhou 'set up seventy-one states, fifty-three under men of the Ji clan'. The lords walled and garrisoned their towns, ruled the local people, and owed the king homage, tribute and troops.

The Zhou also built a lineage order: the eldest son of the principal wife inherited the throne or the house, and younger sons founded branches, fief within fief, so that king and lords were ruler and subjects and also senior and junior lines of one family. The Duke of Zhou is said to have laid down the rites and music that ranked the nobility. The reigns of Cheng and Kang were remembered as an age of peace. Under King Zhao the advance south failed: he led his armies against Chu and was lost with them on the Han River.
facts: King Cheng's reign; 'dwell in this central land'
Xunzi: 71 states, 53 under the Ji clan

steps: Gonghe and King Xuan

In 841 BC the people of Haojing drove out King Li, and for fourteen years ministers ruled: the Gonghe regency, whose first year begins China's exact chronology. King Xuan, who followed, fought the Xianyun in the north and the Huai Yi in the south-east, and the court revived for a time. On the map of 800 BC Chu has spread between the Han and the Yangtze, Qin holds the western frontier as a Zhou dependency, and the royal domain still runs from Guanzhong to Luoyi.

p: After the mid-Western Zhou the royal house weakened. King Li let the Duke of Rong take the profits of the hills, woods and waters for the crown, and set a shaman to watch for critics, until people dared only exchange glances in the street. The Duke of Shao warned him that 'stopping the people's mouths is worse than damming a river', in vain. In 841 BC the people rose, and King Li fled to Zhi (Huozhou, Shanxi), where he died years later without returning.

The fourteen years after his flight are called Gonghe. Sima Qian says the Dukes of Shao and Zhou ruled jointly; the Bamboo Annals and the Tsinghua bamboo chronicle Xinian say a lord, He of Gong, acted as king. Either way, Sima Qian's tables of the states run year by year from the first year of Gonghe, 841 BC, and from then on Chinese history has a continuous, exact chronology. Every earlier date, the Chronology Project's used in this atlas included, is an estimate.

King Xuan (827–782 BC) sent Yin Jifu north against the Xianyun, Duke Mu of Shao south-east against the Huai Yi and Fang Shu south against the Man of Jing, campaigns sung in the Book of Songs. Qin Zhong, chief of the Qin, was charged with fighting the western Rong and died doing so; his son Duke Zhuang beat them and was made Grandee of the Western March. But Xuan's later years brought defeats, among them by the Jiang Rong at Qianmu in 789 BC, and the court declined again.
facts: 841 BC; King Li flees to Zhi

steps: The Fall of the Western Zhou

In 771 BC the Lord of Shen, with Zeng and the Quanrong, stormed Haojing and killed King You, ending the Western Zhou. Next year King Ping moved east to Luoyi; the court lost Guanzhong and the lords grew strong. Compare the maps of 800 and 700 BC: the domain in Guanzhong is gone, Qin has pushed east, the king keeps only a patch around Luoyi, and the lords once shown in the Zhou's pale shade are states in their own right.

p: In King You's second year, 780 BC, an earthquake shook the Jing, Wei and Luo rivers, and the official Bo Yangfu foretold the end of Zhou. You doted on Bao Si and set aside his queen, a daughter of the Lord of Shen, and her son Yijiu, who fled to his grandfather. In 771 BC Shen, with the state of Zeng and the Quanrong, attacked; King You was killed below Mount Li and Haojing was sacked.

The Western Zhou's nearly three centuries left a deep mark. The Zhou taught that Heaven's mandate could pass from house to house and went to the virtuous, an idea that explained why the Shang fell and the Zhou rose, and justified every change of dynasty after. Western Zhou bronzes carry long inscriptions on appointments, gifts, wars and lawsuits; that of the Mao Gong ding, nearly 500 characters, is the longest known. The oldest of the Book of Songs and the early Zhou proclamations in the Book of Documents come from this age too.

The fall of the Western Zhou was also the turning point of the fief system. After the court moved east, with far less land and fewer troops, the lords stopped obeying and swallowed one another, and hegemons gave orders in the king's place. The Eastern Zhou, from 770 BC, is divided into the Spring and Autumn and the Warring States periods; the story continues in The Spring and Autumn Hegemons.
facts: 771 BC; King You killed at Mount Li

spring-autumn.title: The Spring and Autumn Hegemons
spring-autumn.lede: From the Zhou court's move east in 770 BC to the destruction of the Zhi clan in 453 BC, the Zhou kings reigned in name only, while Qi, Jin, Chu, Qin and later Wu and Yue vied to lead the states as hegemon; the age is named after the Lu chronicle, the Spring and Autumn Annals.
steps: The Zhou Move East

In 771 BC the Quanrong sacked Haojing and killed King You; next year King Ping moved the court to Luoyi, and royal power faded. On the map of 700 BC the major states are rough outlines: Zheng, Wey, Song, Lu and Qi east of the royal domain, Yan north, Jin and Qin west, Chu south, Wu and Yue south-east; the rest of the 'Zhou states' stands for small states and the Rong, Di and Yi.

p: Sima Qian says King You set aside his queen and her son Yijiu for Bao Si, so the queen's father, the Lord of Shen, called in the Quanrong; the tale of beacons lit to amuse Bao Si clashes with the Tsinghua bamboo chronicle Xinian and is widely doubted. Yijiu became King Ping, but the Duke of Guo raised a rival king, and for years there were two. Duke Xiang of Qin escorted Ping east, was made a lord and was promised the land west of Mount Qi if he could take it from the Rong. Qin pushed east, and in 688 BC Duke Wu ruled conquered Rong lands as counties, among the earliest on record.

The court grew poorer. Its lands went to the lords who had escorted it or were eaten away by the Rong, and at times it begged from the lords: after King Ping died in 720 BC, the Spring and Autumn Annals record, it sent to Lu for funeral gifts. The age is named after this Lu chronicle, which runs in terse entries from 722 to 481 BC and was traditionally said to have been edited by Confucius. The Zuo Commentary adds year-by-year narratives of all the states and is the main source for the period.

Zheng stood out first. Its founder, a brother of King Xuan, died with King You; his son Duke Wu moved east, absorbed Kuai and Eastern Guo and built a capital at today's Xinzheng. Wu and his son Duke Zhuang (743–701 BC) ran the royal government as chief ministers. Zhuang crushed his brother's revolt in 722 BC and exchanged hostages with the court, which then dismissed him. In 707 BC King Huan led his army and troops from Chen, Cai and Wey against Zheng and was routed at Xuge, shot in the shoulder by a Zheng officer; royal prestige never recovered. After Zhuang died his sons fought over the throne and Zheng declined; historians call him a 'minor hegemon'.
facts: 707 BC, Duke Zhuang of Zheng defeats King Huan

steps: Duke Huan of Qi

Duke Huan took the throne of Qi in 685 BC and made Guan Zhong, who had once shot at him, chief minister. Championing the king against the barbarians, Qi saved Yan and Xing, restored Wey and led the states against Chu; in 651 BC Huan presided at Kuiqiu as the first hegemon. The map of 650 BC, still in outline, shows Qi in northern Shandong, a larger Jin and Qin, and Chu reaching past the Han to the upper Huai.

p: When Duke Xiang of Qi was murdered in 686 BC, two exiled princes raced home. Guan Zhong, serving Prince Jiu, ambushed Prince Xiaobai and hit his belt hook; Xiaobai played dead, reached Linzi first and became Duke Huan (685–643 BC), and on Bao Shuya's advice made Guan his minister. The Discourses of the States say Guan split the capital into wards of gentlemen, artisans and merchants, made the household registers the army's muster, taxed land by its quality and exploited Qi's fish and salt. The Guanzi, which credits him with salt and iron monopolies, was compiled much later.

The Rong and Di pressed hard. In 664 BC Qi marched against the Mountain Rong to save Yan; in 661 BC, when the Di attacked Xing, Guan Zhong said 'the Xia states are close kin and must not be abandoned', and Qi sent help. In 660 BC the Di overran Wey, whose crane-loving duke fell in battle; 730 survivors fled over the Yellow River, and in 658 BC Huan rebuilt Wey at Chuqiu. In 656 BC he led the states against Chu and made a covenant at Shaoling. Later ages called this 'honour the king, expel the barbarians'. 'But for Guan Zhong,' said Confucius, 'we would wear our hair loose and fold our robes to the left.'

Ba, 'hegemon', was first written bo, 'eldest of the lords'. In the king's name the hegemon called covenants, settled disputes and led allied armies against the Rong, Di and oath-breakers; allies attended his court, paid contributions and sent troops but kept their lands. The Zuo Commentary dates Qi's hegemony from 679 BC; Huan 'assembled the lords nine times'. After his death in 643 BC his sons fought for the throne and, Sima Qian says, left him unburied for 67 days.
