Duke Xiang of Song tried to succeed him, but at the Hong River in 638 BC he waited for Chu to form up, lost, and died of his wound. Often counted among the Five Hegemons, he never led the states.
facts: 656 BC, Qi leads the states against Chu
651 BC, the king sends Huan sacrificial meat

steps: Duke Wen of Jin and Chengpu

In 636 BC Chong'er, nineteen years an exile, came home with Qin's help to rule Jin as Duke Wen. He restored the Zhou king, crushed Chu at Chengpu in 632 BC and was named leader of the lords at Jiantu; Jin long led the central states. Blocked by Jin, Duke Mu of Qin turned west against the Rong. The map still shows 650 BC: Jin on the lower Fen, Qin on the Wei, Chu on the Han and middle Yangtze.

p: Jin, first granted to Shu Yu of Tang, lay in southern Shanxi. From 745 BC, when Marquis Zhao gave his uncle Quwo, the Quwo branch fought the senior line at Yi for over sixty years, until in 678 BC Duke Wu of Quwo took over with the king's blessing. His son Duke Xian (676–651 BC) massacred his kinsmen and swallowed Huo, Wei, Geng, Guo and Yu; 'when the lips are gone the teeth feel the cold' comes from his borrowing a road through Yu to take Guo. His favourite Li Ji drove the heir Shensheng to suicide, and the princes Chong'er and Yiwu fled. Chong'er lived twelve years among the Di, then wandered through Wey, Qi, Cao, Song, Zheng, Chu and Qin.

The year Duke Wen (636–628 BC) came home, Prince Dai rose with Di help and drove King Xiang out; next year Wen killed Dai and restored the king, gaining Yangfan, Wen, Yuan and other lands south of the Taihang. In 632 BC Chu besieged Song; Jin attacked Chu's allies Cao and Wey, and the Chu commander Ziyu, ignoring his king, marched north. True to a promise made in exile to King Cheng of Chu, Wen fell back three days' march, then routed Chu at Chengpu with Qi, Qin and Song. That winter he summoned the king; Confucius, says the Zuo Commentary, found this no example to follow, so the Annals say only that 'the Heavenly King hunted at Heyang'.

Duke Mu of Qin (659–621 BC) put Dukes Hui and Wen on the Jin throne, and the houses intermarried so often that 'Qin and Jin' became a byword for a good match; but Jin barred Qin's road east. In 627 BC a Qin army crossed Jin to surprise Zheng; the merchant Xian Gao, posing as a Zheng envoy, presented twelve oxen, and the Qin generals, thinking Zheng forewarned, turned back, to be wiped out by a Jin ambush at Xiao. Mu turned west and, Sima Qian says, 'added twelve states and opened a thousand li', leading the western Rong. At his death 177 people were buried with him; the Yellow Bird in the Book of Songs mourns three.
facts: ruled 636–628 BC, after 19 years in exile
632 BC, Jin, Qi, Qin and Song defeat Chu
627 BC, Jin destroys a Qin army

steps: Jin against Chu

King Zhuang of Chu pushed north: in 606 BC he paraded his army on the Luo and asked the weight of the Zhou cauldrons; in 597 BC he crushed Jin at Bi. Jin and Chu then fought for half a century, until the truce of 546 BC. The 600 BC map, still in outline, shows Jin reaching the Taihang, Chu from the Yangtze gorges to the middle Huai, Zheng, Song and Wey between, and a shrinking royal domain.

p: The Zhou called Chu 'the Jing barbarians'. In 704 BC its ruler Xiong Tong proclaimed himself king, and his son King Wen moved the capital to Ying. Chu swallowed the small states of the Han valley ('Chu has finished off all the Ji states north of the Han', says the Zuo Commentary, Ji being the Zhou royal surname) and ran places such as Shen and Xi as counties under appointed officials, not fiefs. King Zhuang (613–591 BC), Sima Qian says, idled for three years, then 'astonished the world with one cry'. In 606 BC he reached the Luo and asked how heavy the nine cauldrons were. 'It lies in virtue, not in the cauldrons,' replied the Zhou envoy Wangsun Man.

In 597 BC Zhuang besieged Zheng for three months, until its duke came out stripped to the waist, leading a sheep. Xun Linfu's Jin relief army came too late; the deputy Xian Hu crossed the Yellow River on his own, and at Bi Jin broke. Those in the boats hacked at the hands clinging on: 'the fingers in the boats could be scooped up', says the Zuo Commentary. Urged to heap up the Jin dead as a trophy, Zhuang refused, saying the character for 'martial' is made of 'stop' and 'weapon'. In 595 BC Chu besieged Song for nine months, until its people 'exchanged children to eat'; peace followed, with Chu's hegemony at its height.

Jin soon recovered. In 584 BC Jin sent the Chu defector Wuchen to teach Wu chariot warfare and harry Chu from behind; in 575 BC Duke Li beat King Gong of Chu at Yanling, where the king was shot in the eye. Jin destroyed the Red Di in 594–593 BC, and in 569 BC Wei Jiang urged buying land and peace from the Rong and Di with goods. Zheng could only wait 'with victims and jade at both borders'. In 546 BC Xiang Xu of Song gathered Jin, Chu and over ten other states for a truce under which each side's allies attended both courts; for forty years the central plain saw few great battles.
facts: 546 BC, brokered by Xiang Xu of Song

steps: Wu and Yue

Wu and Yue, on the lower Yangtze, rose late. In 506 BC Helü of Wu took the Chu capital Ying; his son Fuchai crushed Yue and marched north. Goujian of Yue struck back, destroyed Wu in 473 BC and led the lords in covenant. The 500 BC map shows Wu from Lake Tai north across the Huai and Yue in today's Zhejiang; its borders are approximate, and Wey, Chen and Cai are left inside their neighbours.

p: Wu claimed descent from Taibo, eldest son of Tai Wang of Zhou. After Wuchen came in 584 BC, King Shoumeng opened ties with the central states and began raiding Chu. In 515 BC Prince Guang had King Liao assassinated and took the throne as Helü (514–496 BC), relying on the Chu exile Wu Zixu. In 506 BC Wu, Cai and Tang routed Chu at Baiju and after five battles entered Ying. Shen Baoxu wept at the Qin court for seven days until Qin sent help, and with revolt at home Wu withdrew. Sima Qian says Sun Wu took part and Wu Zixu flogged the corpse of King Ping of Chu; the Zuo Commentary mentions neither.

In 496 BC Goujian of Yue beat Helü at Zuili, fatally wounding him. Two years later Fuchai crushed Yue at Fujiao, and Goujian, cornered on Mount Kuaiji, sued for peace. Wu Zixu warned that Yue would spend 'ten years breeding and ten years training', but Fuchai turned north, routed Qi at Ailing in 484 BC and drove Wu Zixu to suicide. At Huangchi in 482 BC he disputed precedence with Jin (the Zuo Commentary gives it to Jin, the Discourses of the States to Wu) while Goujian broke into his capital; in 473 BC Yue destroyed Wu. The 'brushwood' in Goujian's 'sleeping on brushwood and tasting gall' was added only in the Song, and Xi Shi's mission to Wu first appears in Eastern Han books.

In Lu power lay with the Three Huan, the Jisun, Shusun and Mengsun, descendants of Duke Huan of Lu who had shared out the duke's army and taxes. In 517 BC Duke Zhao, failing against the Jisun, fled abroad. Confucius (551–479 BC) made his name as a teacher, became Minister of Justice and in 498 BC tried to pull down the three houses' walled towns, but stopped halfway. In 497 BC he left Lu and travelled for fourteen years with his disciples through Wey, Song, Chen, Cai and Chu, teaching, as he had once told Duke Jing of Qi, 'let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son'. Back in Lu in 484 BC, he worked on the classics, traditionally including the Annals.
facts: 506 BC, Wu enters Ying after five battles

steps: The Partition of Jin

Power was passing to ministerial clans. In Jin six ministers devoured one another until four remained: Zhi, Zhao, Han and Wei. In 455 BC Zhi Bo led Han and Wei against Zhao's Jinyang; in 453 BC Han and Wei turned on him and the three destroyed the Zhi. The 453 BC map shows Jin split into Zhao in the north, Wei in the south and Han between; the enclave in Zhao is the Di state of Zhongshan, and Yue reaches into southern Shandong.

p: After Li Ji's intrigues Jin gave no office to the ducal kin, and other clans took over. Duke Wen's three armies had six commanders and deputies, later called the six ministers, drawn over time from the Xi, Luan, Fan, Zhonghang, Zhi, Han, Zhao, Wei and others, who preyed on one another: the Xi fell in 574 BC and the Luan in 550 BC. In 513 BC Zhao Yang and Xun Yin levied iron to cast the penal laws on a cauldron, an early mention of iron; Confucius said Jin was doomed. From 497 BC Zhao Yang fought the Fan and Zhonghang from Jinyang, and by 490 BC both were driven out.

The Zhi were now strongest. Zhi Bo demanded land from Han, Wei and Zhao; Han Kangzi and Wei Huanzi gave way, Zhao Xiangzi refused. In 455 BC Zhi Bo led Han and Wei against Jinyang and flooded the city; Sima Qian says the water came within three boards of the wall top and people hung their pots up to cook. In 453 BC Xiangzi's envoy Zhang Mengtan won Han and Wei over; the three broke the dykes onto Zhi's camp, killed Zhi Bo, wiped out his clan and shared his lands. The Zuo Commentary ends with Zhi Bo's fall. In 403 BC the Zhou king made the three houses lords: the next chapter's story.

In Qi the Tian clan won the people by lending in a large measure and collecting in a small one, and in 481 BC Tian Chang killed Duke Jian and took control. That year the Annals end with the capture of a qilin; the Warring States are usually dated from 475 BC. Every hegemon came from the edge of the Chinese world: Qi, Jin, Chu, Qin, Wu and Yue could expand into Rong, Di, Man and Yi lands and rule conquests as counties, while Zheng, Song, Wey and Lu in the centre were boxed in. Iron reached farm tools, Zheng and Jin published their laws, hereditary office was eroding, and the age of hegemons gave way to wars of conquest.
facts: Huan of Qi from 679 BC; Wen of Jin from 632 BC, Jin then leading for most of a century; Zhuang of Chu from 597 BC; a Jin–Chu truce from 546 BC; finally Fuchai of Wu and Goujian of Yue

Huan of Qi, Xiang of Song, Wen of Jin, Mu of Qin, Zhuang of Chu (Zhao Qi's Mencius commentary, the Shiji Suoyin and others); Huan of Qi, Wen of Jin, Zhuang of Chu, Helü of Wu, Goujian of Yue (the Xunzi)

warring-states.title: The Seven Warring States
warring-states.lede: From the destruction of the Zhi clan by the Han, Zhao and Wei families in 453 BC to Qin's conquest of Qi in 221 BC, seven great states fought for more than two centuries: first Wei led, then Qi and Qin faced each other from east and west, and at last Qin stood alone and united China.
steps: The Seven Take Shape

In 453 BC the Han, Zhao and Wei families of Jin together destroyed the mighty Zhi clan at Jinyang and divided its lands. In 403 BC the Zhou king raised all three to the rank of lords, and in 386 BC Tian He, master of Qi, was recognised too. On the map Zhao lies north, Wei south, and Han, the smallest, in between; Qi and Yan are east, Qin west, Chu and Yue south.

p: By the late Spring and Autumn period six ministerial families ran Jin; by 490 BC four were left, the strongest led by Zhi Yao. Han and Wei gave him the land he demanded, but Zhao Xiangzi refused and withdrew to Jinyang, modern Taiyuan. From 455 BC Zhi and his two allies besieged the city and diverted the Fen River into it until only a few feet of wall stood above water, yet it held out. Zhao's envoy Zhang Mengtan slipped out by night and won Han and Wei over; in 453 BC the three broke the dykes onto the Zhi army, killed Zhi Yao and divided his lands.

Zhao, based at Jinyang, moved its capital to Handan in 386 BC and spanned central and northern Shanxi and southern Hebei. Wei ruled from Anyi, in southern Shanxi, over rich lands on both banks of the Yellow River. Han began at Pingyang, modern Linfen, moved south to Yangzhai and, after conquering Zheng in 375 BC, settled at Xinzheng. Their lands were tangled together, so each needed and hampered the others. In 403 BC the Zhou king recognised them as lords; Sima Guang began his great chronicle with that year, seeing in it the collapse of the old order. In 376 BC, Sima Qian says, they shared out the last of Jin.

The Tian of Qi descended from Chen Wan, a Chen prince who fled to Qi in 672 BC. They won the people by lending grain in a large measure and taking it back in a small one. In 481 BC Tian Chang killed Duke Jian and took control. In 391 BC Tian He sent the last duke off to the coast, and in 386 BC the Zhou king recognised him as lord of Qi. These were the seven powers: Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei. Between them lay Song, Lu, Zheng, Zhongshan and Yue, among others; the Zhou king kept only Luoyang. The era's start is dated to 476, 475, 453 or 403 BC.
facts: Zhi destroyed 453 BC; lords recognised 403 BC
Qin: Yong; Wei: Anyi; Zhao: Jinyang; Han: Pingyang; Qi: Linzi; Chu: Ying; Yan: Ji

steps: Reform and the Primacy of Wei

At first Wei was the strongest state. Marquis Wen employed Li Kui and Wu Qi and took Qin's lands west of the Yellow River. Others followed: Wu Qi reformed Chu, Shen Buhai served Han, and from 356 BC Shang Yang remade Qin. King Hui of Wei moved to Daliang and took the royal title, but Qi beat him twice. On the map Han has absorbed Zheng, and Qin is penned in Guanzhong behind Wei.

p: In this age iron tools spread, new land was ploughed and the population grew, and wars were fought less by nobles in chariots than by peasant infantry, conscripted by the tens of thousands and armed with crossbows. Whoever could register, tax and conscript every household would win. Marquis Wen of Wei (r. 445–396 BC) went first: Li Kui pressed farmers to work the land harder and had the state buy grain in good years and sell it cheaply in bad ones, and Ximen Bao is said to have dug twelve canals at Ye. Li Kui's Canon of Laws is first mentioned centuries later and may never have existed.

Wu Qi took Qin's lands west of the Yellow River for Wei in 409–408 BC. Later, distrusted, he fled to Chu, where King Dao made him chief minister: fiefs reverted after three generations and idle posts were cut to pay for the army. When Dao died in 381 BC the nobles shot Wu Qi dead. In Han, Shen Buhai taught Marquis Zhao the art of controlling officials. In Qin, Duke Xiao's minister Shang Yang reformed in 356 and 350 BC, rewarding farming and fighting, ranking men by merit in war and putting counties under the ruler. Qin law is said to have executed latecomers, but Shuihudi statutes only reprimand or fine lateness for labour service.

King Hui of Wei (r. 369–319 BC) moved his capital from Anyi to Daliang, modern Kaifeng, in 361 or perhaps 339 BC. In 354 BC he besieged Handan, the Zhao capital; Qi's Tian Ji and his strategist Sun Bin marched on Daliang and ambushed the Wei army hurrying home at Guiling, 'besieging Wei to save Zhao'. In 344 BC Hui called himself king. In 341 BC, when Wei attacked Han, Qi came again: Sun Bin lit fewer cooking fires each day to fake desertions, lured the Wei general Pang Juan into a headlong chase and trapped him at Maling under massed crossbows. Pang Juan killed himself, and Wei declined.
facts: 356 and 350 BC; capital moved to Xianyang 350 BC

steps: Vertical and Horizontal Alliances

In the late 4th century BC rulers styled themselves kings, and Qin became the common threat. Travelling advisers urged the others to unite against it, or to side with it. King Huiwen of Qin took Ba and Shu in 316 BC and Chu's Hanzhong in 312 BC; King Wuling of Zhao put his army in nomad dress. On the map Qin holds Sichuan, Chu has taken Yue's heartland, leaving Yue remnants in Fujian, and Zhao and Yan have pushed north.

p: This was the age of the shi, men of learning who sold their ideas to rulers; even a man of humble birth might talk his way into high office. Outside the Ji gate of Linzi, King Xuan of Qi paid over seventy scholars as senior officials to debate without holding office; Zou Yan, Chunyu Kun and Shen Dao taught there, and Mencius came to advise the king. Confucians, Mohists, Daoists, Legalists, Yin-Yang theorists, logicians, strategists and agrarians wrote and argued: the Hundred Schools. The most practical were the diplomatists. An alliance of the six states, strung from north to south, against Qin was 'vertical'; joining Qin, from east to west, was 'horizontal'.

Zhang Yi of Wei, Qin's chief minister from 328 BC, led the horizontal camp. In 316 BC Qin's court debated whether to strike Han or Shu; Zhang Yi wanted to go east, but Sima Cuo argued that Shu would make Qin rich, and King Huiwen agreed: Shu fell that year, and Ba with it. In 313 BC Zhang Yi offered Chu six hundred li of land to break with Qi; King Huai did, was cheated, attacked Qin and lost Hanzhong at Danyang in 312 BC. Sima Qian makes Su Qin Zhang Yi's rival, uniting the six against Qin; silk manuscripts found at Mawangdui in 1973 show he came later, chiefly as Yan's agent in Qi.

Zhao bordered steppe peoples such as the Linhu and Loufan, with the state of Zhongshan in its midst. In 307 BC King Wuling (r. 325–299 BC) put his men into the nomads' short jackets and trousers for riding and shooting, though his uncle Prince Cheng objected. Zhao now had real cavalry: it beat the Linhu and Loufan, founded the commanderies of Yunzhong, Yanmen and Dai, and took Zhongshan in 296 BC. Wuling abdicated in 299 BC, planning to attack Qin from the north, but in 295 BC starved to death at Shaqiu during a palace revolt. Yan under King Zhao drove back the Donghu; on the map it reaches past the Liao River.
facts: Qin takes Ba, Shu and Hanzhong
c. 306 BC (334 BC in another account)

steps: The Rise and Fall of Qi

Around 300 BC Qi and Qin were the great powers of east and west; in 288 BC their kings briefly styled themselves emperors. Qi's conquest of Song in 286 BC alarmed everyone, and in 284 BC Yue Yi of Yan led five states into Qi and took Linzi; Tian Dan won Qi back in 279 BC. In 278 BC Qin took Ying, the Chu capital. The map still shows 300 BC, with Song and Zhongshan.

p: Qi held what is now Shandong, with fish and salt from the sea; its capital Linzi, said to have 70,000 households, was one of the greatest cities of the age. Under King Wei it twice beat Wei, and in 314 BC, when an abdication threw Yan into chaos, King Xuan's troops briefly held the Yan capital. King Min (r. 300–284 BC) went further. From 298 BC he led Han and Wei against Qin and broke through the Hangu Pass; in 286 BC he destroyed Song and pressed on Chu, Han, Zhao and Wei. The Jixia scholars, their advice ignored, drifted away, and Qi's neighbours began to close ranks.

King Zhao of Yan (r. 311–279 BC) came to the throne in a land just ravaged by Qi. He honoured the scholar Guo Wei to attract talent, and Yue Yi, Zou Yan and Ju Xin came; he also sent Su Qin to Qi to steer it into isolation. In 284 BC Yue Yi led the armies of Yan, Qin, Han, Zhao and Wei to victory west of the Ji River, then marched on Linzi, carried off Qi's treasures and in the next few years took over seventy cities. King Min fled to Ju, where Nao Chi, a Chu general sent to help him, killed him. Only Ju and Jimo held out.

In 279 BC King Zhao died; his distrustful successor replaced Yue Yi, who fled to Zhao. Tian Dan struck back from Jimo. He is said to have tied blades to the horns of a thousand oxen and oil-soaked reeds to their tails, and loosed them, blazing, on the Yan camp. The Yan army broke, the seventy cities were retaken and King Xiang returned to Linzi, but Qi never again matched Qin. Qin turned on Chu: Bai Qi marched down the Han River and in 278 BC took Ying, burning the royal tombs at Yiling. King Qingxiang moved to Chen; Ying became Qin's Nan commandery. The poet Qu Yuan is said to have drowned himself that year.
facts: 278 BC; Chu moves its capital to Chen

steps: Changping

King Zhaoxiang of Qin adopted Fan Ju's policy: befriend distant Qi and Chu, attack neighbouring Han and Wei. In 262 BC Qin cut off Han's Shangdang, whose governor went over to Zhao, and the two powers fought it out at Changping, where Bai Qi destroyed the Zhao army in 260 BC. Wei and Chu broke Qin's siege of Handan in 257 BC. On the map Qin holds Hedong, Nanyang and Ying; Shangdang is still Zhao's.

p: Geography favoured Qin. The Guanzhong plain, ringed by passes such as Hangu and Wu, was a 'land sealed on four sides': Qin could strike east at will, while invaders could hardly get in, and Ba and Shu gave it a second granary and a river road into Chu. Fan Ju, arriving in 270 BC, told King Zhaoxiang (r. 306–251 BC) that the chancellor Wei Ran was wrong to march past Han and Wei against distant Qi for land Qin could not hold; every inch taken nearby would be the king's for good. In 266 BC Fan Ju replaced Wei Ran. After crushing Han and Wei at Yique in 293 BC, Qin now ate steadily into Han, Wei and Zhao.

In 262 BC Bai Qi took Yewang, cutting Han's Shangdang commandery off from the rest of Han. Han was ready to cede it to Qin, but its governor, Feng Ting, offered its seventeen towns to Zhao instead, to draw Qin's armies there. King Xiaocheng accepted, against the advice of Lord Pingyang. Qin's Wang He overran Shangdang, and the Zhao veteran Lian Po dug in at Changping and would not fight. Qin agents in Handan put it about that Qin feared only Zhao Kuo, son of the great general Zhao She. In 260 BC the king gave the well-read but untried Zhao Kuo the command, and Qin secretly sent Bai Qi to command.

Zhao Kuo attacked at once. Bai Qi fell back, sent flying columns to cut his retreat and supplies, and King Zhaoxiang went to Henei to send every man over fifteen to block Zhao's relief. After 46 days without food Zhao Kuo was shot dead leading a breakout, and his army surrendered. Sima Qian writes that Bai Qi buried 400,000 prisoners alive; the figure is probably exaggerated, but a mass grave dug up at Yonglu near Gaoping in 1995 shows the massacre was real. In 259 BC Qin besieged Handan. Lord Xinling of Wei had his king's tally stolen to seize a Wei army, and with Chu lifted the siege in 257 BC. In 256 BC Qin ended the Zhou.

259–257 BC, lifted by Wei and Chu

steps: Qin Conquers the Six

In 247 BC Zheng, aged thirteen, became king of Qin; he took power in 238 BC and, guided by Li Si, set out to destroy his rivals one by one. Between 230 and 221 BC Qin conquered Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi. The map still shows the seven states of 260 BC, with Chu and Qi still looking like great powers; on the next map, 221 BC, all six belong to Qin.

p: After Changping the other states joined forces twice more. In 247 BC Lord Xinling led five armies that drove Qin back to the Hangu Pass; in 241 BC Chu, Zhao, Wei, Han and others attacked again in vain, and Chu moved east to Shouchun. Zheng, born at Handan in 259 BC, reigned at first under the chancellor Lü Buwei. Taking power in 238 BC, he crushed Lao Ai's revolt, dismissed Lü Buwei and, on Li Si's advice, cancelled an order expelling foreign officials. In Qi, King Jian heeded his minister Hou Sheng, said to be in Qin's pay, and for forty years neither helped the others nor prepared for war.

Qin took the weakest first: in 230 BC the official Teng overran Han and captured King An. Zhao's general Li Mu had twice beaten Qin, so Qin bribed a royal favourite to have him killed for treason. In 228 BC Wang Jian took Handan and King Qian; a Zhao prince ruled on in Dai. In 227 BC Crown Prince Dan of Yan sent Jing Ke to stab the king of Qin with a dagger hidden in a map; he failed. Qin took the Yan capital, Ji, in 226 BC, and King Xi fled to Liaodong, killing Dan to appease Qin. In 225 BC Wang Ben flooded Daliang until its walls fell, and Wei surrendered.

Before the war on Chu, the young general Li Xin said 200,000; the veteran Wang Jian said 600,000. Li Xin and Meng Tian went, and Xiang Yan of Chu routed them. The king rode to Pinyang to apologise to Wang Jian and gave him his 600,000. Wang Jian waited behind his ramparts, struck as the Chu army withdrew and in 223 BC captured King Fuchu; Xiang Yan fell fighting. In 222 BC Wang Ben took Liaodong and King Xi, then ended Dai; Wang Jian subdued the lands south of the Yangtze. In 221 BC Wang Ben swept south to Linzi, and King Jian of Qi surrendered without a fight. Zheng took the title of emperor.
facts: king from 247 BC, in power from 238 BC
Li Xin 200,000, defeated; Wang Jian 600,000, victorious
Han 230, Zhao 228 (Dai 222), Wei 225, Chu 223, Yan 222, Qi 221 BC

qin-unification.title: The Qin Dynasty
qin-unification.lede: The united Qin lasted only fifteen years, from the conquest of the last rival to its fall, yet it set the pattern of imperial rule for two thousand years.
steps: The First Emperor

In 221 BC King Zheng took a new title, First Emperor, expecting his heirs to reign for ten thousand generations. Rather than enfeoff his sons, he divided the realm into 36 commanderies run by appointed officials, standardised writing, weights, coins and axles, and built highways. On the map the Qin empire borders the Xiongnu to the north and the Yuezhi to the west.

p: His ministers proposed the title Supreme August. Zheng kept 'August', added the 'Emperor' of the ancient sage rulers and called himself the First Emperor, to be followed by the Second and Third for ever. He abolished posthumous names, which let sons judge fathers and subjects their lords. The chancellor Wang Wan urged him to make his sons kings in distant Yan, Qi and Chu, but Li Si objected that the Zhou kings' kinsmen had ended up fighting one another like enemies. The realm was instead divided into 36 commanderies, each with a governor, a commander and an inspector appointed by the court. The empire's weapons were melted into twelve bronze giants at Xianyang, and 120,000 wealthy families were moved there.

Unification was more than conquest. The six states had written differently; Li Si and others standardised the Qin small seal script, while clerks used the quicker clerical script for daily business. Weights and measures followed Shang Yang's standards, and official weights bore the emperor's edict of 221 BC. The knife, spade and cowrie coins of the old states gave way to gold and the round bronze banliang coin with its square hole. Carts were built to one width, and highways ran from Xianyang to the old lands of Yan, Qi, Wu and Chu. Over 1,100 bamboo slips found at Shuihudi in Hubei in 1975 show how closely Qin law ran granaries, labour service and justice.

As emperor he made five great tours, sacrificed on Mount Tai and set up inscriptions praising his deeds. In 213 BC, on Li Si's advice, he had all histories but Qin's burned, along with private copies of the Odes, the Documents and the philosophers, sparing books on medicine, divination and farming. The next year over 460 scholars and magicians accused of slandering him were buried alive at Xianyang, many of them probably magicians who had failed to find the elixir of life. Over 700,000 convicts built his palaces and his tomb at Mount Li. In 1974 farmers digging a well east of the tomb found the Terracotta Army, an estimated 8,000 figures.
facts: gold and the bronze banliang coin

steps: Walls in the north, conquests in the south

In 215 BC Meng Tian led 300,000 men against the Xiongnu and took the Ordos. The next year Qin set up 34 (some texts say 44) counties and joined the old walls of Qin, Zhao and Yan into one line from Lintao to Liaodong. In the south, Qin armies crossed the Nanling mountains, dug the Lingqu canal to carry grain and in 214 BC set up three commanderies. The map is still that of 221 BC, with the Ordos in Xiongnu hands and the south still Yue land: both became Qin's in the years after.

p: Qin, Zhao and Yan had each built walls against the northern nomads. In 215 BC Lu Sheng, a magician sent to sea in search of immortals, came back with a book of prophecy: 'Qin will be destroyed by the Hu', the northern barbarians. The emperor at once sent Meng Tian with 300,000 men against the Xiongnu, and Qin took the grasslands of the Ordos, inside the great northern loop of the Yellow River. The next year it built 34 (some texts say 44) walled counties along the river and filled them with convict settlers. The Xiongnu ruler Touman withdrew north, and Qin's frontier reached the Yin mountains.

Meng Tian then joined and extended the old walls; Sima Qian says the result ran from Lintao to Liaodong, more than ten thousand li. It was built mostly of rammed earth and stone, and for long stretches ran north of the brick Ming wall seen today. In 212 BC Meng Tian also built the Straight Road, some 700 km from Yunyang near Xianyang to Jiuyuan on the Yellow River, so that an army could reach the frontier in days. For over a decade the Xiongnu kept away, but the building, the garrisons and the grain convoys weighed heavily on the people.

The Yue peoples lived across today's Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam. According to the Huainanzi, Qin sent 500,000 men south in five columns; their commander Tu Sui killed a chief of the Western Ou, but the Yue took to the forests, raided by night and killed Tu Sui himself. To bring up grain the official Lu dug the Lingqu canal at today's Xing'an, linking the Xiang and Li rivers and so the Yangtze and Pearl systems, a waterway used for two thousand years. In 214 BC Qin set up three commanderies, with Ren Xiao and Zhao Tuo among their officials, and sent convicts and merchants to settle among the Yue.

steps: Revolt and fall

In 210 BC the First Emperor died on his fifth tour. According to Sima Qian, Zhao Gao and Li Si forged his will, drove the heir Fusu to suicide and enthroned the younger son Huhai. The next summer 900 conscripts delayed by rain rose under Chen Sheng and Wu Guang at Dazexiang, and the old kingdoms rose with them. In 206 BC Liu Bang reached Xianyang, and the dynasty ended after fifteen years.

p: In the summer of 210 BC the emperor died at Shaqiu, in today's Hebei. Sima Qian says he had summoned his eldest son Fusu, then with the army in the north, to conduct the funeral. Instead Zhao Gao, keeper of the seals, plotted with Li Si and the younger son Huhai: they hid the death, masked the smell of the corpse by loading the carriages with salted fish and forged orders for Fusu and Meng Tian to kill themselves, which both did. A Han bamboo text now at Peking University, the Zhao Zheng Shu, says the dying emperor himself chose Huhai, so the story is still debated. The Second Emperor killed his siblings and many ministers.

In the seventh month of 209 BC, 900 poor men bound for frontier duty at Yuyang were stopped by heavy rain at Dazexiang, in today's Anhui, and could no longer arrive on time. Lateness, Sima Qian says, meant death, so two of their leaders, Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, killed their officers and rose in the names of Fusu and the Chu general Xiang Yan. 'Are kings, lords, generals and ministers born to it?' Chen Sheng asked. He took Chen and proclaimed the kingdom of Zhangchu, and the nobles of the old states restored their kingdoms. Qin statutes from Shuihudi, though, punish lateness for labour service only with reprimands and fines, so some historians doubt the story.

The minister Zhang Han armed the convicts working on the emperor's tomb; Chen Sheng was murdered by his own driver, and Xiang Liang fell at Dingtao. But in 207 BC Xiang Liang's nephew Xiang Yu smashed the main Qin army at Julu, and Zhang Han surrendered, and Sima Qian says Xiang Yu later massacred over 200,000 of his men at Xin'an. At court Zhao Gao had Li Si cut in two, drove the Second Emperor to suicide and made Ziying king of Qin, who promptly had Zhao Gao killed. In the winter of 207–206 BC Liu Bang entered the Guanzhong plain, and Ziying surrendered by the roadside with the imperial seal. Xiang Yu soon arrived, killed Ziying and burned Xianyang.

han-xiongnu.title: Han and the Xiongnu
han-xiongnu.lede: From the siege at Baideng to the inscription at Yanran: three centuries of marriage alliances and war between Han China and the Xiongnu, which opened the road to the west.
steps: Baideng and the heqin peace

As Qin collapsed, Modu killed his father, made himself chanyu, crushed the Donghu and drove off the Yuezhi, building the first empire to unite the steppe. In 200 BC the Han founder Liu Bang marched north in person and was surrounded for seven days on Baideng hill near Pingcheng. He escaped by a ruse, and Han turned to heqin: a princess and yearly gifts of silk, wine and grain.

p: Sima Qian tells how Modu, heir of the chanyu Touman, was sent as a hostage to the Yuezhi and escaped on a stolen horse. He trained his men to shoot wherever his whistling arrow flew, on pain of death, and aimed it at his favourite horse, then his favourite wife, and finally his father, becoming chanyu in 209 BC. The Donghu, thinking him weak, demanded his best horse, a wife and then land; he fell on them and destroyed them, drove off the Yuezhi and took back the Ordos. He is said to have had over 300,000 archers. On the map the Xiongnu reach from Manchuria to the Western Regions, a larger realm than the new Han.

In 201 BC Xin, a vassal king guarding the frontier at Mayi, defected to the Xiongnu. That winter Liu Bang led 320,000 men, mostly infantry, north in such cold that two or three in ten lost fingers. Modu hid his best troops and herds, and Han envoys saw only old men and thin cattle. Hurrying ahead to Pingcheng, today's Datong, Liu Bang was surrounded on Baideng hill by 400,000 horsemen, ranged by colour, Sima Qian says: white on the west, grey on the east, black on the north, chestnut on the south. For seven days no help came. Han agents bribed Modu's queen to persuade him to open a corner of the ring; what exactly Chen Ping had devised was kept secret.

On Liu Jing's advice, in 198 BC Liu Bang made the first heqin treaty: a woman of the imperial clan, styled a princess, married the chanyu, Han sent fixed amounts of silk floss, cloth, wine and rice each year, and the two rulers became brothers. Liu Bang had meant to send his own daughter, but Empress Lü wept until he gave way. After his death Modu wrote proposing to marry the empress. The general Fan Kuai offered to ride across the steppe with 100,000 men; Ji Bu reminded the court that even the founder had been trapped at Pingcheng, and she sent a humble reply. For sixty years Han paid and recovered its strength, but the raids never stopped.

steps: Zhang Qian's mission

Xiongnu captives told the young Emperor Wu that the Xiongnu had killed the king of the Yuezhi and made his skull a drinking cup, and that the Yuezhi had fled west, nursing their hatred. Seeking them as allies, Han called for envoys. A palace attendant, Zhang Qian, set out around 139 or 138 BC; twice held by the Xiongnu, he came back to Chang'an thirteen years later.

p: Zhang Qian, from Hanzhong, left Longxi with over a hundred men and a guide of Xiongnu birth, Ganfu. They were caught as soon as they entered the Xiongnu-held Hexi corridor and taken to the chanyu, who asked how Han could send envoys to the Yuezhi beyond his lands. He kept Zhang Qian more than ten years and gave him a Xiongnu wife, who bore him a son, but Zhang Qian never gave up his envoy's staff. The map, still the layer of 200 BC, shows the Yuezhi in the Hexi corridor and far beyond; by the time Zhang Qian left, they had long been driven from their old lands and were moving west.

After about ten years Zhang Qian slipped away westward and after several weeks reached Dayuan, in the Ferghana valley. Its king sent him on with guides to Kangju, and Kangju passed him to the Yuezhi. They had conquered Bactria and settled north of the Oxus, the Amu Darya, in rich land with few enemies, and had no thought of revenge. After more than a year he gave up. Returning along the Kunlun mountains through Qiang country, he was captured again, and escaped only when the chanyu's death threw the Xiongnu into civil war. He reached Chang'an in 126 BC; of the hundred-odd men who set out, two came back.

His report on Dayuan, the Wusun, Kangju, the Yuezhi, Bactria, Parthia and India became the core of Sima Qian's chapter on the western lands. In Bactria he had seen cloth and bamboo staffs from Shu, today's Sichuan, brought by merchants through India, and he concluded that a road ran that way too. In 123 BC he guided Wei Qing's army to water and pasture and was made Marquis of Bowang. In 119 BC he went west again, to the Wusun, with 300 men, 600 horses, herds of cattle and sheep and a fortune in gold and silk, sending deputies on to Dayuan, Kangju, Bactria, Parthia and India. Sima Qian said he had 'pierced the void', opening a road where none had been.

steps: Wei Qing, Huo Qubing and Mobei

After a failed ambush at Mayi in 133 BC ended the heqin peace, Wei Qing led seven campaigns against the Xiongnu and retook the Ordos, and Huo Qubing twice swept through the Hexi corridor, opening the way west. In 119 BC each led 50,000 horsemen across the Gobi. Wei Qing routed the chanyu, Huo Qubing crushed the Wise King of the Left, and the Xiongnu court withdrew far to the north.

p: In 133 BC Han hid more than 300,000 men near Mayi and had a local magnate lure the chanyu south with the promise of the town. On the way the chanyu saw herds with no herdsmen, grew suspicious, captured a Han officer and learned the truth; from then on the two sides were at war. In 129 BC Wei Qing, once a horseman in the household of the emperor's sister, led his first campaign and struck Longcheng, where the Xiongnu gathered to sacrifice. In 127 BC he retook the Ordos, where Han set up two commanderies, and in 124 BC he surprised the Wise King of the Right by night, taking 15,000 captives. He was made Grand General.

Huo Qubing, Wei Qing's nephew, first fought at eighteen, leading 800 light horsemen far ahead of the army, and was made Champion Marquis. In 121 BC, barely twenty, he twice swept through the Hexi corridor, in spring past the Yanzhi mountains and in summer by Juyan to the Qilian mountains; Sima Qian credits the summer campaign alone with over 30,000 killed or captured. That autumn the Xiongnu King Hunye killed his fellow King Xiutu and surrendered with over 40,000 people. The corridor passed to Han, cutting the Xiongnu off from the Qiang. A Xiongnu song recorded later laments that without the Yanzhi mountains their women had no colour for their cheeks.

In 119 BC Emperor Wu sent 100,000 cavalry, half under each commander, with 140,000 horses in all and hundreds of thousands of foot soldiers and porters behind, across the Gobi. Wei Qing, marching from Dingxiang, met the chanyu Yizhixie and circled his armoured wagons into a fort. At dusk a gale filled the air with sand and the Han wings closed in; the chanyu escaped with a few hundred riders, and 19,000 of his men were killed or taken. Huo Qubing, marching from Dai, crushed the Wise King of the Left, took over 70,000 and sacrificed to Heaven on Mount Langjuxu. The cost was high: of 140,000 horses, fewer than 30,000 came back.

steps: Dayuan and the Hexi corridor

Han organised the Hexi corridor into four commanderies, Wuwei, Zhangye, Jiuquan and Dunhuang, and built walls and watchtowers out to the Jade Gate. To get the 'heavenly horses' of Dayuan, Emperor Wu twice sent Li Guangli to the Ferghana valley; his army returned in 101 BC. Envoys and caravans now used the road that would much later be called the Silk Road.

p: With King Hunye's surrender the Hexi corridor passed to Han. The annals of the History of the Han say Wuwei and Jiuquan were founded in 121 BC and Zhangye and Dunhuang carved out of them in 111 BC, but the same book's treatise on geography gives other dates, and historians still argue over them. Han extended its wall and beacon towers west from Lingju, today's Yongdeng in Gansu, all the way past Dunhuang to the Jade Gate and Yang passes, and moved settlers and soldier-farmers into the corridor. The map is still the layer of 200 BC, with the Yuezhi in the corridor.

Zhang Qian had reported that Dayuan bred fine horses that sweated blood, which Emperor Wu came to call heavenly horses. Around 104 BC a Han envoy offered a thousand pieces of gold and a golden horse for the stallions of Ershi; Dayuan refused and had the envoys killed on their way home. The emperor made Li Guangli, brother of his favourite Lady Li, General of Ershi and sent him west with 6,000 cavalry and tens of thousands of young toughs. The oasis states shut their gates, and only a few thousand starving men reached Yucheng, where they were beaten. After two years only one or two in ten came back to Dunhuang, and the furious emperor barred the Jade Gate against them.

In 102 BC Li Guangli set out again with 60,000 men, 100,000 oxen and over 30,000 horses, while 180,000 troops guarded the frontier behind him. He besieged the Dayuan capital for more than forty days and cut off its water, until the nobles killed their king and let the Han army choose: a few dozen of the best horses and over 3,000 others. Only about 10,000 men and 1,000 horses came back through the Jade Gate in 101 BC, lost less in battle than to their officers' greed. The western states now sent envoys, grapes and alfalfa were planted near the capital, and silk went west. The name 'Silk Road' was popularised only in 1877, by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen; a few earlier uses are known.
facts: dozens of the best, over 3,000 others

steps: The Protectorate of the Western Regions

After Emperor Wu the Xiongnu weakened under attacks from Han and the Wusun and a run of disasters. In 60 BC the Xiongnu king who ruled the Western Regions surrendered, and Emperor Xuan made Zheng Ji the first Protector-General, based at Wulei. Soon the Xiongnu split: one chanyu, Huhanye, became a Han vassal; the other, Zhizhi, fled west and was hunted down.

p: Emperor Wu's last years brought defeats: Li Ling surrendered to the Xiongnu in 99 BC, Li Guangli lost his whole army and went over to them in 90 BC, and the emperor renounced further distant wars. But the Xiongnu fared worse. In 72–71 BC five Han armies marched while Chang Hui led 50,000 Wusun horsemen from the west, taking nearly 40,000 captives. That winter a blizzard dropped more than two metres of snow in a day on the chanyu's army; fewer than one in ten came home. The Dingling, Wuhuan and Wusun then attacked from north, east and west, and the Xiongnu lost their grip on the west.

Han's foothold in the west began with soldier-farmers, whom Zheng Ji led with oasis troops to defeat Jushi, near Turfan, in 68 BC. In 60 BC, amid a fight over the Xiongnu throne, the Rizhu king who governed the Western Regions came over to Zheng Ji with some 12,000 people, and the Xiongnu office that taxed the oasis states was abolished. Emperor Xuan made Zheng Ji Protector-General of both the northern and southern roads round the Tarim basin. From Wulei, east of today's Luntai, he oversaw 36 states, later over 50. Each kept its king; the protector settled disputes, raised troops and guarded the roads, so the map does not draw them inside Han.

In 57 BC five rival chanyus claimed the throne, and the Xiongnu ended up split between Huhanye and Zhizhi. In 51 BC Huhanye came to pay homage to Emperor Xuan, who received him as a guest ranking above the Han princes. Zhizhi moved west to Kangju and killed a Han envoy. In 36 BC Chen Tang, deputy to the Protector-General Gan Yanshou, forged an imperial order, raised over 40,000 men and stormed Zhizhi's fortress near today's Taraz in Kazakhstan, killing the chanyu. Whoever offended mighty Han, Gan Yanshou and Chen Tang wrote, would be punished, however far away. In 33 BC the palace lady Wang Zhaojun married Huhanye, and the frontier stayed quiet for decades.
facts: Wulei, east of today's Luntai, Xinjiang

steps: The Xiongnu split; Yanran

After Wang Mang seized the throne, relations with the Xiongnu broke down and the Western Regions were lost. In AD 48 the Xiongnu split again, and the Southern Xiongnu settled inside the frontier. In 89 Dou Xian and his Southern Xiongnu allies crushed the Northern Xiongnu at Mount Jiluo and had Ban Gu's inscription carved on Mount Yanran. Two years later the northern chanyu fled west, all but vanishing from Chinese records.

p: In AD 9 Wang Mang replaced the Han with his own Xin dynasty, swapped the chanyu's Han seal for one of lower rank and later gave him an insulting title. The Xiongnu raided year after year, and the oasis states went over to them. In the early Eastern Han the Xiongnu were torn by feuds and by drought and locusts that left the land 'red for thousands of li'. In 48 Bi, a grandson of Huhanye who ruled eight southern tribes, took the title Huhanye and submitted to Han: these were the Southern Xiongnu, who later settled at Meiji, in today's Inner Mongolia, and guarded the frontier for Han. The map is still the layer of AD 1; they appear only in the 100 snapshot.

The Northern Xiongnu still held Mongolia and the Western Regions. In 73 Dou Gu and Geng Zhong beat them in the Tian Shan and took Yiwu, today's Hami. Ban Chao, an officer with the army, went to Shanshan with 36 men, wiped out a Xiongnu embassy in a night attack and won the king over; he would spend thirty years in the west. In 87 the Xianbei killed the northern chanyu, and 58 tribes, 200,000 people, came south to surrender. The regent, Empress Dowager Dou, gave command of a new campaign to her brother Dou Xian so that he could redeem himself: he had had a marquis of the imperial clan assassinated.

In 89 Dou Xian and Geng Bing led over 40,000 Han, Southern Xiongnu and Qiang horsemen in three columns and routed the northern chanyu at Mount Jiluo; 81 tribes, over 200,000 people, surrendered. Dou Xian climbed Mount Yanran, usually placed in Mongolia's Khangai range, and had Ban Gu, who rode with him, compose an inscription for the rock; 'carving the stone at Yanran' became a byword for frontier glory. In 2017 a Chinese–Mongolian team identified it on a cliff in Mongolia's Dundgovi province. In 91 Geng Kui beat the northern chanyu again in the Altai, and he fled west. Whether his people were related to the Huns who later reached Europe is still debated.
facts: by Ban Gu; identified in Mongolia in 2017

three-kingdoms.title: The Three Kingdoms
three-kingdoms.lede: From the Yellow Turbans to the fall of Wu: the century of division after the collapse of the Han, the age later retold in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
steps: The Yellow Turbans

By the late second century the Eastern Han court was a battleground of eunuchs and empresses' kin; scholars who protested were purged, and land-grabbing and famine drove peasants from their fields. In 184 Zhang Jue, leader of the Way of Great Peace, raised hundreds of thousands of followers in yellow headbands across eight provinces. The rising was crushed within the year, but power passed to provincial governors and their armies.

p: Zhang Jue, from Julu in Ji province, called himself the Great Worthy Teacher and healed the sick with charms, holy water and spells. In ten years he gathered hundreds of thousands of followers in eight provinces, organised in 36 divisions of six or seven thousand to over ten thousand under their own commanders. They spread a prophecy: 'The blue sky is dead, the yellow sky shall rise; in the jiazi year, all under heaven shall prosper', and chalked jiazi on the gates of government offices, even in the capital. The rising was set for the fifth day of the third month of the jiazi year, 184, and one leader, Ma Yuanyi, had won over eunuchs in the palace.

A month before the date a disciple betrayed the plan. Ma Yuanyi was torn apart by chariots in Luoyang and over a thousand others were killed. Zhang Jue rose at once, in the second month, as General of Heaven, with his brothers Zhang Bao and Zhang Liang as Generals of Earth and of Man, and the Yellow Turbans burned government offices and sacked towns. Emperor Ling lifted the ban on the partisan scholars, lest they join the rebels, and sent Huangfu Song, Zhu Jun and Lu Zhi against them. Zhang Jue fell ill and died; by the year's end his brothers had been killed, and the rebel dead numbered in the hundreds of thousands. Remnants held out for some twenty years.

In 188, on Liu Yan's advice, the court turned some provincial inspectors into governors with full military and civil power. Emperor Ling died in 189. The regent He Jin plotted against the eunuchs and was murdered by them; Yuan Shao stormed the palace and killed over two thousand eunuchs. In the chaos the general Dong Zhuo seized Luoyang and replaced the young emperor with his half-brother, the boy Emperor Xian. In 190 the eastern governors rose under Yuan Shao; Dong Zhuo burned Luoyang and moved the court to Chang'an, where Wang Yun and Lü Bu killed him in 192. The warlords then fought for the provinces, and Sun Ce crossed the Yangtze to take the south-east.
facts: Zhang Jue, Zhang Bao, Zhang Liang
hundreds of thousands in eight provinces, 36 divisions

steps: Guandu

In 196 Cao Cao brought Emperor Xian to Xu and from then on issued orders in his name. By 199 Yuan Shao held four northern provinces, and he marched south with 100,000 men. In 200 the two armies faced each other for months at Guandu, near today's Zhengzhou, until Cao Cao, on a defector's tip, burned Yuan Shao's grain at Wuchao and the Yuan army fell apart.

p: Cao Cao's father was the adopted son of a powerful eunuch, and Cao Cao made his name fighting the Yellow Turbans and Dong Zhuo. In 192 he took the surrender of over 300,000 Yellow Turbans and formed the best into his Qingzhou army. In 196 he brought the fugitive Emperor Xian to Xu, today's Xuchang, and settled refugees around it as state farmers; the first harvest, a million hu of grain, fed his armies. In 198 he executed Lü Bu at Xiapi and controlled much of the land south of the Yellow River. North of it Yuan Shao, of a family that had given top ministers for four generations, destroyed Gongsun Zan in 199 and prepared to march on Xu.

Early in 200 Cao Cao crushed a rebellion by Liu Bei in Xu province; Liu Bei fled to Yuan Shao, leaving Guan Yu a prisoner. When Yuan's general Yan Liang besieged Baima, on the Yellow River, Cao Cao feinted, and Guan Yu rode into the enemy ranks and killed Yan Liang; another of Yuan's generals, Wen Chou, fell at Yanjin. Cao Cao fell back on Guandu. For months the armies faced each other: Yuan's men built mounds and towers to shoot into Cao's camp, and Cao smashed the towers with stone-throwers; Yuan dug tunnels, and Cao dug trenches to meet them. Cao's grain ran low and he thought of retreat, but Xun Yu urged him to hold on.

In the tenth month Xu You, one of Yuan Shao's advisers, defected and told Cao Cao that Yuan's grain was parked at Wuchao under Chunyu Qiong with some 10,000 men. Cao Cao led 5,000 foot and horse there by night, reportedly under Yuan banners, and set it ablaze. Yuan's generals Zhang He and Gao Lan, failing to take Cao's camp, went over to him, and the Yuan army dissolved. The Records of the Three Kingdoms give Yuan 100,000 picked troops and 10,000 horse and Cao under 10,000; the fifth-century commentator Pei Songzhi already suspected Cao's numbers were played down. Yuan Shao died in 202, his sons fought each other, and by 207 Cao Cao held the north.
facts: Cao Cao's night raid burns Yuan Shao's grain at Wuchao
Yuan 100,000 foot and 10,000 horse; Cao under 10,000, perhaps understated

steps: The Red Cliffs

In 208 Cao Cao marched on Jing province; its governor died, his son surrendered, and Liu Bei fled south. Zhuge Liang won over Sun Quan, who sent Zhou Yu with 30,000 men to join Liu Bei. That winter the armies met at the Red Cliffs on the Yangtze. Cao's troops were sick, Huang Gai's fire ships set his fleet ablaze, and Cao Cao retreated north, leaving the realm to be split in three.

p: Liu Bei had taken refuge with Liu Biao, governor of Jing province, at Xinye. In 207 he called three times on the recluse Zhuge Liang, who laid out a plan: take Jing and Yi provinces, make peace with the peoples of the west and south, ally with Sun Quan, and at the right moment strike north from both. In the seventh month of 208 Cao Cao, newly chancellor, marched south. Liu Biao died and his son surrendered at Xiangyang. Liu Bei retreated with over 100,000 refugees at ten li a day; Cao's 5,000 picked horsemen caught him at Changban, and he fled with a few dozen riders, abandoning his family. Cao took Jiangling with Jing's fleet and stores.

Zhuge Liang went with Lu Su to see Sun Quan at Chaisang. Cao Cao wrote to Sun Quan that he had 800,000 men in his navy and looked forward to a hunt with him in Wu. Most of Sun's ministers urged surrender; Lu Su and Zhou Yu argued for war. Zhou Yu reckoned Cao's northerners at no more than 150,000 or 160,000, and worn out; Liu Biao's former troops, at most 70,000 or 80,000, were not to be trusted; and northerners new to river warfare would fall sick in the south. Sun Quan gave Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu 30,000 men to join Liu Bei's 20,000 or so. At the Red Cliffs they won the first clash, and Cao fell back to Wulin on the north bank.

Seeing that Cao's ships lay bow to stern, Huang Gai proposed fire. He sent a letter offering to defect, then sailed dozens of ships packed with oil-soaked brushwood towards the north bank. Before a strong south-east wind they were set alight a short way out, and the fire spread from the fleet to the camps ashore. Cao Cao retreated on foot by the Huarong road, where sick soldiers laying straw over the mud were trampled to death. He later wrote to Sun Quan that disease, not Zhou Yu, had made him burn his own ships. The site is disputed; most scholars place it in today's Chibi in Hubei, not at Huangzhou, where Su Shi wrote his famous rhapsody.
facts: 30,000 under Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu; about 20,000 with Liu Bei

steps: Three kingdoms

In 220 Cao Pi ended the Han and founded Wei; in 221 Liu Bei proclaimed himself emperor of Han at Chengdu, the state called Shu; in 229 Sun Quan became emperor of Wu, ruling from Jianye. The 262 snapshot shows Wei in the north, Shu in Sichuan, Hanzhong and the south-west, and Wu along the Yangtze down to northern Vietnam. Zhuge Liang led five campaigns against Wei and died in camp in 234.

p: After the Red Cliffs, Liu Bei took southern Jing province, won Yi province in 214 and in 219 took Hanzhong, killing Cao Cao's general Xiahou Yuan at Mount Dingjun. That year Guan Yu struck north at Fancheng and, as the Han river flooded, destroyed Yu Jin's army, but Lü Meng of Wu slipped upriver with soldiers dressed as merchants and took Jiangling; Guan Yu was captured and killed. Cao Cao died early in 220, and that winter Cao Pi made the last Han emperor abdicate. Liu Bei, emperor from 221, marched on Wu to retake Jing, was routed by Lu Xun's fire attack at Yiling in 222 and died at Baidicheng in 223, entrusting his son Liu Shan to Zhuge Liang.

As chancellor, Zhuge Liang ran Shu. He restored the alliance with Wu, put down a rising in the south in 225 and in 227 presented his famous memorial and marched to Hanzhong. Between 228 and 234 he led five campaigns north; the 'six campaigns from Mount Qi' come from the Romance, and only two went by Qishan. In the first, three Wei commanderies came over to him, but his vanguard commander Ma Su disobeyed orders and was routed at Jieting, and Zhuge Liang had him executed. He built 'wooden oxen' and 'gliding horses' to carry grain over the Qinling tracks. In 234 he faced Sima Yi at Wuzhang Plains for over a hundred days and died there, aged 54.

After him Jiang Wan and Fei Yi ran Shu, while Jiang Wei's repeated campaigns drained it. In Wei, Sima Yi conquered Liaodong in 238, and in 249, while the regent Cao Shuang was out of Luoyang with the emperor at the Gaoping tomb, he seized the capital and had Cao Shuang killed; from then on the Sima family ruled Wei. In Wu, Sun Quan's death in 252 brought years of bloody feuds. The Tongdian records 4.43 million registered people in Wei around 263, 940,000 in Shu and 2.3 million in Wu in 280, together less than a seventh of the Eastern Han at its height: war had taken a terrible toll, but many people had also slipped off the registers into the service of local magnates.

steps: Wei takes Shu; the Jin

In 263 Sima Zhao, master of Wei, sent three armies against Shu. Jiang Wei held Zhong Hui at the Jiange pass, but Deng Ai led his men some 700 li across roadless mountains by the Yinping track, broke through at Jiangyou and Mianzhu and reached Chengdu, where Liu Shan surrendered. Two years later Sima Zhao's son Sima Yan made the last Wei emperor abdicate and founded the Jin.

p: Sima Yi and then his sons crushed three revolts in the Huai valley; after his death in 251 Sima Shi and Sima Zhao held power in turn and deposed one emperor. In 260 the young emperor Cao Mao, refusing to be a puppet, declared that Sima Zhao's ambitions were known to every man in the street and led a few hundred guards and servants against him. Jia Chong, Sima Zhao's ally, had an officer, Cheng Ji, stab the emperor to death, and Cao Huan was enthroned. To win the prestige he needed to replace the Cao house, Sima Zhao resolved to conquer Shu. The 262 snapshot on the map shows the last moment of the three-way balance.

In the autumn of 263 three Wei armies marched. Zhong Hui led over 100,000 men through the Qinling valleys into Hanzhong, while Deng Ai and Zhuge Xu, each with over 30,000, came south from Longxi to pin down Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei slipped away to the pass at Jiange, where Zhong Hui could not break through and his supplies ran thin. Deng Ai proposed going round by the Yinping track. For more than 700 li his men crossed empty mountains, cutting paths and building plank roads; at one slope Deng Ai wrapped himself in felt and rolled down, while his soldiers clung to trees and rock in single file. They emerged at Jiangyou, whose commander surrendered.

Zhuge Liang's son Zhuge Zhan fought them at Mianzhu and died. In the eleventh month Deng Ai reached Chengdu, and Liu Shan, advised by Qiao Zhou, came out bound to surrender; Shu had lasted 43 years. Made Duke of Anle in Luoyang, he is said to have told Sima Zhao that he was too happy there to miss Shu. In 264 Zhong Hui had Deng Ai arrested and plotted with Jiang Wei to rule Shu himself, but his troops mutinied and killed them both, and Deng Ai was then killed by men sent by Wei Guan. Sima Zhao, now King of Jin, died in 265; that winter his son Sima Yan took the throne from Cao Huan and founded the Jin at Luoyang.
facts: eleventh month of 263; Liu Shan surrenders
Zhong Hui over 100,000; Deng Ai and Zhuge Xu over 30,000 each
twelfth month of 265 (early 266 in the Western calendar)

steps: Jin conquers Wu

Wu's last emperor, Sun Hao, was cruel and capricious. After a decade of preparation, Emperor Wu of Jin sent six armies, over 200,000 men, against Wu in the winter of 279, while Wang Jun's fleet sailed down the Yangtze from Sichuan, burning through the iron chains across the river. In the third month of 280 Sun Hao surrendered at Jianye. The map now shows the 280 layer: Jin rules all of China.

p: Sun Hao came to the throne of Wu in 264. Suspicious and bloodthirsty, he had officials who displeased him flayed or blinded, built lavish palaces and for a time moved his capital to Wuchang, to his people's disgust. For Jin, Yang Hu commanded at Xiangyang from 269, setting his soldiers to farm until he had ten years' grain in store and winning over people across the border by fair dealing, while he and the Wu general Lu Kang treated each other with chivalrous respect. Lu Kang died in 274. Yang Hu urged an invasion again and again, but Jia Chong and others opposed it, and before he died in 278 he named Du Yu to succeed him.

In Yi province Wang Jun spent seven years building a fleet. His largest craft, hulls lashed together, were 120 paces across, carried over 2,000 men and had wooden walls and towers on deck with room to ride horses. In the eleventh month of 279 six Jin armies, over 200,000 men in all, advanced from the lower Yangtze to Jiangling, while Wang Jun and Tang Bin sailed down from Sichuan. Wu had strung iron chains across the river's narrows and planted iron spikes under water. Wang Jun sent great rafts ahead, manned by straw dummies in armour, to catch the spikes, then burned through the chains with huge torches soaked in sesame oil.

When Jin had taken Xiling and Jiangling, some advised waiting for winter, as summer was coming with its floods and disease. Du Yu replied that the army's momentum was like splitting bamboo: after the first few joints the rest part at the touch of the blade, words that became the idiom for an unstoppable advance. In the third month of 280 Wang Jun's fleet reached the Stone Fortress at Jianye ahead of the other armies, and Sun Hao came out with his hands bound, bringing his coffin. Jin took over 2.3 million people and 230,000 soldiers; the reunited empire registered about 16 million. It did not last: from 291 the princes of the Jin house fought one another, and the north soon fell apart again.
facts: third month of 280; Sun Hao surrenders

sixteen-kingdoms.title: The Sixteen Kingdoms
sixteen-kingdoms.lede: From Liu Yuan's rising in 304 to the Northern Wei's conquest of the north in 439, Xiongnu, Jie, Xianbei, Di, Qiang and Han Chinese founded more than twenty states in northern China, while the Jin court survived south of the Yangtze.
steps: The Fall of the Western Jin

After Emperor Wu of Jin died, his princes fought each other from 291 to 306, the War of the Eight Princes. The peoples settled inside the frontier seized their chance: in 304 the Xiongnu noble Liu Yuan founded a state called Han, and the Ba-Di leader Li Xiong took Chengdu. In 311 Han armies sacked Luoyang; in 316 Chang'an fell. The map still shows the united Jin of 280.

p: The Western Jin's unity lasted barely ten years. Believing that Cao Wei had fallen because its princes were powerless, Emperor Wu gave his kinsmen fiefs and armies, and after conquering Wu he disbanded most provincial troops. He died in 290. His heir, Emperor Hui, was mentally incapable, and Empress Jia Nanfeng fought the regent Yang Jun for power. Her coup of 291, in which Yang Jun was killed, began the War of the Eight Princes: one prince after another seized the court, and in 301 Sima Lun, Prince of Zhao, briefly took the throne. By 306, when Sima Yue, Prince of Donghai, came out on top, the Luoyang region lay in ruins.

By then many peoples lived in the north. Since the Eastern Han the Southern Xiongnu had been settled in Bing province, modern Shanxi, where Cao Cao split them into five divisions; Xianbei groups such as the Murong, Tuoba and Duan had taken over the Xiongnu steppe and neared the Great Wall; Di and Qiang lived in Guanzhong and Longyou. In 299 Jiang Tong warned that half of Guanzhong's million people were not Chinese. The princes hired their horsemen; Sima Ying, Prince of Chengdu, relied on Liu Yuan. In 304 Liu returned to Zuoguo, near Lishi, as chanyu and then King of Han, claiming the Han emperors as maternal kin; in 308 he became emperor.

Liu Yuan died in 310; his son Liu Cong seized the throne and sent Liu Yao, Wang Mi and the Jie leader Shi Le raiding across the plain. Sima Yue died in the third month of 311, and in the fourth Shi Le's horsemen caught the 100,000 men escorting his coffin at Ningping and wiped them out, the chief minister Wang Yan among them. In the sixth month Han troops stormed Luoyang, burned the palaces and killed over 30,000 people; Emperor Huai was taken to Pingyang and killed in 313. Emperor Min was enthroned at Chang'an; in 316 Liu Yao besieged it until people ate one another, and the emperor surrendered.

steps: The Eastern Jin and the Two Zhaos

After Chang'an fell, Sima Rui founded the Eastern Jin at Jiankang: king in 317, emperor in 318. In 319 the northern Han state split into Liu Yao's Zhao at Chang'an and the Later Zhao of Shi Le, a Jie, at Xiangguo. On the map of 320 Han Zhao holds Guanzhong, Later Zhao Hebei and the Central Plain, Cheng Han Sichuan, Former Liang Hexi, Dai the northern frontier and the Murong Liaoxi.

p: Sima Rui, a great-grandson of Sima Yi, had been posted in 307 to Jianye, renamed Jiankang in 313 to avoid Emperor Min's name. He had little standing in the south until Wang Dao of the Langya Wang clan won him the great southern families, such as those of Gu Rong and He Xun. Under the new emperor Wang Dao ran the court and his cousin Wang Dun commanded the armies upriver: 'the Wang and the Sima share the realm', people said. Northerners came south in waves and were settled in 'lodged' provinces named after their old homes; Tan Qixiang estimated some 900,000 migrants by the Liu Song, a sixth of the south's people.

After Liu Cong's death in 318 the consort kinsman Jin Zhun killed the new ruler and the Liu clan. Liu Yao marched from Chang'an against him, took the throne on the way and in 319 renamed the state Zhao. Shi Le, a Jie from Shangdang once sold as a slave by Jin officials, broke with Liu Yao in 319 as King of Zhao at Xiangguo, modern Xingtai. Zu Ti, a Jin general who crossed the Yangtze in 313, won back much land south of the Yellow River; after his death in 321 it fell to the Later Zhao. In 328 Shi Le captured Liu Yao at Luoyang, and the Former Zhao ended the next year.

Li Te of the Ba-Di had led refugees from the north-west into Sichuan; his son Li Xiong took Chengdu in 304 and proclaimed the state of Cheng in 306, which Li Shou renamed Han in 338: hence Cheng Han. Zhang Gui, a Han Chinese, became governor of Liang province in 301, and his family held Hexi from Guzang, modern Wuwei, still nominally loyal to the Jin: the Former Liang. The Tuoba Xianbei chief Tuoba Yilu, a Jin ally, became Duke of Dai in 310 and King in 315, ruling from Shengle. Murong Hui of the Murong Xianbei held Jicheng in Liaoxi and took in refugees; in 337 his son Murong Huang declared himself King of Yan.
facts: 304–329, the Xiongnu Liu clan; capital Chang'an from 319
319–351, the Jie leader Shi Le; capital Xiangguo, Ye from 335

steps: The Former Yan and the Former Qin

After Shi Hu's death in 349 the Later Zhao collapsed, and Ran Min, a Han Chinese, took the throne at Ye. The Former Yan swept south, captured Ran Min in 352 and moved to Ye in 357; the Di Fu clan founded the Former Qin in 351. Jin's Huan Wen took Sichuan in 347 and Luoyang in 356. On the map of 360 Yan holds Hebei, the Central Plain and Liaoxi, Qin Guanzhong, Former Liang Hexi.

p: Shi Le died in 333, and his nephew Shi Hu seized power, moving the capital to Ye in 335. He drafted 100,000 men at a time for his palaces and taxed his people hard, but revered the Central Asian monk Fotudeng, who spread Buddhism across the north. After his death in 349 his sons killed one another. In 350 his adopted grandson Ran Min, a Han Chinese, killed the emperor Shi Jian, proclaimed a state of Wei and ordered the slaughter of the Jie and other non-Chinese; the History of Jin's figure of over 200,000 dead is doubtful. The Later Zhao ended in 351, and uprooted peoples streamed home, many dying on the way.

Murong Huang's Former Yan defeated Goguryeo, destroyed the Yuwen Xianbei and in 342 moved to Longcheng, modern Chaoyang. His son Murong Jun, king from 348, took Ji, modern Beijing, in 350. In 352 his general Murong Ke captured Ran Min at Liantai, Yan took Ye, and Murong Jun proclaimed himself emperor at Ji; in 357 he moved to Ye. Meanwhile, after the Di chief Fu Hong was poisoned in 350, his son led their people from Fangtou to Guanzhong and in 351 became Heavenly King of Qin at Chang'an. In 357 the founder's nephew Fu Jian killed his cruel cousin Fu Sheng, took power and made the Han Chinese Wang Meng his minister.

In the south Huan Wen, governor of Jing province, sailed up the Yangtze late in 346 and in 347 took Chengdu; the Cheng Han ruler Li Shi surrendered. Huan Wen's prestige soared. In 354 he attacked the Former Qin and reached Bashang outside Chang'an, but the Qin stripped the fields and hunger forced him back. In 356 he beat the Qiang leader Yao Xiang on the Yi River and recovered Luoyang, then asked in vain for the capital to return there. The Former Yan retook Luoyang in 365. On the map of 360 the Jin border runs near Luoyang, Yan and Qin face each other across the Yellow River, and Dai lies to the north.
facts: 337–370, the Murong Xianbei; capitals Longcheng, Ji, then Ye
351–394, the Di Fu clan; capital Chang'an

steps: The Fei River

With Wang Meng as minister, Fu Jian's Former Qin conquered the Former Yan in 370, took Sichuan from the Jin in 373 and absorbed the Former Liang and Dai in 376, uniting the north. On the map of 383 Qin stretches from Liaodong to Hexi, bordering the Jin along the Huai and Han. That year Fu Jian marched south; Xie Xuan's Beifu army routed him on the Fei River, and the north fell apart.

p: Wang Meng, of humble birth, enforced the law, executing lawless Di nobles, and encouraged farming and schools. In 369 Murong Chui beat Huan Wen's invasion of the Former Yan at Fangtou, then, distrusted at his own court, fled to the Qin. In 370 Wang Meng routed the Yan army on the Lu River and took Ye, ending the Former Yan. Qin took Hanzhong and Sichuan from the Jin in 373; in 376 Zhang Tianxi of the Former Liang surrendered, and Dai fell apart after its defeated king Tuoba Shiyijian died. Xiangyang fell in 379. Dying in 375, Wang Meng had urged Fu Jian to spare the Jin and beware the Xianbei and Qiang.

Fu Jian left Chang'an in the eighth month of 383 with, the History of Jin says, over 600,000 foot and 270,000 horse; his brother Fu Rong took 250,000 ahead to Shouyang, in modern Anhui. From Jiankang the Jin chief minister Xie An sent Xie Shi and Xie Xuan with about 80,000 men, chiefly the Beifu army Xie Xuan had raised from northern refugees. In the eleventh month, facing the Qin across the Fei, Xie Xuan asked them to draw back so he could cross. Fu Jian agreed, meaning to strike mid-river, but the withdrawal turned to chaos; the captured Jin officer Zhu Xu shouted that Qin was beaten, the army broke, and Fu Rong was killed.

As the Qin fled, the story goes, every gust of wind and cry of a crane sounded like pursuit, and before the battle Fu Jian had taken the trees on Mount Bagong for Jin troops: both became proverbs for panic. Xie An read the news over a game of weiqi and remarked only that 'the youngsters have beaten the enemy'. Modern historians think the recorded Qin numbers inflated and believe only the vanguard fought. Qin's unity was fragile anyway: conquered leaders still commanded their own followers, Fu Jian trusted Murong Chui and Yao Chang completely, and he had scattered 150,000 Di households to distant garrisons, leaving Guanzhong itself thinly held.
facts: Former Yan 370; Former Liang and Dai 376
Qin nearly 900,000, Jin about 80,000; far fewer Qin troops fought

steps: The Former Qin Breaks Up

After the Fei River the subject peoples broke away: in 384 the Xianbei Murong Chui founded the Later Yan and the Qiang Yao Chang the Later Qin, who strangled Fu Jian in 385; in 386 Tuoba Gui restored Dai as Wei, the Northern Wei. The map of 400 shows Wei in Hebei and Shanxi, Later Yan in Liaoxi, Southern Yan in Shandong, Later Qin in Guanzhong and four Liang states in Hexi.

p: Murong Chui left Fu Jian for Hebei, became King of Yan at Xingyang in 384 and emperor in 386, ruling from Zhongshan, modern Dingzhou: the Later Yan. His nephews Murong Hong and Murong Chong rose in Guanzhong and took Chang'an in 385; their Western Yan moved east to Changzi and fell to the Later Yan in 394. Fu Jian fled Chang'an and was captured and strangled by Yao Chang in 385. Yao Chang took Chang'an in 386 as emperor of the Later Qin. Fu Jian's kinsman Fu Deng fought on in eastern Gansu until Yao Xing killed him in 394, ending the Former Qin. The Later Qin took Luoyang in 399 and brought Kumarajiva to Chang'an in 401.

Tuoba Gui, Shiyijian's grandson and at first a Later Yan client, became King of Dai at Niuchuan in 386 and soon renamed the state Wei. In 395 the Yan crown prince Murong Bao invaded and, retreating, was surprised at Canhe Slope, probably near Liangcheng in Inner Mongolia, and tens of thousands of prisoners were killed. The next year Murong Chui marched in person, saw the heaped bones at Canhe, fell ill with grief and died. In 397 the Wei took Zhongshan, and Murong Bao fled to Longcheng. In 398 Tuoba Gui moved to Pingcheng, modern Datong, as emperor; Murong De took his followers south and founded the Southern Yan, later based at Guanggu in Shandong.

Lü Guang, a Di general of Fu Jian's, took Kucha in 384 and came back with Kumarajiva; in 386 he founded the Later Liang at Guzang. In 397 Tufa Wugu of the Hexi Xianbei founded the Southern Liang around modern Xining; that year Juqu Mengxun of the Lushui Hu set up the Northern Liang under the Han Chinese Duan Ye, whom he killed in 401, ruling from Zhangye. In 400 Li Gao, a Han Chinese, became Duke of Liang at Dunhuang: the Western Liang. The Qifu Xianbei's Western Qin, founded in 385, is missing from the map: it submitted to the Later Qin in 400 and revived in 409. The Later Liang submitted to the Later Qin in 403.
facts: Former Yan 337–370, Later Yan 384–409, Southern Yan 398–410; the Western Yan (384–394) is not one of the Sixteen
386, by Tuoba Gui; capital Pingcheng and imperial title 398
395; tens of thousands of Later Yan prisoners killed

steps: Liu Yu's Northern Campaigns

Late in the Eastern Jin the Beifu general Liu Yu crushed the usurper Huan Xuan, then conquered the Southern Yan in 410 and the Later Qin in 417, but Helian Bobo of the Tiefu Xiongnu took Chang'an in 418. In 420 Liu Yu became emperor of Song. On the map of 420 Song reaches the Yellow River; Xia holds Guanzhong, Wei Hebei and Shanxi, Northern Yan Liaoxi, and Western Qin, Northern Liang and Western Liang the west.

p: After the Fei River Xie An was sidelined, and power passed to Sima Daozi and his son. In 399 the Daoist leader Sun En rose in eastern Zhejiang; in 402 Huan Wen's son Huan Xuan took Jiankang, and in 403 he made himself emperor of Chu. Liu Yu, a poor man from Jingkou, had risen in the Beifu army. In 404 he and Liu Yi rose against Huan Xuan and restored Emperor An; from then on Liu Yu ran the court. He beat off Sun En's successor Lu Xun, destroyed rivals such as Liu Yi, and in 413 sent Zhu Lingshi to recover Sichuan from the separatist Qiao Zong. The Jin's army and government were his.

The Southern Yan ruler Murong Chao kept raiding south for captives. In 409 Liu Yu marched north through the Daxian pass and besieged Guanggu; it fell early in 410, and Murong Chao was beheaded at Jiankang. In 416 the Later Qin's Yao Xing died amid Xia raids, and his sons fought over the throne. Liu Yu's armies took Luoyang in the tenth month, and the next year he led a fleet up the Yellow River, beating off Wei horsemen with a crescent of chariots. In the eighth month of 417 Wang Zhen'e sailed up the Wei River to Chang'an, and Yao Hong surrendered: the greatest northern victory since the Jin moved south.

Helian Bobo, son of the Tiefu Xiongnu chief Liu Weichen, had been a Later Qin general; in 407 he proclaimed himself Heavenly King of Great Xia, and in 413 began his capital, Tongwancheng, north of modern Jingbian. At the end of 417 Liu Muzhi, who held Jiankang for Liu Yu, died, and Liu Yu hurried south, leaving his young son Liu Yizhen at Chang'an. The Jin commanders there killed one another; in 418 Helian attacked, Liu Yizhen fled, his army was destroyed at Qingni, and Helian proclaimed himself emperor at Bashang. That year Liu Yu had Emperor An strangled; in 420 Emperor Gong abdicated, ending the Eastern Jin and opening the Southern Dynasties.
facts: 420, sixth month; end of the Eastern Jin (317–420)

steps: The Northern Wei Unites the North

Emperor Taiwu of the Northern Wei came to the throne in 423 and took the Xia capital Tongwancheng in 427, Longcheng from the Northern Yan in 436 and Guzang from the Northern Liang in 439; Xia itself was gone by 431. The north was one again, facing the Liu Song: the Northern and Southern Dynasties had begun. On the map of 439 Wei reaches from Liaoxi to Hexi, while Song holds Shandong and Huaibei.

p: After Liu Yu's death in 422 the Wei took Huatai from the Song that year, and Luoyang and Hulao in 423. Tuoba Tao, Emperor Taiwu, succeeded in 423 and, advised by the Han Chinese minister Cui Hao, campaigned repeatedly against the Rouran, a steppe khaganate since 402. Helian Bobo died in 425; Taiwu turned west, stormed Tongwancheng in 427 and captured the Xia ruler Helian Chang in 428. His brother Helian Ding fell back to Pingliang, destroyed the Western Qin in 431 and set out across the Yellow River against the Northern Liang, but the Tuyuhun caught him and handed him to the Wei. Earlier the Western Qin had ended the Southern Liang (414) and the Northern Liang the Western Liang (421).

The Northern Yan in Liaoxi grew out of the Later Yan. In 407 the Han Chinese general Feng Ba killed the Later Yan ruler Murong Xi and enthroned Gao Yun, an adopted son of Murong Bao; when Gao Yun was murdered in 409, Feng Ba took the throne, so the Northern Yan is dated from 407 or 409. In 436 the Wei besieged Longcheng, and Feng Hong fled with his people to Goguryeo, where he was killed in 438. In the ninth month of 439 Juqu Mujian surrendered Guzang to Taiwu; his brothers fled west to Gaochang. Over 30,000 households, monks and scholars among them, were moved to Pingcheng, carrying Hexi's learning and Buddhism into the Wei.

From Liu Yuan's rising in 304 to 439 the north knew 135 years of division and war. The name Sixteen Kingdoms comes from the Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms by the Northern Wei historian Cui Hong, who covered sixteen states that held land and claimed titles; Dai, Ran Wei, the Western Yan, Chouchi and others are left out, as is the Wei itself. 'Five Hu' is the old collective name for the Xiongnu, Jie, Xianbei, Di and Qiang, yet three of the sixteen were founded by Han Chinese. Through the wars the peoples of the north mingled and intermarried, northern gentry served the new rulers, and Buddhism took root in Chinese society.
facts: Xiongnu: Han Zhao 329, Xia 431, Northern Liang 439; Jie: Later Zhao 351; Xianbei: Former Yan 370, Later Yan 409, Southern Yan 410, Southern Liang 414, Western Qin 431; Di: Cheng Han 347, Former Qin 394, Later Liang 403; Qiang: Later Qin 417; Han Chinese: Former Liang 376, Western Liang 421, Northern Yan 436

north-south.title: The Northern and Southern Dynasties
north-south.lede: From Liu Yu's Song in 420 to the Sui conquest of the Chen in 589, the Song, Qi, Liang and Chen ruled the south, while in the north the Wei split into Eastern and Western Wei, which became the Northern Qi and Northern Zhou.
steps: Liu Yu's Song

In the sixth month of 420 Liu Yu took the Eastern Jin throne at Jiankang and founded the Song, or Liu Song: the Southern Dynasties begin. On the map it reaches the Yellow River, with Luoyang and Shandong, won in 409–417. North of the river is the Northern Wei at Pingcheng; the Xia has held Guanzhong since 418; the Western Qin, Northern and Western Liang hold the west, the Northern Yan Liaoxi, the Rouran the steppe.

p: Liu Yu came from a poor family at Jingkou, modern Zhenjiang, and farmed and cut reeds before joining the Beifu army, raised by Xie Xuan around 377 from northern refugees; it had routed the Former Qin on the Fei River in 383. Rising against Sun En's rebels from 399, Liu Yu overthrew the usurper Huan Xuan in 404 and ran the Jin court from then on. He destroyed the Southern Yan in 410, recovered Sichuan in 413, took Luoyang in 416 and Chang'an in 417, ending the Later Qin. Hurrying home to prepare his accession, he left a young son in Guanzhong; in 418 the Xia took Chang'an.
