For a century the great northern clans who had fled south, such as the Wang of Langya and the Xie of Chenjun, had shared power with the Jin throne; the nine-rank system gave their sons the best posts by birth, and the Wang and the Sima, people said, 'shared the realm'. Liu Yu, a soldier, broke the pattern: every later southern dynasty was founded by a general, armies and key provinces went to princes, confidential business to low-born clerks. The great clans kept their prestige, married among themselves and served each dynasty in turn, but lost real command. Liu Yu also registered the refugees where they lived, widening the tax base.

When Liu Yu died in 422, Emperor Mingyuan of Wei struck south and by 423 had taken Huatai, Luoyang and Hulao, where Mao Dezu held out for some two hundred days; the Song lost Henan south of the Yellow River. Emperor Wen, Liu Yilong, came to the throne in 424; in 430 his general Dao Yanzhi briefly retook four Henan strongholds, losing them the next year. Meanwhile Emperor Taiwu of Wei, Tuoba Tao, took the Xia capital Tongwan (427) and destroyed the Northern Yan (436) and the Northern Liang (439), uniting the north. The Song, holding Huaibei and Shandong, now faced a united Wei.

steps: The Yuanjia Campaign

In 450 Emperor Wen of Song launched the Yuanjia campaign to retake Henan, but his army failed before Huatai. Emperor Taiwu of Wei struck back and by the year's end stood at Guabu on the Yangtze, across from Jiankang; he withdrew early in 451, leaving the Huai country in ruins. The map is still 439: the Wei has united the north, with the Rouran beyond; the Song holds the south with Huaibei and Shandong.

p: Emperor Wen reigned for thirty years, 424–453, re-registering households, encouraging farming and, from 438, opening academies at Jiankang for Confucian learning, metaphysics, history and letters: the 'Yuanjia peace'. In 436, out of suspicion, he had his best general, Tan Daoji, killed; Tan cried that the emperor was pulling down his own Great Wall. In the second month of 450 Taiwu besieged the Song town of Xuanhu for forty days in vain. In the seventh month the Song struck: Wang Xuanmo besieged Huatai for months, and Liu Yuanjing's western column reached Shan, near Sanmenxia. In the tenth month Taiwu crossed the Yellow River; Wang fled and the Song armies withdrew.

Taiwu came south in five columns, bypassing Pengcheng and Shouyang, and in the twelfth month reached Guabu, near Nanjing, where his men cut reeds for rafts and threatened to cross; Jiankang was put under martial law. Looking out from the Shitou fortress, Emperor Wen sighed that had Tan Daoji lived the northern horsemen would never have come so far. Early in 451 the Wei turned back, failing in a month's siege of Xuyi. They left scorched earth; returning swallows, it was said, nested in the trees. Taiwu was murdered by a eunuch in 452, Emperor Wen by his heir in 453. The poet Xin Qiji later called the campaign rash.

The Wei was ruled by Xianbei nobles, but it needed the great Han clans. Cui Hao of the Qinghe Cui, Taiwu's most trusted adviser, championed the Daoist Kou Qianzhi, and Taiwu turned to Daoism, in 440 naming his reign 'Perfect Lord of Great Peace'. In 446, after weapons were found in a Chang'an monastery, he had monks killed and temples and scriptures burned. In 450 Cui Hao was executed for writing too frankly of the Tuoba's origins; related clans, says the History of Wei, were wiped out. Emperor Wencheng restored Buddhism in 452, and from 460 the monk Tanyao carved five caves at Yungang, their Buddhas thought to stand for five Wei emperors.
facts: 450, seventh to tenth month; Huatai holds
begun 460, the five caves of Tanyao

steps: Xiaowen Moves to Luoyang

In 466–469, during a Song civil war, the Northern Wei took Huaibei and Shandong; in 479 Xiao Daocheng replaced the Song with the Southern Qi. Emperor Xiaowen of Wei brought in the equal-field system, moved his capital to Luoyang in 494 and made the Xianbei take Chinese dress, speech and names. On the map of 500 Wei and Qi meet on the Huai; the Qi keeps Hanzhong, Xiangyang and Sichuan. In 502 the Liang replaced it.

p: After Emperor Wen the Song princes killed one another. In 465 the brutal young emperor Liu Ziye was murdered and his uncle became Emperor Ming; in 466 most provinces backed another prince, and war followed. Ming won, but commanders who had backed his rival, among them Xue Andu at Pengcheng, went over to the Wei for fear of punishment. The Wei occupied Pengcheng and in the first month of 469 took Dongyang in Qingzhou: the land north of the Huai was lost, and the Huai became the frontier. Ming purged his kin again; after his death in 472 power slipped to the general Xiao Daocheng, who took the throne in 479.

Emperor Xiaowen came to the throne in 471 not yet five, and his grandmother, the Empress Dowager Feng, long ruled for him. From 484 officials drew salaries; an edict of 485 created the equal-field system, allotting land to each adult; from 486 village headmen registered every household for a new tax. The state now reached its farmers directly, and the system lasted into the mid-Tang. Feng died in 490. Pingcheng was remote, hard to supply and the old nobility's stronghold. In 493 Xiaowen marched south with 300,000 men, ostensibly against the Qi; in the autumn rains at Luoyang his ministers begged him to halt, and he declared the capital would move instead.

In Luoyang Xiaowen banned Xianbei dress and forbade officials under thirty to speak Xianbei at court; Xianbei who moved south were registered as natives of Luoyang and could not be buried in the north. In 496 the Tuoba became the Yuan, and other clans took Chinese names: the Qiumuling became Mu, the Helai He. Ranking the great families, he set eight Xianbei clans beside Han houses such as the Cui, Lu, Zheng and Wang and had them intermarry, fusing the two nobilities. The crown prince, who opposed the move, was deposed and killed. The Longmen caves were begun. But the soldiers left on the Six Garrisons were forgotten, storing up trouble.

steps: The Wei Splits

From 523 the Wei's Six Garrisons rose, and the revolt spread to Hebei and the north-west. In 528 Erzhu Rong massacred the court at Heyin. Gao Huan, a garrison man, then took control; in 534 Emperor Xiaowu fled to Yuwen Tai, and the Wei split into the Eastern Wei at Ye and the Western Wei at Chang'an (535). On the map of 540 the south is the Liang of Xiao Yan, founded in 502, reaching the Huai and Hanzhong.

p: The Six Garrisons were built along the Yin Mountains in the early Wei against the Rouran: from west to east Woye, Huaishuo, Wuchuan, Fuming, Rouxuan and Huaihuang. Their commanders were Xianbei nobles, their soldiers once the empire's best. After the move to Luoyang the Xianbei who went south became officials; those left behind sank into hereditary soldiers without prospects, squeezed by their commanders. In 523, after a Rouran raid brought famine, the men of Huaihuang killed their commander, and Poliuhan Baling rose at Woye (perhaps in 524). In 525 the Wei crushed him with Rouran help and moved over 200,000 garrison people to Hebei, where they rose again under Ge Rong.

Luoyang then had over 1,300 temples, says the Record of the Monasteries of Luoyang, and the Empress Dowager Hu's nine-storey Yongning pagoda reportedly rose over a hundred metres. Early in 528 Emperor Xiaoming died suddenly, probably poisoned by his mother, who enthroned an infant. Erzhu Rong, chief of the Qihu at Xiurong, marched south and made Yuan Ziyou emperor. In the fourth month he drowned the dowager and the infant in the Yellow River and massacred the court at Heyin: 1,300 dead by one account, over 2,000 by another. That year he routed Ge Rong with 7,000 horsemen. In 530 the emperor had him killed and was killed by the Erzhu.

Gao Huan of Huaishuo rose in 531 with the garrison refugees, crushed the Erzhu at Hanling the next year and set up Emperor Xiaowu. In 534 Xiaowu fled west to Yuwen Tai, a Wuchuan man, at Chang'an. Gao Huan enthroned another emperor and moved the court to Ye, driving 400,000 households from Luoyang within three days: the Eastern Wei. Yuwen Tai poisoned Xiaowu and in 535 set up the Western Wei. The east was populous and rich, the north-west poor, yet in 537 Yuwen Tai, with under 10,000 men, routed Gao Huan at Shayuan. Gao Huan told his Xianbei that the Han fed them, and the Han that the Xianbei fought for them.
facts: 528, Erzhu Rong slaughters the Wei court

steps: Hou Jing's Rebellion

The map still shows 540: the two Weis and the Liang, whose Emperor Wu, Xiao Yan, had reigned for almost fifty peaceful years. After the Eastern Wei strongman Gao Huan died in 547, his general Hou Jing went over to the Western Wei, then the Liang. In 548 he rebelled at Shouyang and crossed the Yangtze; in 549 he took Jiankang's palace city, and the old emperor died a prisoner. The richest land in the south lay waste.

p: Xiao Yan, a distant kinsman of the Qi emperors, had been one of a prince's 'Eight Friends'. In 500 the Qi emperor put his brother to death; Xiao Yan rose at Xiangyang, took Jiankang the next year and in 502 founded the Liang. The Wei meanwhile took Shouyang in 500 and Hanzhong in 505. In 507 a Wei army said to be a million strong besieged Zhongli, south of the Huai, until in the spring floods Liang fire ships under Wei Rui burned its pontoon bridges. The histories claim 100,000 drowned and as many killed, surely too many. The Huai remained the border, and the Liang regained Shouyang in 526 and Hanzhong in 535.

Emperor Wu promoted Confucian learning and above all Buddhism. He gave up meat and wine, banned meat for monks, and from 527 four times gave himself to the Tongtai monastery as a servant, ransomed by his ministers at vast cost. The Tang poet Du Mu wrote of the 'four hundred and eighty temples'. Crown Prince Xiao Tong compiled the Wen Xuan, and Gao Huan feared that northern scholars saw the Liang as the true dynasty. But the emperor indulged princes and great clans; one official, wrote Yan Zhitui, had never ridden and took a prancing horse for a tiger. When Hou Jing asked for a Wang or Xie bride, he was told they were too grand.

Hou Jing, a Huaishuo man, held Henan with 100,000 troops. In 547 he offered the Liang thirteen provinces; the emperor accepted and sent his nephew Xiao Yuanming north, to be routed and captured at Hanshan. In 548 Hou Jing was beaten at Woyang and fled to Shouyang with 800 men. Fearing the Liang would trade him for peace, he rebelled, joined by a disgruntled prince, Xiao Zhengde. He crossed at Caishi and besieged the palace city, Taicheng. Relief armies of 100,000 held back; of the 100,000 inside, fewer than 4,000 could man the walls. Taicheng fell in 549; the old emperor, kept short of food, died two months later, hence the tradition that he starved.
facts: 549; Emperor Wu dies two months later

steps: Qi, Zhou and Chen

After Hou Jing the Liang fell apart: the Eastern Wei took the Huai lands, the Western Wei Sichuan (553) and Jiangling (554), setting up Xiao Cha's Western Liang. Gao Yang's Northern Qi (550, at Ye) and Yuwen Jue's Northern Zhou (557, at Chang'an) replaced the two Weis, and Chen Baxian founded the Chen (557). On the map of 560 the Chen holds only the land south of the Yangtze; the Qi has the Huai lands, the Zhou Sichuan and Xiangyang.

p: Hou Jing enthroned Xiao Gang, then killed him in 551 and became emperor of Han, while the Liang princes fought: Xiao Yi at Jiangling killed his nephew Xiao Yu, whose brother Xiao Cha at Xiangyang turned to the Western Wei, and Xiao Ji claimed the throne in Chengdu. In 552 Wang Sengbian and Chen Baxian took Jiankang; Hou Jing was killed fleeing, and Xiao Yi became Emperor Yuan. Asked to distract Xiao Ji, the Western Wei general Yuchi Jiong took Chengdu in 553. In 554 Yu Jin stormed Jiangling; Emperor Yuan burned 140,000 scrolls, surrendered and was killed, and over 100,000 people were reportedly marched north, most as slaves. Xiao Cha was made Western Liang emperor.

Chen Baxian, of humble birth in Wuxing, Zhejiang, made his name in the far south fighting the self-made emperor Li Ben (Ly Bi) in Jiaozhou from 545, and in 549 marched north from Guangzhou against Hou Jing. In 555 the Northern Qi sent the captive Xiao Yuanming south and forced Wang Sengbian to accept him; Chen struck from Jingkou, killed Wang and enthroned a son of Emperor Yuan. In 556 he routed a Qi army north of Jiankang, and in the tenth month of 557 took the throne. His Chen was the smallest southern dynasty, defied upriver by Wang Lin until 560. With Jiankang's émigré clans ruined, it leaned on southern strongmen.

Gao Huan's eldest son Gao Cheng was assassinated in 549; in 550 the second, Gao Yang, deposed the Eastern Wei emperor and founded the Northern Qi, with Ye as capital and Jinyang as military base, and built walls against the Rouran and the rising Turks. In the west the weaker Yuwen Tai remodelled government on the Rites of Zhou with Han advisers such as Su Chuo, created the fubing militia under eight 'pillars of state' and twelve generals, gave Han officers Xianbei names and bound Xianbei soldiers and north-western gentry into the so-called Guanlong bloc. He died in 556; early in 557 his son Yuwen Jue became Heavenly King of Zhou.
facts: 557: Yuwen Jue in the first month, Chen Baxian in the tenth

steps: The Zhou Unites the North

In 573 the Chen general Wu Mingche retook the Huai lands from the Qi. In 577 Emperor Wu of Zhou conquered the misruled Qi, reuniting the north; in 578 the Zhou crushed Wu Mingche, and in 579 took the Huai lands. On the map of 580 the Zhou holds the north and Sichuan to the Yangtze, with the Western Liang as its client; the Chen keeps the south. That year Yang Jian, father-in-law of the dead Zhou emperor, took power.

p: The Northern Qi was stronger than the Zhou, but its Xianbei generals and Han officials were at each other's throats, and its ruler Gao Wei trusted favourites. In 572, believing a rhyme spread by Zhou agents, he killed his best general, Hulü Guang, and in 573 forced the Prince of Lanling to take poison. Zhou and Qi both showered silk on the Turkic khagan, who boasted of his two dutiful sons in the south. In 573 Emperor Xuan of Chen sent Wu Mingche north with 100,000 men. He took Qinjun, Liyang and Hefei, then dammed the Fei, flooded Shouyang and stormed it, killing Wang Lin: the Chen frontier was back on the Huai.

For fifteen years Yuwen Tai's nephew Yuwen Hu ruled the Zhou, killing two emperors. In 572 Emperor Wu had him killed and took power. In 574 he banned Buddhism and Daoism, laicising monks, nuns and priests and seizing temple lands, and he recruited Han farmers into the militia until 'half the Chinese were soldiers'. Late in 576 he invaded the Qi, routed its army at Pingyang and took Jinyang; early in 577 he entered Ye. Conquering the Qi brought him over three million households and twenty million people. A Chen thrust at Pengcheng ended in 578 with Wu Mingche trapped and captured at Lüliang; in 579 the Zhou took everything north of the Yangtze.

Emperor Wu died in 578, in his thirties, on campaign against the Turks. His heir, Emperor Xuan, was debauched and cruel; in 579 he handed the throne to his small son, styling himself 'Heavenly Emperor', and died in 580. His father-in-law Yang Jian belonged to the Guanlong bloc: his father Yang Zhong was one of the twelve generals, his wife a daughter of Dugu Xin, one of the eight pillars. Courtiers forged a will making him regent and chancellor. Then Yuchi Jiong rose at Ye, followed by Sima Xiaonan in Hubei and Wang Qian in Sichuan; Yuchi and Wang were killed, Sima fled to the Chen. Ye was razed and its people moved to Anyang.

steps: The Sui Reunites China

In the second month of 581 Yang Jian took the Zhou throne at Chang'an and founded the Sui as Emperor Wen. He abolished the Western Liang in 587; late in 588 over half a million Sui troops moved on the Chen in eight columns, and early in 589 they took Jiankang and the last Chen ruler. The map shows the Sui from the Great Wall to Lingnan: divided since the fall of the Western Jin in 316, China was one again.

p: Yang Jian massacred the Zhou imperial clan and rebuilt the state. At the centre he set up three departments over six ministries; in the provinces he cut three tiers of government to two; his simpler Kaihuang code became the model for the Tang; and he kept the equal-field system and the militia and hunted down hidden households. In 582 he began a new capital, Daxing, south-east of Han Chang'an, and moved in the next year. In 583 his armies beat the Turks, whose empire then split in two. When Emperor Xuan of Chen died in 582, Yang Jian called off an invasion, since one does not attack a mourner, but kept building warships upriver.

On Gao Jiong's advice the Sui threatened invasion at every southern harvest, wearing the Chen out with call-ups, and sent agents to burn its granaries; at Yong'an, modern Fengjie, Yang Su built five-decked warships. In 588 an edict listing the crimes of Chen Shubao was copied 300,000 times and spread across the south. In the tenth month 518,000 men under Yang Guang advanced in eight columns from Sichuan to the sea, while Chen Shubao, trusting the river, feasted on. On New Year's Day 589 Heruo Bi crossed at Guangling and Han Qinhu by night to Caishi; within the month Jiankang fell, and Chen Shubao was hauled out of a palace well with two consorts.

The victors razed Jiankang's walls and palaces and ploughed the site, governing from the Shitou fortress; the capital of six dynasties fell silent. In Lingnan the chieftainess Lady Xian brought her people over, carrying Sui rule to Hainan. The north won with the registered farmers of the equal-field system, a militia of Xianbei and Han, and a united Guanlong bloc; the southern aristocracy never recovered from Hou Jing. Yet the Sui drew on both halves: the historian Chen Yinke traced Sui and Tang institutions to the Northern Wei and Qi, the Liang and Chen, and the Western Wei and Zhou. Treating the age as parallel Southern and Northern Dynasties goes back to Li Yanshou's early Tang histories of the South and the North.
facts: South: Song 420–479, Qi 479–502, Liang 502–557, Chen 557–589. North: Northern Wei 386–534, Eastern Wei 534–550, Western Wei 535–557, Northern Qi 550–577, Northern Zhou 557–581

tang.title: The Height of the Tang
tang.lede: From the Xuanwu Gate to the An Lushan rebellion: the Tang's century of greatness and its undoing.
steps: Heavenly Qaghan

In 626 Li Shimin, Prince of Qin, killed his brothers, the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji, at the Xuanwu Gate of the palace in Chang'an, and two months later became emperor as Taizong. In 630 Li Jing broke the Eastern Turks and Tang troops captured Illig Qaghan, and the chiefs of the north-west hailed Taizong as 'Heavenly Qaghan'. The map still shows 589: the Tang had inherited the Sui lands.

p: After the Tang was founded in 618, Li Shimin, the second son, won its decisive wars against Xue Ju's son Xue Rengao, Liu Wuzhou, Wang Shichong and Dou Jiande, which made him a threat to the crown prince Li Jiancheng and their brother Li Yuanji. On 2 July 626 Li Shimin and his men, among them Yuchi Jingde and Zhangsun Wuji, lay in wait at the Xuanwu Gate on the north side of the palace; he shot Li Jiancheng himself, and Yuchi Jingde killed Li Yuanji. Emperor Gaozu named him heir and soon abdicated. Taizong's ministers Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui and the outspoken Wei Zheng helped make his Zhenguan reign a model of good government.

In the chaos at the end of the Sui the Eastern Turks had grown strong, and northern warlords, Li Yuan among them, had accepted their overlordship. In the autumn of 626, less than three weeks after Taizong's accession, Illig Qaghan reached the Wei River just north of Chang'an with over 100,000 horsemen; Taizong rode out to parley and bought a treaty with gold and silk. Then heavy snows killed the Turks' herds, and the Tiele tribes under them rebelled. Taizong struck in the winter of 629. Early in 630 Li Jing took Dingxiang in a night attack with 3,000 horsemen and fell on Illig's camp near the Yin mountains; Illig was captured.

Taizong did not slaughter the surrendered Turks. About 100,000 were settled along the Great Wall in new prefectures and area commands under their own chiefs, the first of the Tang's 'loose-rein' prefectures for frontier peoples. That spring the chiefs of the north-west came to Chang'an and asked Taizong to take the title Tian Kehan, 'Heavenly Qaghan', which he used thereafter in his letters to them. The Tang emperor was now overlord of the steppe as well as of China. The Turkic Khaganate had split into eastern and western halves around 583; on the map of 589 the Eastern Turks hold the Mongolian steppe and the Western Turks the lands beyond the Altai.

steps: The Four Garrisons

Under Taizong and Gaozong the Tang conquered Gaochang, broke the Western Turks and garrisoned Kucha, Khotan, Kashgar and Suyab, the Four Garrisons. Meanwhile Songtsen Gampo united Tibet, and in 641 the Tang married Princess Wencheng to him. Tibet then fought the Tang for the Tarim Basin until Wang Xiaojie retook the garrisons in 692. The map shows 700, under Wu Zetian, at the height of the rivalry.

p: In 640 Hou Junji conquered the oasis kingdom of Gaochang, near Turfan, and the Tang set up its Anxi Protectorate there, later moving it to Kucha, taken in 648. In 657 Su Dingfang crushed the Western Turkic qaghan Ashina Helu, and for a time Tang suzerainty reached beyond the Pamirs. Kucha, Khotan and Kashgar commanded the routes north and south of the Taklamakan, while Suyab, near modern Tokmok in Kyrgyzstan, stood on the steppe beyond the Tianshan; at times Karashahr took its place. The garrisons were small and relied on the obedience of the oasis cities and on military farms.

Early in the seventh century Songtsen Gampo united the Tibetan plateau and made Rasa, modern Lhasa, his capital. In 641 Taizong sent him Princess Wencheng, a lady of the imperial clan, with craftsmen, books and Buddhist images; tradition holds that the Buddha statue in the Jokhang temple is the one she brought. After Songtsen Gampo died, the family of his minister Gar Tongtsen ruled Tibet, swallowed the Tuyuhun of Qinghai and pushed into the Tarim. In 670 the Tibetans overran the Tang outposts, the garrisons were given up, and a Tang army under Xue Rengui was crushed at Dafeichuan. For twenty years the garrisons changed hands.

In 690 Wu Zetian replaced the Tang with her own Zhou dynasty. In 692 her generals Wang Xiaojie and Ashina Zhongjie routed the Tibetans and retook the Four Garrisons, and this time 30,000 Chinese troops were posted to Kucha to stay; critics who wanted to save the cost were overruled. In 699 the Tibetan king destroyed the overmighty Gar family; its leader Gar Trinring killed himself, and his brother and son went over to the Tang. In 702 the Tang added a Beiting Protectorate north of the Tianshan. On the map of 700 Tibet is vast, but the Tang hold the Tarim oases.

steps: Kaiyuan

Xuanzong came to the throne in 712 and the next year began the Kaiyuan era, which with able ministers such as Yao Chong and Song Jing became a byword for prosperity. In 742 the registers counted about 48.9 million people, and Chang'an was among the largest cities in the world. Yet the old militia had withered, and the frontiers were held by military governors with some 490,000 professional troops. The Tang lands in the Western Regions are drawn in by this atlas.

p: After Wu Zetian's fall the court went through years of turmoil. When Emperor Zhongzong died suddenly in 710, poisoned by the Empress Wei according to the histories, Li Longji destroyed her faction and put his father Ruizong on the throne, succeeding him in 712. Ministers such as Yao Chong, Song Jing and Zhang Jiuling cut surplus offices, re-registered households that had fled the tax rolls and moved the grain of the Yangtze and Huai north to the capital. Du Fu later recalled Kaiyuan's 'days of fullness', when even small towns held ten thousand households. In 742 the registers counted some 8.5 million households; the true population was probably considerably higher.

Chang'an's outer wall ran for about 36 kilometres around some 84 square kilometres, with over a hundred walled wards and two great markets; its population is usually put at around a million. Japanese envoys, students from Silla, Sogdian merchants, Persians and Arabs came and went; the Japanese scholar Abe no Nakamaro served the Tang for decades, and Zoroastrian shrines and a Church of the East temple stood among the Buddhist monasteries. In 742 Li Bai was summoned to court; after leaving in 744 he met Du Fu at Luoyang. The monk Jianzhen began his attempts to sail to Japan, succeeding on the sixth in 753.

Beneath the prosperity the army was changing. The fubing militia relied on farmers serving in rotation, and as land concentrated and households fled the registers it broke down; by the Kaiyuan years the state hired professionals instead. To face the Turks, Tibetans and Khitans, frontier regions were placed under military governors, jiedushi, who controlled a region's troops, revenue and military farms. The Zizhi Tongjian lists for 742 nine governors and one commissioner in the far south, with about 490,000 troops and 80,000 horses, far more than the court held near the capital. That year An Lushan became governor of Pinglu in the north-east.

steps: Talas

In 747 the Tang general Gao Xianzhi led an army over the Pamirs against Little Balur. In 750 he attacked the kingdom of Shi, around Tashkent, and captured its king, whose son appealed to the new Abbasid caliphate. In July 751 Gao led about 30,000 men to Talas, near modern Taraz in Kazakhstan. After five days the Karluks in his army changed sides, and the Tang were routed.

p: In the early eighth century the Tang in Central Asia faced the Tibetans to the south, the Arabs advancing from the west, and Turkic peoples of the steppe such as the Türgesh and Karluks, all shown on the map around the Four Garrisons. The Tibetans reached the Tarim through Little Balur, around modern Gilgit in Pakistan. In 747 Gao Xianzhi, a general of Goguryeo descent, set out from Kucha with 10,000 men, passed Kashgar, crossed the Darkot Pass at over 4,000 metres, overwhelmed the Tibetan garrison and captured the king of Little Balur. Aurel Stein, who later followed the route, rated the feat very highly. Gao was made military governor of the Four Garrisons.

Further west, the Umayyad Caliphate on the map fell in 750 to the Abbasids, whose governor of Khurasan, Abu Muslim, ran Central Asia. That year Gao accused the king of Shi of failing in his duties as a vassal, lured him into surrender and sent him to Chang'an to be beheaded, carrying off great treasure. The prince of Shi escaped and sought Arab help. In 751 Gao struck first, marching some 700 li with 30,000 men to Talas, where he met an Arab army under Ziyad ibn Salih. After five days the Karluks turned on the Tang, and according to the Zizhi Tongjian only a few thousand survived.

The Arab historian Ibn al-Athir wrote that 50,000 Tang soldiers were killed and 20,000 captured, figures plainly inflated. One prisoner, Du Huan, spent more than ten years in the Islamic world and came home by sea in 762; fragments of his account survive in the Tongdian, compiled by his kinsman Du You, among the earliest Chinese eyewitness descriptions of the Arab lands. A later story says prisoners from Talas brought papermaking to Samarkand, but it comes from an eleventh-century writer, and paper probably reached Central Asia earlier. Talas did not end Tang power in the west; the rebellion four years later did.

steps: An Lushan

In 755 An Lushan, military governor of three frontier commands, rose at Fanyang, modern Beijing, and within five weeks took Luoyang. In 756 Tongguan fell and Xuanzong fled towards Sichuan; at Mawei his guards killed the chief minister Yang Guozhong and forced the death of Yang Guifei. With Uyghur help the Tang retook both capitals, but the war ended only in 763.

p: An Lushan, a frontiersman of Sogdian and Turkic parentage from Yingzhou, spoke several languages and began as a broker in the border markets. War service and flattery won him the favour of Xuanzong and Yang Guifei, and by 751 he governed three commands with about 180,000 troops, over a third of the frontier armies. The chief minister Yang Guozhong feuded with him and kept warning that he would rebel. On 16 December 755 An marched south with 150,000 men, among them Tongluo, Xi and Khitan horsemen, claiming 200,000. Hebei gave way; the rebels crossed the Yellow River and took Luoyang, and at the new year An proclaimed himself emperor of Yan.

The Tang held the pass of Tongguan. In the sixth month of 756, pressed by Yang Guozhong, Xuanzong ordered its commander Geshu Han to attack; his army, said to be 200,000 strong, was destroyed and the pass was lost. Xuanzong fled. At the Mawei post station his guards killed Yang Guozhong and made the emperor order Yang Guifei's death. While he went on to Sichuan, the crown prince took the throne at Lingwu as Suzong. Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan held Suiyang for about ten months, blocking the road to the Yangtze. In 757 An Lushan was murdered by his son, and Guo Ziyi, with Uyghur cavalry, retook Chang'an and Luoyang.

Shi Siming, who had submitted, rebelled again, retook Luoyang in 759 and was killed by his own son Shi Chaoyi, whose suicide early in 763 ended the war. To finish quickly, the court made surrendered rebel generals military governors where they stood, and Hebei became a land of semi-independent provinces. The registered population fell from 52.9 million in 755 to 16.9 million in 764, but that mostly measures the collapse of the registers and the flight of people; the often repeated claim of 36 million dead is not credible. Du Fu, in rebel-held Chang'an, wrote that 'the state is broken, but the hills and rivers remain'.

steps: Tibet and the provinces

To fight the rebels the Tang pulled its troops out of the north-west, and Tibet moved in. A Tibetan army briefly held Chang'an in 763; over the next decades Tibet took Longyou and the Hexi Corridor, and the cut-off garrisons of Anxi and Beiting fell. On the map of 800 Tibet reaches almost to Chang'an. Inside China military governors ran their provinces, and those in Hebei paid no taxes at all.

p: In the tenth month of 763, just as the rebellion ended, over 200,000 Tibetans with Tuyuhun and Tangut allies marched east, and Emperor Daizong fled. The Tibetans held Chang'an for fifteen days, set up a puppet emperor and left loaded with plunder. For decades they raided the capital region almost every autumn, and the court had to send troops each year to 'guard against the autumn'. The Hexi oases, cut off, fell one by one: Liangzhou in 764, then Ganzhou, Suzhou and Guazhou; Shazhou, modern Dunhuang, held out until about 786. Beiting, out of contact with the court, held on until about 790 and Anxi longer still.

The Uyghurs had replaced the Turks as masters of the steppe in 744. Twice their cavalry helped the Tang retake the capitals, plundering Luoyang for their pains. Afterwards they sold horses to the Tang for silk, often at forty bolts a horse, a heavy drain on the treasury. In 763 the Uyghur qaghan converted to Manichaeism, a rare case of a major state adopting it. In 787 the minister Li Mi urged Emperor Dezong to ally with the Uyghurs, Nanzhao and the Arabs against Tibet, and the next year a Tang princess married the Uyghur qaghan. On the map Tibet lies between Nanzhao to the south-west and the Uyghurs to the north.

Inside China the provinces became the dynasty's chronic illness. In Hebei, Weibo, Chengde and Lulong were held by former rebel officers, who passed them from father to son or let the soldiers choose, and sent no taxes. Dezong's attempt to bring them to heel in 781 set off a chain of revolts, and in 783 mutinous troops drove him from Chang'an. In 780 Yang Yan's two-tax system, levied twice a year on property and land, replaced the old taxes tied to the equal-field system. With the revenues of the Yangtze and Huai and the palace armies of the Shence, the Tang lasted another century, and in 821–822 made peace with Tibet.

five-dynasties.title: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms
five-dynasties.lede: From the fall of the Tang in 907 to the surrender of the Northern Han in 979, five dynasties followed one another in the north while ten kingdoms, most of them in the south, ruled the rest.
steps: The End of the Tang

From about 875 Wang Xianzhi and Huang Chao led a revolt in Henan and Shandong, and at the end of 880 Huang took Chang'an. The rising failed in 884, but the Tang never recovered: the rebel turned loyalist Zhu Wen held Bianzhou, modern Kaifeng, the Shatuo Turk Li Keyong held Taiyuan, and governors ruled the rest. In 907 Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor. The map still shows 900.

p: The late Tang lived on the revenues of the Yangtze and Huai valleys, while taxes and the price of salt kept rising and drought and locusts struck the north-east. Late in 874 the salt smuggler Wang Xianzhi rose at Changyuan, and Huang Chao, another smuggler, joined him the next year. Wang was killed in 878; Huang led the rebels south and in 879 sacked Guangzhou, where, an Arab account claims, 120,000 foreigners died, probably an exaggeration. In 880 he turned north, took Luoyang and the Tong Pass, and at the end of the year entered Chang'an and proclaimed himself emperor of Great Qi. Emperor Xizong fled to Chengdu.

The rebellion was crushed not by the court's armies but by the governors. In 882 Huang's general Zhu Wen went over to the Tang, was renamed Quanzhong, 'Perfect Loyalty', and became governor of Xuanwu at Bianzhou. Li Keyong, chief of the Shatuo Turks, brought his horsemen south, retook Chang'an in 883 and became governor of Hedong at Taiyuan. In 884 Huang Chao was beaten and died near Mount Tai. That year Zhu Wen feasted Li Keyong at Bianzhou and attacked him in the night; Li escaped over the wall in a storm, and they became mortal enemies. Over twenty years Zhu absorbed the commands of Henan and Shandong.

In 903 Zhu Wen seized Emperor Zhaozong from Li Maozhen, governor of Fengxiang, and massacred the palace eunuchs. In 904 he moved the emperor to Luoyang and had Chang'an's palaces and houses torn down and their timber floated away; the great city never recovered. That year he murdered Zhaozong and set up a boy emperor, and in 905 more than thirty officials were killed and thrown into the Yellow River. In 907 Zhu Wen took the throne as emperor of the Later Liang. The Tang on the map looks whole, but Yang Xingmi in Huainan, Qian Liu in Zhejiang, Wang Jian in Sichuan and others already ruled on their own.

steps: Liang against Jin

The Later Liang ruled from Kaifeng and Luoyang but never subdued Jin in Hedong, where Li Cunxu, who succeeded Li Keyong in 908, fought it across Hebei for fifteen years. The map of 910 also shows Qi at Fengxiang, Yan at Youzhou and the Khitans on the steppe; in the south stand Wu, Wuyue, Former Shu, Chu, Min, Southern Han (an empire only from 917) and Jingnan, seven of the Ten Kingdoms.

p: Zhu Wen ruled his army by terror: if an officer fell, his whole unit was executed, and soldiers' faces were tattooed against desertion. In 908 the young Li Cunxu broke the Liang siege of Luzhou, modern Changzhi, in a morning fog, and Zhu Wen sighed, 'A son should be like Li Yazi!' (Li Cunxu's boyhood name). At the end of 910 two Hebei commands nominally under the Liang went over to Jin, and early in 911 Jin crushed the Liang at Baixiang. In 912 Zhu Wen was murdered by one son, who was overthrown by another, Zhu Youzhen. Jin took Youzhou in 913, capturing the self-styled emperor Liu Shouguang, and Weibo in 915.

Most founders of the southern states were soldiers who had risen in the chaos of the late Tang. Yang Xingmi ruled Huainan from Yangzhou and was made Prince of Wu in 902; Qian Liu ruled Zhejiang from Hangzhou and became King of Wuyue in 907, the year Wang Jian proclaimed the Former Shu at Chengdu. Ma Yin ruled Hunan from Changsha, Wang Shenzhi Fujian from Fuzhou, and Liu Yin Lingnan from Guangzhou, where his brother founded the Southern Han in 917. Gao Jixing held Jiangling as Jingnan. The count of ten comes from Ouyang Xiu's New History of the Five Dynasties, which leaves out Qi, Yan and others.

The southern states lasted because they were more peaceful and growing richer. As war ravaged the north, people streamed south, and the Yangtze and Huai lands, Zhejiang, Fujian and Sichuan filled up. In 910 Qian Liu built a stone sea wall at Hangzhou, and Wuyue kept a corps dredging the waterways around Lake Tai; its Yue celadon was shipped overseas. Wang Shenzhi courted foreign merchants, and Fuzhou, Quanzhou and Guangzhou were busy ports. Chu grew tea and sold it in the north for silk and warhorses. The south acknowledged the northern court for legitimacy and trade, the north needed southern tea and salt, and they mostly left each other alone.
facts: Wu, Wuyue, Former Shu, Chu, Min, Southern Han (from 917), Jingnan

steps: The Later Tang

In 923 Li Cunxu, Prince of Jin, proclaimed the Later Tang, took Kaifeng by surprise and ended the Liang; in 925 he conquered the Former Shu in seventy days. On the map of 926 the Later Tang, reaching from the Great Wall to Sichuan, is the largest of the Five Dynasties; the south is unchanged, and the Khitans have just swallowed Balhae. That year Li Cunxu died in a mutiny.

p: In 915 the Liang tried to split up Weibo; its troops mutinied and went over to Jin, and the two sides faced each other across the Yellow River. At Huliubei in 918 both lost heavily, and Jin's best general, Zhou Dewei, was killed. In 923 Li Cunxu proclaimed himself emperor at Weizhou, modern Daming, as heir of the Tang. In the tenth month, with the main Liang army north of the river, he struck from the south bank and reached Kaifeng within days; the last Liang emperor had an aide kill him. The Later Tang ruled from Luoyang; Qi submitted, and in 924 Gao Jixing of Jingnan became Prince of Nanping.

In the ninth month of 925 Zhuangzong, as Li Cunxu is known, sent his son Li Jiji and Guo Chongtao against Shu, where Wang Jian's pleasure-loving heir Wang Yan surrendered seventy days later. But Zhuangzong was obsessed with the theatre, acted under the stage name 'Li Tianxia', favoured actors and eunuchs and was mean with rewards. Early in 926 Guo Chongtao was wrongly put to death and the Weibo garrison mutinied; Li Siyuan, sent against it, was proclaimed by the mutineers and marched on Luoyang. In the fourth month Zhuangzong was killed by his own guards, and Li Siyuan became Mingzong. Again and again, Five Dynasties emperors fell to their own troops.

On the steppe Yelü Abaoji had become khagan of the Khitans in 907. In 905 (or, by another account, 907) he had sworn brotherhood with Li Keyong at Yunzhou, modern Datong, but then befriended the Liang, and Jin and the Khitans became enemies. In 916 Abaoji proclaimed himself emperor; in 917 his army besieged Youzhou for two hundred days, and in 918 he began a capital in today's Bairin Left Banner, Inner Mongolia. Early in 926 he took the Balhae capital and made the kingdom a vassal, Dongdan, but died on the way home; his son Deguang succeeded. The name Liao, already on the map, was probably adopted in 947, or in 938.

steps: The Sixteen Prefectures

In 936 Shi Jingtang, Later Tang governor of Hedong, rebelled at Taiyuan and bought Khitan help by offering to be their vassal and 'son' and to cede the Sixteen Prefectures. Khitan cavalry destroyed the Later Tang, Shi founded the Later Jin, and the prefectures passed to the Liao in 938. In the south the Later Shu arose in 934, and in 937 the Southern Tang replaced Wu.

p: After Mingzong died in 933, his son lasted four months before Mingzong's adopted son Li Congke, governor of Fengxiang, overthrew him. Li Congke distrusted Shi Jingtang, Mingzong's son-in-law and commander of the strong Hedong army, and in 936 ordered him away from Taiyuan. Shi rebelled and was besieged. He appealed to the Khitans, promising to be their vassal, to treat Deguang as his father, to cede the Sixteen Prefectures and to send 300,000 bolts of silk a year. In the ninth month Deguang came south and routed the Later Tang army, and in the eleventh he crowned Shi emperor of Great Jin. Li Congke burned himself to death in Luoyang.

In 938 the Later Jin, now ruling from Kaifeng, handed over the registers of the sixteen prefectures, among them Youzhou, Yunzhou and Shuozhou: modern Beijing, Tianjin and northern Hebei and Shanxi. The Khitans made Youzhou their Southern Capital; on the map these lands are the block of Liao territory south of the Yan mountains. Shi Jingtang, ten years older than Deguang, was mocked as the 'son emperor', and many of his generals chafed. An Chongrong, governor of Chengde, liked to say, 'Are emperors a breed apart? Whoever has the strongest troops and horses becomes one.' Late in 941 he rebelled against submission to the Khitans, and early in 942 he was killed.

In the south, too, power passed to strong ministers and governors. After the conquest of Shu the Later Tang sent Meng Zhixiang to Chengdu; exploiting the turmoil at court he took eastern Sichuan too, and in 934 proclaimed the Later Shu, dying that year and leaving the throne to his son Meng Chang. In Wu power lay with the minister Xu Wen, whose adopted son Xu Zhigao, based at Jinling, took the Wu throne in 937 as emperor of Qi. In 939 he took back his birth surname as Li Bian, claimed Tang descent and renamed his state Tang. Avoiding war, the Southern Tang became the richest state of the south.
facts: 937, by Xu Zhigao (Li Bian); capital Jinling

steps: The Khitans in Kaifeng

Shi Jingtang's heir refused to be a vassal, and after three invasions the Khitans took Kaifeng early in 947 and ended the Later Jin. Deguang proclaimed the Liao there, but risings drove him north and he died on the way. Liu Zhiyuan of Hedong took the throne and Kaifeng, founding the Later Han. In the south Min had fallen in 945; Fujian was split between the Southern Tang, Wuyue and Qingyuan.

p: Shi Jingtang died in 942. His nephew and heir Shi Chonggui, advised by the minister Jing Yanguang, would call himself the Khitan emperor's grandson but not his subject, and war followed. Khitan invasions in 944 and 945 were beaten back; at Yangcheng in 945 Deguang escaped on a camel. In the winter of 946 the Khitans came a third time, and the Jin commander Du Chongwei surrendered his army on the Hutuo River, leaving Kaifeng defenceless. Early in 947 Shi Chonggui surrendered, Deguang entered the city, and Shi was taken north. In the second month Deguang held court in Kaifeng as a Chinese emperor and proclaimed the Great Liao.

The Khitan army drew no pay and lived by plunder, which it called 'gathering grass', until the country around Kaifeng and Luoyang lay empty and risings broke out everywhere. In the third month Deguang turned for home, saying he had not known the Chinese were so hard to rule, and in the fourth he died at Luancheng. Liu Zhiyuan of Hedong, a Shatuo like Shi Jingtang, had proclaimed himself emperor at Taiyuan; in the sixth month he entered Kaifeng and named his dynasty Han. He died in 948, and under his young son power lay with generals such as Guo Wei. The Later Han, shortest of the Five Dynasties, lasted four years.

Min fell apart from within. After Wang Shenzhi died in 925 his heirs made themselves kings and emperors and murdered one another, and in 943 Wang Yanzheng set up a rival state at Jianzhou. In 945 the Southern Tang took Jianzhou and Wang Yanzheng surrendered. Fuzhou wavered until a Wuyue army beat the Southern Tang there in 947 and kept it. Quanzhou and Zhangzhou were held by the Min officer Liu Congxiao in the Southern Tang's name, and in 949 became the Qingyuan command under him: on the map of 950 Fujian is split in three. In Hunan the Ma brothers were tearing Chu apart; the Southern Tang took it in 951.
facts: 947–951, the shortest of the Five Dynasties

steps: Shizong of the Later Zhou

At the end of 950 Guo Wei rebelled against the Later Han and took Kaifeng, founding the Later Zhou early in 951; Liu Zhiyuan's brother Liu Chong set up the Northern Han at Taiyuan under Liao protection. Guo's adopted son Chai Rong, Shizong, who succeeded in 954, beat the Northern Han and the Liao at Gaoping and, as the map of 958 shows, pushed the Zhou to the Yangtze.

p: The emperor had already killed Guo Wei's family in Kaifeng; Guo crossed the Yellow River and the emperor died in the fighting. In the twelfth month, as Guo led the army north against the Khitans, his soldiers at Chanzhou tore up a yellow banner, wrapped it round him and hailed him emperor, a scene the Chenqiao mutiny would repeat. Guo Wei lightened taxes and died in 954. Liu Chong of the Northern Han struck south with Liao troops, and Shizong marched in person. At Bagongyuan near Gaoping his right wing fled, but Shizong rode into the fight, and Zhao Kuangyin and the palace troops turned defeat into victory.

Shizong then executed some seventy officers who had fled, and rebuilt the palace army: the old and weak were dismissed, and Zhao Kuangyin recruited the best soldiers in the realm for the Palace Command. From then on the palace army was stronger than any governor's. In 955 the minister Wang Pu proposed a plan: take the Yangtze and Huai lands first, then Lingnan and Sichuan, then the Liao-held Yan region, and the Northern Han last, very much the order the Song would follow. That year the Zhou took four north-western prefectures from the Later Shu, closed over 30,000 unlicensed monasteries and melted down bronze images for coin.

From the end of 955 to 958 Shizong led three campaigns against the Southern Tang, whose general Liu Renzhan held Shouzhou for over a year and was dying when it gave in. In 958 Li Jing ceded fourteen prefectures north of the Yangtze, dropped the imperial title and became a vassal. In Hunan a Chu officer drove out the Southern Tang in 952, and Zhou Xingfeng later ruled there as governor of Wuping, the name on the map, appointed by the Later Zhou; Chu's Lingnan prefectures went to the Southern Han. In 959 Shizong attacked the Liao and in forty-odd days took three prefectures, but fell ill and died, not yet forty.
facts: Southern Tang cedes the lands north of the Yangtze

steps: The Song Reunite China

In 960 Zhao Kuangyin, commander of the Later Zhou palace army, was proclaimed emperor by his troops at Chenqiao and founded the Song. He took the south first: Jingnan and Hunan in 963, the Later Shu in 965. The map of 970 still shows the Southern Han, the Southern Tang, Wuyue, Qingyuan and the Northern Han; they ended in 971, 975, 978, 978 and 979.

p: Shizong's heir was a small child. On the first day of 960 the frontier reported a joint Liao and Northern Han invasion, and Zhao Kuangyin was sent north. The army camped at Chenqiao, north-east of Kaifeng, and at dawn the officers, prompted by his brother Zhao Guangyi and his secretary Zhao Pu, draped a yellow robe on him and proclaimed him emperor. Back in Kaifeng the palace commanders, Shi Shouxin among them, were his sworn brothers, and power changed hands almost without bloodshed. He named the dynasty after Songzhou, where he had been governor. The invasion was never heard of again, and many historians believe the mutiny was staged.

Taizu, as Zhao Kuangyin is known, set about taking command away from the generals. In a famous story he persuaded Shi Shouxin and other veteran commanders over wine in 961 to give up their posts; the story comes from later anecdotes and its details are doubtful, but junior men did take over the palace army then. The governors' troops, revenue and courts passed to the centre, and civil officials took over the prefectures. The conquests went south first: in 963 an army sent through Jingnan to Hunan took both; in 965 Wang Quanbin took Chengdu and the Later Shu; in 971 Pan Mei took Guangzhou and the Southern Han.

Li Yu, the last Southern Tang ruler and a fine poet, submitted humbly but could not save his state. In 974 Song troops crossed the Yangtze at Caishi on a pontoon bridge, and at the end of 975 took Jinling. Taizu died in 976 and his brother Zhao Guangyi succeeded as Taizong. In 978 Chen Hongjin of Quanzhou, the Qingyuan of the map (renamed Pinghai in 964), and Qian Chu of Wuyue handed over their lands, Wuyue's without a fight. In 979 Taizong took Taiyuan, the Northern Han surrendered, and old Jinyang was burnt. After seventy years of division China was one again, but for the Liao-held lands around Youzhou and Yunzhou.
facts: Former Shu 925, Wu 937, Min 945, Chu 951, Jingnan 963, Later Shu 965, Southern Han 971, Southern Tang 975, Wuyue 978, Northern Han 979

song-liao-jin.title: Song, Liao, Xia and Jin
song-liao-jin.lede: For more than a century the Song shared China with the Liao, the Western Xia and the Jin, by war and by treaty.
steps: Chanyuan

In the autumn of 1004 the Liao regent, Empress Dowager Xiao Chuo, and Emperor Shengzong led a great army south to Chanzhou on the Yellow River. Some Song ministers urged flight; the chief minister Kou Zhun persuaded Emperor Zhenzong to go to the front. A Song crossbow killed the Liao commander, and peace followed: Song would pay silver and silk every year, and the peace lasted more than a century.

p: Emperor Shengzong of Liao came to the throne in 982 as a boy, and his mother Xiao Chuo, the Empress Dowager Chengtian, ruled for him. She relied on able men such as Han Derang and Yelü Xiuge and threw back the Song invasion of 986. The Liao governed each people by its own customs: a northern administration ran the Khitans and other herders, while a southern one, modelled on the Tang, governed the Chinese counties, whose farms and taxes were a mainstay of the state. For years Liao armies raided south and the Song defended the Hebei towns and waterways; neither side could break the other.

In the intercalary ninth month of 1004 the regent and the emperor marched south with an army said to number 200,000. Unable to take Yingzhou and other towns, they went round them and in the eleventh month reached Chanzhou, modern Puyang, about 150 kilometres from Kaifeng. The Song court panicked: Wang Qinruo urged moving the capital to Jinling, Chen Yaosou to Chengdu. Kou Zhun refused and pressed Zhenzong to lead the army himself. Outside Chanzhou the Liao commander Xiao Talin was killed by a bolt from a Song siege crossbow. Zhenzong crossed the river and appeared on the city gate, and his troops' cheers, the History of Song says, carried for miles.

Neither side wanted a long war, and the Song envoy Cao Liyong went back and forth between the camps. In the twelfth month, by then January 1005, a treaty was sworn. Song would send Liao 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year; the two emperors would call each other brother; the border would stand, neither side would build new forts or dig new channels, and fugitives would be returned. Critics said the Song had bought peace, but the payments cost far less than war, and much of the silver came back through the border markets. For more than a century there was no major war between them.
facts: 100,000 taels of silver, 200,000 bolts of silk

steps: The Western Xia

The map still shows 1000, when the Tanguts of the north-west were only the Dingnan command, now submitting to the Song, now raiding it. They went on to take the Hexi Corridor, and in 1038 Li Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor of Great Xia, the Western Xia. The Song refused to recognise him and lost battle after battle. In 1044 they made peace for yearly gifts of silver, silk and tea.

p: The Tanguts were a Qiang people. At the end of the Tang their chief Tuoba Sigong helped put down Huang Chao and was made governor of Dingnan, with the imperial surname Li; his family held Xiazhou and its neighbours in what is now northern Shaanxi and the Ordos. When the early Song reclaimed these lands, Li Jiqian rebelled in 982 and in 1002 took Lingzhou. His son Li Deming paid homage to both Song and Liao for gifts and trade while expanding west, destroying the Ganzhou Uyghurs. Deming's son Li Yuanhao pushed on, and by about 1036 he held the whole Hexi Corridor.

Yuanhao set out to be the Song's equal. He ordered Tangut men to shave the crowns of their heads, had his minister Yeli Renrong devise a Tangut script, organised a government and an army, and made Xingqing, modern Yinchuan, his capital. In 1038 he declared himself emperor. Emperor Renzong stripped him of his titles and closed the border markets, and war followed. The Song lost at Sanchuankou in 1040; in 1041 an army was ambushed at Haoshuichuan and its commander Ren Fu killed; in 1042 Ge Huaimin's army was wiped out at Dingchuan. Only under Fan Zhongyan and Han Qi, who built forts and trained frontier troops, did the Shaanxi front hold.

The Liao used the war to squeeze the Song, and in 1042, threatening to reclaim land south of the passes, won an extra 100,000 taels of silver and 100,000 bolts of silk a year. The Xia kept winning battles but suffered from the closed border. In 1044, after talks conducted through the frontier town of Yanzhou, Yuanhao dropped the imperial title for 'Lord of the Xia State' and nominally acknowledged Song overlordship; the Song gave him 72,000 taels of silver, 153,000 bolts of silk and 30,000 jin of tea a year and reopened the markets. That year Yuanhao also beat an invading Liao army. His state now reached west to the Jade Gate.
facts: 72,000 taels of silver, 153,000 bolts of silk, 30,000 jin of tea

steps: Jingkang

On the map of 1100 the Liao still rule the north, but the Jurchens were rising on their north-eastern frontier. In 1115 Wanyan Aguda proclaimed the Jin, and within a decade the Liao was gone. The Song, allied with the Jin, twice failed to take Yanjing. In 1125 the Jin turned on the Song, and in January 1127 took Kaifeng and carried off the emperors Huizong and Qinzong.

p: The Jurchens lived in what is now Heilongjiang and Jilin under Liao rule, and resented the Liao envoys who came each year demanding gyrfalcons and other tribute. In 1114 Aguda, chief of the Wanyan clan, rose with 2,500 men and beat a Liao army at Chuhedian. In 1115 he proclaimed himself emperor of the Great Jin and routed a huge army led by the Liao emperor Tianzuo in person. The Liao Supreme Capital fell in 1120, the Central and Western Capitals in 1122. Tianzuo fled into the mountains and was captured in 1125. The Khitan prince Yelü Dashi led his followers west and founded the Qara Khitai in Central Asia.

Emperor Huizong saw the Liao collapsing and hoped to recover the Sixteen Prefectures. Around 1120 envoys crossing the Bohai Gulf agreed the 'Alliance on the Sea': the two states would attack the Liao together, the prefectures would go to the Song, and the Song would pay the Jin what it had paid the Liao. In 1122 Tong Guan twice failed to take Yanjing, and the Jin took it instead. They handed it and six prefectures over only after stripping them of people and wealth, and demanded a million strings of cash a year besides. In the winter of 1125 two Jin armies marched south, and Huizong abdicated in favour of his son Qinzong.

Early in 1126 the Jin besieged Kaifeng. Li Gang organised the defence, and the Jin withdrew only after the Song promised to cede three frontier commands, Taiyuan, Zhongshan and Hejian, and pay an enormous indemnity. Qinzong then went back on the cession. That autumn the Jin returned, and in January 1127 Kaifeng's outer city fell. In the fourth month the Jin carried off Huizong, Qinzong and thousands of consorts, princes, officials and craftsmen, with the court's ritual vessels, books and treasure. In the fifth month Qinzong's brother Zhao Gou took the throne at Yingtian, modern Shangqiu, and the Southern Song began.

steps: Shaoxing

Emperor Gaozong once fled out to sea from the Jin, and later settled at Lin'an, modern Hangzhou. In 1140 Yue Fei beat the Jin at Yancheng and came within reach of Kaifeng, but Gaozong and his chief minister Qin Hui wanted peace. The treaty of 1141 made the Song a Jin vassal, with the border on the Huai River and the Dasan Pass, the line on the map. Early in 1142 Yue Fei was put to death.

p: In 1129 the Jin prince Wanyan Zongbi, the Wuzhu of Chinese stories, crossed the Yangtze and took Jiankang and Lin'an, and Gaozong spent months on his ships off the Zhejiang coast. As the Jin withdrew in 1130, Han Shizhong's fleet trapped Wuzhu's army at Huangtiandang on the Yangtze for 48 days, 8,000 men against 100,000 by Song accounts, until the Jin cut a channel and escaped. The Jin then set up a puppet state of Qi under the turncoat Liu Yu as a buffer, and the Song held the Yangtze. In 1134 Yue Fei recovered Xiangyang, and in 1138 Lin'an became the 'temporary residence', in practice the capital.

Yue Fei ran a famously disciplined army; the Jin were said to admit that it was easier to shake a mountain than the Yue family army. In 1140 the Jin tore up a peace made the year before and Wuzhu marched south. Yue Fei beat Wuzhu's elite cavalry at Yancheng in the seventh month and won again at Yingchang. His grandson Yue Ke wrote that the vanguard reached Zhuxian, 45 li from Kaifeng; some historians doubt it, and the battle accounts may be embellished. Still, no Southern Song army came closer to the old capital. Then, says the History of Song, Gaozong sent twelve gold-lettered orders in one day recalling him.

Gaozong feared his generals' power and wanted his mother back from captivity. In 1141 he and Qin Hui called Han Shizhong, Zhang Jun and Yue Fei to court and promoted them out of their commands, then jailed Yue Fei for treason. In the eleventh month the treaty was agreed: the Song became a Jin vassal, with the border on the Huai and at the Dasan Pass, and paid 250,000 taels of silver and 250,000 bolts of silk a year; the Jin sent back Huizong's coffin and the empress dowager. On 27 January 1142 Yue Fei was put to death. Asked for the evidence, Qin Hui is said to have replied that it 'need not exist'.
facts: 250,000 taels of silver, 250,000 bolts of silk

mongols.title: The Mongols and the Yuan
mongols.lede: Rising from the steppe, the Mongols destroyed the Xia, the Jin and the Song, became the first northern people to rule all of China, and within a century were back on the steppe.
steps: Genghis Khan

In spring 1206 Temujin called an assembly of the tribes, a kurultai, at the source of the Onon River, where he was proclaimed Chinggis Khan, better known as Genghis Khan, and the Great Mongol State was born. The map still shows 1142: only 'Mongol tribes' on the plateau, with the Jin and the Western Xia to the south. Those two neighbours would be his first targets.

p: In the 12th century the Mongolian plateau was divided among rival peoples: Tatars in the east, Kereit in the centre, Naiman in the west, Merkit in the north, and the Mongols, one tribe among many. The Jin kept them divided, often backing the Tatars. Temujin's birth year is given as 1155, 1162 or 1167. According to the Secret History of the Mongols, the Tatars poisoned his father Yesugei, and the abandoned family lived by fishing and hunting. As a young man he served Ong Khan of the Kereit, his father's sworn brother, and with Jamukha crushed the Merkit, who had carried off his wife Borte.

Over the next twenty years he destroyed his rivals one by one: the Tatars in 1202, Ong Khan, who had turned on him, in 1203, and the Naiman of Tayang Khan in 1204; Jamukha was handed over by his own men and executed. At the 1206 assembly Temujin regrouped his people into 95 hereditary units of a thousand under loyal commanders, cutting across the old tribes, and enlarged his guard, the keshig, to 10,000 men. A captured Uyghur scribe, Tata-tonga, began writing Mongolian in the Uyghur alphabet, and Shigi Qutuqu became chief judge. What the word Chinggis meant is still debated.

The new state turned south at once. The Western Xia came first: raided in 1205 and 1207, it saw its capital Zhongxing besieged in 1209. The Mongols tried to flood the city from the Yellow River, but the dyke burst and swamped their own camp; even so, Emperor Xiangzong gave a daughter in marriage and became a vassal. The Jin had been the Mongols' overlords, but when the Prince of Wei took the Jin throne in 1208, Temujin refused to bow to his envoy. In 1211 he crossed the Jin border walls and routed the main Jin army at Yehuling, opening a war of more than twenty years.
facts: source of the Onon, Khentii, Mongolia

steps: The End of Xia and Jin

The Mongols took the Jin capital, Zhongdu, in 1215, and the Jin fell back south of the Yellow River. In 1227 Genghis Khan died campaigning against the Western Xia, which surrendered and was destroyed. In 1234 a Mongol and Song army stormed Caizhou and the last Jin emperor hanged himself. The map still shows the 1142 snapshot; by now neither state existed.

p: After Yehuling the Mongols raided Hebei, Shandong and Shanxi year after year. In 1214 Emperor Xuanzong of Jin bought a truce with a princess and great quantities of gold and silk, then moved his capital from Zhongdu to Kaifeng. Genghis Khan called this a breach of faith and took Zhongdu in 1215. In 1217 he left the war in north China to his general Muqali; after Khwarazm's governor at Otrar massacred a Mongol caravan in 1218, he led the main army west in 1219. The Mongols reached the Indus and the Kipchak steppe and came home only in 1225.

The Western Xia had once helped the Mongols against the Jin, but the allies fell out and wore each other down. When the Xia refused troops for the western campaign, Genghis Khan returned and attacked in 1226, taking Ganzhou, Liangzhou and Lingzhou, and in 1227 he besieged Zhongxing. He died in camp in August 1227; the place is disputed, and his grave has never been found. His death was kept secret. The last Xia ruler, Li Xian, came out to surrender and was killed, and a state of nearly 190 years was gone, much of its Tangut literature with it.

Ögedei, khan from 1229, followed his father's plan of going round the Jin defences through Song land. In 1231 three columns advanced; Tolui's forced its way through Song-held Hanzhong to come up behind the Jin. Early in 1232 the main Jin army was destroyed in the snow at Sanfengshan. Subutai besieged Kaifeng, where an epidemic struck; the History of Jin claims 900,000 dead in fifty days, surely an exaggeration. Emperor Aizong fled to Guide, then Caizhou. The Song joined in, sending Meng Gong with 20,000 men and 300,000 shi of grain. Caizhou fell in February 1234 and Aizong hanged himself. The Jin had lasted 120 years.

steps: Xiangyang

In 1268 the Mongol general Aju and Liu Zheng, a Song commander who had defected, closed in on Xiangyang and Fancheng, twin cities on the Han River. Lü Wenhuan held out for years while relief failed. In 1273 trebuchets broke Fancheng and Lü surrendered Xiangyang, opening the way to the Yangtze. The Jin still on the map had long been Mongol land; in 1271 Kublai named his dynasty Yuan.

p: After the Jin fell, a Song attempt to retake Kaifeng and Luoyang ended in rout, and from 1235 the two sides were at war. The Song held out in mountain forts in Sichuan and behind the rivers of the Huai and Yangtze. In 1259 the khan Möngke died before the Diaoyu fortress, of disease or perhaps a wound. His brother Kublai, besieging Ezhou, made terms with the Song minister Jia Sidao and went north to fight their brother Ariq Böke for the throne. The winner moved his centre into China, building Dadu from 1267 and naming his dynasty Yuan in 1271, after a phrase in the Book of Changes.

In 1261 Liu Zheng, the Song commander at Luzhou, went over to the Mongols. He urged Kublai to stop battering the Sichuan forts and take Xiangyang instead, then follow the Han into the Yangtze. Xiangyang and Fancheng faced each other across the river, joined by a pontoon bridge. From autumn 1268 Aju and Liu ringed them with forts, cut them off by land and water, built 5,000 warships and trained 70,000 sailors. Song relief armies were beaten back, Fan Wenhu's among them in 1271. In 1272 Zhang Shun and Zhang Gui broke in with 3,000 men in a hundred light boats carrying salt and cloth; neither survived.

A weapon from the west broke the deadlock. Kublai asked the Ilkhanate for engineers, and Ismail and Ala al-Din reached Dadu in 1271 and built counterweight trebuchets that hurled stones of 150 jin, about 90 kg; the Chinese called them 'Muslim catapults'. Early in 1273 the Yuan burned the pontoon bridge and stormed Fancheng. When a stone hit a tower of Xiangyang the city lost heart, and in March Lü Wenhuan surrendered; he later guided the Yuan downriver. The siege had lasted nearly five years, six by the traditional count. In 1274 Bayan led 200,000 men down the Han into the Yangtze.

steps: Yamen

In 1276 Bayan reached Lin'an, and the grand empress dowager Xie surrendered with the child emperor. Loyalists crowned two young princes in turn and fell back to the Guangdong coast. In March 1279 Zhang Hongfan destroyed the last Song fleet at Yamen, and Lu Xiufu leapt into the sea with the seven-year-old emperor on his back. On the map the Yuan reach from Mongolia to Yunnan.

p: Bayan's army entered the Yangtze in 1274 and in 1275 routed the main Song army under Jia Sidao at Dingjiazhou; the river towns surrendered one by one. Early in 1276 the Yuan reached Lin'an, the dowager Xie sent out the imperial seal, and the emperor and his clan were taken north to Shangdu. The court had given up; the resistance had not. The emperor's brothers Zhao Shi and Zhao Bing escaped, and Zhao Shi was crowned at Fuzhou. Hunted by the Yuan and shut out of Quanzhou by Pu Shougeng, the court drifted along the coast; Zhao Shi died in 1278 and Zhao Bing succeeded.

In 1278 the court moved to Yamen, an inlet south of Xinhui where two hills stand like a gate to the sea. Zhang Shijie lashed over a thousand ships together. Zhang Hongfan, a Chinese general in Mongol service, and Li Heng closed in and cut the Song off from water and firewood. On 19 March 1279 the Yuan attacked on the morning and evening tides, the Song line broke, and Lu Xiufu jumped into the sea with Zhao Bing. The History of Song speaks of 100,000 bodies afloat, probably an exaggeration. The captured chancellor Wen Tianxiang saw it all; refusing to serve the Yuan, he was executed at Dadu in 1283.

After Yamen the Yuan ruled all of China, the first northern dynasty to do so. On the map they hold Mongolia, Manchuria, north China and the south, and in the south-west the kingdom of Dali, conquered by Kublai in 1253. Tibet is drawn apart, though the Yuan governed it through a Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs and the Sakya lamas; Goryeo was a vassal. The Yuan branch secretariats were the origin of China's provinces. To the west the Chagatai, the Ilkhanate and the Golden Horde owned Kublai as great khan in name only. His two invasions of Japan, in 1274 and 1281, both failed; the second fleet was wrecked by a typhoon.

steps: The Red Turbans

In 1351 the Yuan court drafted 150,000 labourers to tame the Yellow River, and the White Lotus leaders Han Shantong and Liu Futong seized the moment to rise. Their followers wore red headbands and became the Red Turbans, and the revolt spread across the Huai and the middle Yangtze. By the late 1350s the south no longer obeyed the court, though the map still shows the Yuan of 1279.

p: The late Yuan court was unstable. Around Toghon Temür's accession in 1333 the strongmen El Temür and then Bayan held power; the History of Yuan says Bayan even proposed killing everyone surnamed Zhang, Wang, Liu, Li or Zhao. Paper money issued in 1350 set off runaway inflation. In 1344 the Yellow River broke its dykes at Baimao, flooding Shandong and Henan for years and bringing famine and disease. In 1351 the chancellor Toghto put Jia Lu in charge; with 150,000 labourers and 20,000 soldiers he forced the river back into its old bed within the year, but also gathered a multitude of hungry men in one place.

Han Shantong preached that the Buddha Maitreya would descend and a King of Light appear, and his followers proclaimed him a descendant of the Song emperor Huizong; Liu Futong is said to have claimed a famous Song general as his ancestor. The story goes that they buried a one-eyed stone figure at Huanglingang and spread a rhyme that when it was dug up the realm would rise. The plot leaked in May 1351 and Han was caught and killed, but Liu took Yingzhou and others followed: Xu Shouhui made himself emperor of Tianwan at Qishui, and Guo Zixing seized Haozhou early in 1352, where a poor young monk called Zhu Yuanzhang joined him that spring.

The court could still strike back. In 1354 Toghto besieged Zhang Shicheng at Gaoyou with an army said to number a million, but on the verge of victory he was dismissed after court intrigue and his army melted away. In 1355 Liu Futong enthroned Han Shantong's son Han Lin'er as the 'Lesser King of Light' of a revived Song, and in 1357 sent three armies north: one neared Dadu, another burned Shangdu and fought its way into Goryeo. The campaign failed, but it bled the Yuan of their best troops, leaving the court to depend on feuding strongmen such as Kökö Temür. With the southern grain cut off, Dadu went hungry.

steps: The Ming Take Dadu

Having destroyed Chen Youliang and Zhang Shicheng, Zhu Yuanzhang proclaimed himself emperor at Yingtian in January 1368 and named his dynasty Ming. In September Xu Da's army entered Dadu; the last Yuan emperor had fled north days before. The Yuan withdrew to the steppe as the Northern Yuan. The map shows 1400: the Ming south of the Great Wall and in Liaodong, the Northern Yuan on the steppe.

p: Zhu Yuanzhang was born to poor farmers at Haozhou. In 1344 drought and epidemic killed his parents and eldest brother; he became a novice at the Huangjue monastery, then spent three years begging on the road. After joining Guo Zixing he built his own army and in 1356 took Jiqing, renaming it Yingtian, today's Nanjing. In 1363 he fought Chen Youliang's far larger fleet on Lake Poyang for over thirty days, until Chen fell to an arrow; in 1367 he took Suzhou and captured Zhang Shicheng. Han Lin'er, the rebels' nominal sovereign, had drowned crossing the Yangtze, widely believed to be Zhu's doing.

In late 1367 Xu Da and Chang Yuchun marched north with 250,000 men, proclaiming that they would drive out the barbarians and restore China. They took Shandong and Henan, secured the Tong Pass and made for Dadu. On the night of 10 September 1368 Toghon Temür fled with his family; on the 14th the Ming entered and renamed the city Beiping. He died at Yingchang in 1370, and the Ming called him Shundi, the emperor who bowed to Heaven's will. His son reigned on at Karakorum, and in 1372 Kökö Temür routed a Ming expedition into Mongolia, killing tens of thousands; the Ming turned to defence.

The Ming then mopped up the rest of the Yuan: Yunnan in 1382, Naghachu's army in Liaodong in 1387. In 1388 Lan Yu led 150,000 men across the steppe to Buir Lake and captured over 70,000 of the Northern Yuan's people; the emperor Tögüs Temür escaped, only to be murdered by a kinsman, and the Mongols fell into long civil wars. The Ming on the map is borrowed from the 1500 layer. In 1400 the Ming were at war with themselves: Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, would seize the throne in 1402 and move the capital to Beijing. In 1392 Yi Seong-gye had founded Joseon in Korea as a Ming vassal.

ming-qing.title: From Ming to Qing
ming-qing.lede: From the battlefields of Korea to the Taiwan Strait: ninety years in which the Manchus rose beyond the Great Wall, replaced the Ming and united China under the Qing.
steps: The Imjin War

In May 1592 Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who had just unified Japan, landed some 160,000 men at Busan. Within three weeks they held Hanseong, today's Seoul, and two months later Pyongyang. King Seonjo fled to Uiju on the Yalu and appealed to his overlord, the Ming emperor. China sent armies twice, and the war dragged on for seven years, until Hideyoshi died in 1598 and the Japanese went home.

p: Hideyoshi ended a century of civil war in Japan in 1590 and then declared that he would march through Korea to conquer the Ming. Joseon had known two hundred years of peace and its army was unready. The first wave of nine divisions, about 158,000 men with many matchlocks, drove north under Konishi Yukinaga and Kato Kiyomasa. The turn came at sea: Yi Sun-sin, naval commander of Left Jeolla, beat the Japanese at Okpo, Sacheon (where his turtle ships first fought), Hansando and elsewhere and cut their sea route north, while 'righteous armies' harried them on land. The Jurchen chief Nurhaci offered troops to help Korea; the Koreans politely declined.

In summer 1592 a few thousand Ming horsemen under Zu Chengxun were beaten at Pyongyang. In January 1593 Li Rusong, son of the Liaodong commander Li Chengliang, crossed the Yalu with over 40,000 men and in February took Pyongyang with his guns, but was checked soon after at Byeokjegwan, north of Seoul. Stalemate followed. The negotiators Shen Weijing and Konishi patched together a peace, and in 1596 a Ming embassy invested Hideyoshi as 'King of Japan'. Legend says he tore up the patent, which in fact survives in Osaka; certainly he rejected the terms, and in 1597 he sent some 140,000 men back.

Early in the second invasion the Korean fleet was nearly wiped out at Chilcheollyang; Yi Sun-sin, restored to command, beat off a far larger Japanese fleet at Myeongnyang with 13 ships. Larger Ming armies under Xing Jie and Yang Hao fought the Japanese around Ulsan. Hideyoshi died in September 1598 and his armies were recalled; in December Yi and the Ming admiral Chen Lin caught the retreating fleet at Noryang, where Yi and the Ming general Deng Zilong fell. The History of Ming speaks of hundreds of thousands of men lost, surely an inflated figure; but Liaodong was left weak, and Nurhaci profited.
facts: Li Rusong, Chen Lin (Ming); Yi Sun-sin (Korea)

steps: Sarhu

In 1616 the Jurchen chief Nurhaci proclaimed himself khan at Hetu Ala and named his state Jin, the Later Jin. In 1618 he declared Seven Grievances against the Ming and took Fushun. The next year the Ming sent about 100,000 men in four columns; Nurhaci massed his forces and beat them one by one around Sarhu in five days. On the map the land beyond the Liaodong wall is still marked 'Jurchens'.

p: The Jurchens were descendants of the founders of the Jin dynasty. The Ming held them in check with garrison titles, tribute missions and horse markets. Nurhaci, born in 1559, lost his grandfather and father in 1583 when Ming troops attacking the fort of Gure killed them by mistake; legend says he began with thirteen suits of armour they left him. He bowed to the Ming, took tribute to Beijing and was named 'dragon-tiger general', while uniting the Jianzhou and swallowing the Haixi tribes. In 1599 he had a Manchu script made from the Mongol alphabet, and in 1615 he organised his people into the Eight Banners, both army and society.

In 1618 Nurhaci listed seven grievances, the killing of his father and grandfather among them, and took Fushun, whose commander Li Yongfang went over to him. The alarmed Ming added a Liaodong levy to the land tax and sent Yang Hao to gather troops from across the empire, with Korean and Yehe allies: 470,000 men on paper, about 100,000 in fact. In April 1619 four columns set out to converge on Hetu Ala. Nurhaci, so the story goes, resolved to meet many roads with one. With some 60,000 bannermen he destroyed Du Song's column at Sarhu, then routed Ma Lin and ambushed Liu Ting; only Li Rubai's column got away.

By the Ming's own count more than 300 officers and 45,800 men died, and in Liaodong the Ming were now on the defensive. The Later Jin took Kaiyuan and Tieling and annexed the Yehe in 1619, took Shenyang and Liaoyang in 1621, and in 1625 made Shenyang their capital, later called Mukden. In 1626 Yuan Chonghuan threw Nurhaci back from Ningyuan with European cannon; Nurhaci died months later, and the sources disagree on whether he had been wounded there. His son Hong Taiji renamed his people Manchu in 1635 and his state Qing in 1636. The Liaodong levy, raised year after year, bore heavily on the peasants of the Ming.

steps: On 25 April 1644 Li Zicheng's Shun army broke into Beijing and the Chongzhen emperor hanged himself on Coal Hill, ending Ming rule in the north. Wu Sangui, who held the Shanhai Pass, refused to submit and turned to the Qing. On 27 May the Qing and Wu routed Li at the pass, and on 6 June the Qing entered Beijing. The map still shows the Ming of 1600; by now the Qing held Liaodong and Inner Mongolia.

p: The late Ming crisis began with weather and money. The Little Ice Age brought drought and locusts, and from about 1628 the starving of northern Shaanxi rose. To save money the court cut the postal relays, and Li Zicheng, a courier at Mizhi, lost his job and joined the rebels. To pay for its wars the court piled three surcharges on the land tax, together over ten million taels a year. Li took the title 'Dashing King' after Gao Yingxiang was executed in 1636, and promised land and no taxes. A famous rhyme welcoming him is credited to his adviser Li Yan, whose very existence some historians doubt.

Li took Xi'an in 1643, proclaimed the Shun dynasty early in 1644 and drove through Shanxi on Beijing as garrison after garrison surrendered. On the morning of 25 April the capital fell. Chongzhen hanged himself on Coal Hill, today's Jingshan, with only the eunuch Wang Cheng'en beside him; the Ming had lasted 276 years. The Shun stayed in Beijing just 42 days, torturing Ming officials for silver as discipline collapsed. Wu Sangui's father was held in the city, and his concubine Chen Yuanyuan was reportedly seized by the general Liu Zongmin. A poem by Wu Weiye made her the reason for Wu's choice; his motives were surely more mixed.

Hong Taiji had died in 1643, leaving the Qing throne to his five-year-old son Fulin, with Fulin's uncle Dorgon as regent. Wu sent for help, and Dorgon rode hard for the pass. In late May Li arrived with about 60,000 men; the armies fought along the Shi River until Qing cavalry burst out from Wu's right and the Shun army broke. Li fell back to Beijing, killed Wu's family, had himself crowned and fled west. On 6 June the Qing entered Beijing, claiming to avenge the Chongzhen emperor; in October the boy Shunzhi was enthroned there again, and Beijing became the Qing capital. Wu became a prince of the Qing.

steps: The Southern Ming

After the pass the Qing pushed south. In 1645 they stormed Yangzhou and took Nanjing, ending the Hongguang regime, and an order that all men shave their heads in the Manchu fashion set the south ablaze. Ming princes fought on in Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi and the south-west. The 'Southern Ming' on the map is the Yongli court and its allies in 1650, from Guangdong and Guangxi to Yunnan, Guizhou and southern Sichuan.

p: When Beijing fell, the ministers at Nanjing, the Ming southern capital, crowned the Prince of Fu as the Hongguang emperor. His court was torn by faction under Ma Shiying and Ruan Dacheng, and the four generals north of the Yangtze looked after themselves. The Qing first crushed Li Zicheng in Shaanxi, then sent Dodo south.
