On 20 May 1645 he took Yangzhou, defended by Shi Kefa, and the city was sacked for ten days; a survivor's account speaks of over 800,000 dead, a figure that cannot be trusted. Nanjing opened its gates in June; Hongguang was captured and later executed. Li Zicheng died the same year in Hubei; how he died is disputed.

After Nanjing, Dorgon ordered every man to shave his forehead and wear the queue within ten days: keep your hair and lose your head, went the saying. Towns that had submitted rose again; Jiangyin held out for 81 days, and Jiading was massacred three times. Other Ming princes took up the cause. The Prince of Tang reigned at Fuzhou as the Longwu emperor, propped up by Zheng Zhilong; when Zheng went over to the Qing in 1646, Longwu was caught and killed. A rival court at Guangzhou lasted barely forty days. At the end of 1646 the Prince of Gui took the throne at Zhaoqing as the Yongli emperor; his court would last longest.

Zhang Xianzhong was killed in Sichuan in 1647, and his generals Sun Kewang and Li Dingguo led his army into Guizhou and Yunnan; Li Zicheng's veterans also joined the Ming, and yesterday's 'roving bandits' became the backbone of the resistance. In November 1650 Shang Kexi and Geng Jimao took Guangzhou after a ten-month siege and massacred its people; the same month Kong Youde took Guilin and captured the minister Qu Shisi, who was executed weeks later. In 1652 Sun and Li joined the Yongli court, and Li Dingguo twice beat the Qing, driving Kong Youde to suicide and killing the prince Nikan: the last great Ming counter-offensive.

steps: Koxinga Takes Taiwan

In April 1661 Zheng Chenggong, known in the West as Koxinga, sailed from Jinmen with some 25,000 men, landed at Lu'ermen on Taiwan and besieged Fort Zeelandia, the Dutch East India Company's stronghold. Nine months later, in February 1662, the governor Frederick Coyett surrendered, ending 38 years of Dutch rule. 'Dutch Formosa' on the map is its extent in 1650; Zheng's bases at Xiamen and Jinmen lie inside the Qing.

p: Zheng Chenggong was born in 1624 at Hirado in Japan to Zheng Zhilong, master of the south China sea trade, and a Japanese mother. In 1645 the Longwu emperor gave him the imperial surname, which made him 'Lord of the Imperial Surname', Koxinga in the Dutch rendering of its Hokkien form. When his father went over to the Qing in 1646, he refused to follow and fought on from Xiamen and Jinmen for the Yongli emperor, who made him Prince of Yanping. In 1659 he and Zhang Huangyan sailed up the Yangtze, took Zhenjiang and besieged Nanjing, but he lingered before the walls and was routed. He needed a safer base.

South-west Taiwan was then held by the Dutch East India Company. It had built Fort Zeelandia at Tayouan, in today's Tainan, in 1624, driven the Spanish from the north in 1642 and brought in settlers from Fujian to grow sugar and hunt deer. He Bin, an interpreter for the Dutch, defected to Zheng with a chart of the Lu'ermen channel. On 30 April 1661 Zheng's fleet rode the high tide through it; days later Fort Provintia surrendered. Zeelandia was too strong to storm, so Zheng starved it. A relief fleet from Batavia arrived in August and was beaten at sea, and in December a German deserter advised attacking the Utrecht redoubt outside the walls.

On 25 January 1662 the redoubt was shot to pieces; Coyett signed a surrender on 1 February and sailed for Batavia. Zheng renamed Taiwan Dongdu, the Eastern Capital, set up a prefecture and two counties and put his soldiers to farming. The Qing had answered in 1661 by moving the coast's population from Shandong to Guangdong 30 to 50 li inland to starve him of supplies, and executed his father. Zheng died of illness in June 1662, aged 37; that year Wu Sangui also put the Yongli emperor to death in Kunming, ending the Southern Ming. Zheng's son Zheng Jing renamed the island Dongning and held out across the strait.

steps: The Three Feudatories and Taiwan

In 1673 the Kangxi emperor decided to abolish the three great fiefs of the south. Wu Sangui rose in Yunnan, Geng Jingzhong and Shang Zhixin followed, and war engulfed southern China for eight years, until Kunming fell in 1681. In 1683 Shi Lang destroyed the Zheng fleet off Penghu and Zheng Keshuang surrendered Taiwan. The map still shows 1650; its Southern Ming and Dutch Formosa were long gone.

p: The early Qing had conquered the south with Chinese generals who had changed sides. Wu Sangui held Yunnan, Shang Kexi Guangdong and Geng Jingzhong Fujian. These Three Feudatories kept large armies, appointed their own officials and raised their own taxes, yet drew huge subsidies from the court; it was said that half the empire's revenue went to them. In 1673 the ageing Shang Kexi asked to retire to Liaodong and leave his son in command. The 19-year-old Kangxi seized the chance and ordered all three fiefs disbanded. Most ministers warned of revolt; Kangxi reckoned it would come sooner or later anyway.

In December 1673 Wu Sangui killed the governor of Yunnan and rose in revolt. Geng Jingzhong in Fujian and Wang Fuchen in Shaanxi joined him in 1674, Shang Zhixin in Guangdong in 1676, and Zheng Jing crossed from Taiwan to seize the southern Fujian coast; most of the south was lost. Wu quickly took Hunan but halted at the Yangtze, giving the Qing time to recover. Kangxi directed the war from Beijing, relying heavily on Chinese Green Standard troops; Wang and Geng gave in in 1676, Shang in 1677. Wu proclaimed himself emperor of Zhou at Hengzhou in 1678 and died that autumn. In December 1681 Kunming fell and his grandson killed himself.

With the south secure, Kangxi turned to Taiwan. Zheng Jing died in 1681, and the minister Feng Xifan killed his eldest son and set up the boy Zheng Keshuang, dividing the Zheng camp. Kangxi gave command of the Fujian fleet to Shi Lang, a former officer of Koxinga's whose father and brother Koxinga had executed. In July 1683 Shi attacked Penghu with over 200 ships and 20,000 men and in a week destroyed the Zheng fleet under Liu Guoxuan; Zheng Keshuang surrendered. Some at court wanted to abandon the island, but Shi argued for keeping it, and in 1684 Taiwan became a prefecture of Fujian. The ban on sea trade was lifted that year.

late-qing.title: The Late Qing
late-qing.lede: Seventy years of rebellion and foreign war brought two thousand years of empire to an end.
steps: The Opium War

From 1757 the Qing let Western merchants trade only at Guangzhou (Canton). British traders found something China would buy, Indian opium, and silver drained out. In 1839 Lin Zexu destroyed their stocks at Humen; in 1840 Britain went to war. The Treaty of Nanking of 1842 ceded Hong Kong Island and opened five ports, the first of the 'unequal treaties'.

p: The Qing confined trade with the West to Guangzhou, where it passed through licensed Chinese merchants, the Cohong. Britain bought tea, silk and porcelain in quantity but had little that China wanted, so it paid in silver. The East India Company monopolised opium grown in Bengal, and private traders smuggled it onto the Guangdong coast. By the late 1830s about 40,000 chests a year were arriving; silver flowed out instead of in, its price rose, and addiction spread among officials and soldiers. After debate at court, the Daoguang Emperor chose a ban.

Lin Zexu reached Guangzhou as imperial commissioner in March 1839. He blockaded the foreign factories until the British surrendered more than 20,000 chests, and in June had them destroyed on the beach at Humen. Charles Elliot, the British Superintendent of Trade, called for force. In June 1840 a British expedition arrived off Guangdong, sailed north, seized Dinghai in Zhejiang and in August appeared off Dagu, near Tianjin. The emperor dismissed Lin and sent Qishan to negotiate, but neither government accepted the draft he agreed with Elliot. In 1841 the British occupied Hong Kong Island, attacked Guangzhou and moved up the coast, taking Xiamen, Dinghai and Ningbo.

Reinforced in 1842, the British took Wusong, where the commander Chen Huacheng was killed, and in July stormed Zhenjiang, cutting the Grand Canal that carried grain to Beijing. With Nanjing under their guns, the Qing envoys Qiying and Yilibu signed the Treaty of Nanking aboard HMS Cornwallis on 29 August. China ceded Hong Kong Island, opened Guangzhou, Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai, paid 21 million silver dollars, abolished the Cohong and agreed to settle its tariffs with Britain. Agreements in 1843 added consular jurisdiction and most-favoured-nation treatment, and the United States and France soon won similar treaties.

steps: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom

Early in 1851 Hong Xiuquan, a Hakka from Guangdong who had repeatedly failed the civil service examinations, rose in revolt at Jintian in Guangxi and founded the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. In 1853 his armies took Nanjing, which as Tianjing, the Heavenly Capital, held out for eleven years. Common estimates put the dead at 20 to 30 million, some studies higher; no war of the century killed more.

p: Hong Xiuquan, from Hua county near Guangzhou, failed even the lowest examination several times. He had read a Christian tract by the Chinese evangelist Liang Fa, and after a severe illness became convinced that he was God's second son, the younger brother of Jesus, sent to rid the world of demons. With Feng Yunshan he founded the God Worshippers in the hills of Guangxi, winning over ten thousand followers among poor Hakka farmers, charcoal burners and miners. Famine, banditry and feuds between Hakka and older settlers made fertile ground for revolt. In January 1851 the God Worshippers rose at Jintian.

Breaking out of Yong'an in 1852, the Taipings marched north, failed to take Changsha, captured Wuchang in January 1853 and sailed down the Yangtze to take Nanjing in March. Their land programme promised equal shares and common property, though little of it was carried out; they banned opium and foot-binding, segregated men and women, and denounced Confucian books and idols as demonic. A northern expedition came close to Tianjin before it was wiped out. In 1856 the leaders turned on each other: Yang Xiuqing and Wei Changhui were killed, and in 1857 Shi Dakai marched away with his troops.

The Qing's Banner and Green Standard armies lost battle after battle, and the court came to rely on regional armies raised by Han Chinese gentry: Zeng Guofan's Xiang (Hunan) Army, later Li Hongzhang's Huai (Anhui) Army, and near Shanghai the foreign-officered Ever Victorious Army. The Taiping generals Li Xiucheng and Chen Yucheng still won victories, but in 1861 the Xiang Army took Anqing and closed in from upriver. Hong died in June 1864; Tianjing fell in July and was sacked. With the Nian and Muslim revolts as well, the Qing needed over twenty years to restore order.

steps: Outer Manchuria lost

During the Second Opium War Russia exploited the Qing's troubles. The Treaty of Aigun of 1858 gave it about 600,000 km² north of the Amur; in 1860, after British and French troops took Beijing and burned the Old Summer Palace, the Treaty of Peking added about 400,000 km² east of the Ussuri. The map still draws these lands inside the Qing; on the 1900 snapshot they are Russian.

p: In October 1856 Chinese officers boarded the Arrow, a ship once registered in Hong Kong, and arrested its Chinese crew. Britain used the incident as a pretext to attack Guangzhou; France joined in over the execution of a missionary, Auguste Chapdelaine. The allies took Guangzhou at the end of 1857, captured the governor-general Ye Mingchen, and seized the Dagu forts. In June 1858 the Treaties of Tianjin with Russia, the United States, Britain and France opened ten more ports, including Hankou and Nanjing, admitted foreign envoys to Beijing and let foreigners travel and preach inland; opium was soon legalised as 'foreign medicine'.

In the north Russia moved at the same time. Nikolay Muravyov, Governor-General of Eastern Siberia, led flotillas down the Amur and planted posts and settlers along it. In May 1858, under threat of force, he made the Qing general Yishan sign a treaty at Aigun: about 600,000 km² north of the Amur and south of the Stanovoy Range passed to Russia, and the land east of the Ussuri was to be held jointly. Only the Sixty-Four Villages opposite Aigun stayed under Qing rule. The territory had been Qing since the Treaty of Nerchinsk of 1689. The emperor refused to ratify, to no avail.

Repulsed at Dagu in 1859, an Anglo-French army returned in 1860, took Dagu and Tianjin and in September routed Sengge Rinchen's troops at Baliqiao as the Xianfeng Emperor fled to Rehe. In October the allies entered Beijing, and after looting it Lord Elgin ordered the Old Summer Palace burned. Prince Gong signed the Convention of Peking, ceding the tip of Kowloon to Britain, opening Tianjin and raising the indemnities to 8 million taels each. In November the Russian envoy Nikolay Ignatyev secured the land east of the Ussuri, where Russia had already founded Vladivostok, 'Ruler of the East'.

steps: The war with Japan

In 1894, the Jiawu year, the Qing and Japan went to war over Korea. The Beiyang Fleet was mauled off the Yalu and destroyed at Weihaiwei the next year. By the Treaty of Shimonoseki of April 1895 China recognised Korea's 'independence', ceded Taiwan, Penghu and Liaodong and paid 200 million taels. The map still shows Taiwan as Qing; on the 1900 snapshot it is Japanese.

p: Around the time the Taiping fell, officials such as Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang and Zuo Zongtang launched the Self-Strengthening Movement: arsenals and a navy yard, students sent to America, mines, a steamship company and the first railways; from 1861 a new office, the Zongli Yamen, handled foreign affairs. Japan, after the Meiji Restoration of 1868, modernised faster still. It sent troops to Taiwan in 1874, annexed the Ryukyu Islands in 1879 and turned to Korea, the most important of the Qing's tributaries. In 1885 the two agreed at Tianjin that each would notify the other before sending troops there.

In 1894 the Donghak rebellion broke out in Korea; its government asked the Qing for troops, and Japan sent a larger force of its own. On 25 July Japanese warships attacked Chinese ships off Pungdo and sank the transport Kowshing; war was declared on 1 August. In mid-September the Qing army was routed at Pyongyang, and on the 17th the Beiyang Fleet fought the Japanese for about five hours off the Yalu, losing five ships; Deng Shichang went down with the Zhiyuan. In November Japan took Port Arthur (Lüshun) and massacred civilians and surrendered soldiers; Chinese sources usually put the dead at about 20,000.

Early in 1895 Japan attacked Weihaiwei by land and sea; the fleet was destroyed and Admiral Ding Ruchang took his own life. Li Hongzhang, wounded by an assailant during the talks, signed the treaty with Itō Hirobumi on 17 April: China recognised Korea's independence, ceded Taiwan, Penghu and Liaodong, paid 200 million taels, opened four more cities and let Japanese build factories. Russia, Germany and France made Japan return Liaodong for another 30 million taels. On Taiwan a short-lived Republic of Formosa led resistance for about five months. Defeat spurred calls for reform, but in 1898 the Guangxu Emperor's Hundred Days' Reform was ended by a coup of the Empress Dowager Cixi, and six reformers were executed.
facts: 200 million taels, plus 30 million for Liaodong

steps: The Boxer War

After the war with Japan the powers scrambled for leases and spheres of influence. The Boxers, crying 'Support the Qing, destroy the foreign', spread through Shandong and Zhili and in June 1900 besieged Beijing's legations, and the court declared war. In August an eight-nation force took Beijing and Cixi fled to Xi'an. The map now shows the 1900 snapshot: Outer Manchuria is Russian, Taiwan Japanese, Korea the Korean Empire.

p: In November 1897 two German missionaries were killed at Juye in Shandong. Germany seized Jiaozhou Bay and the next year forced a 99-year lease. Russia followed with Port Arthur and Dalian, Britain with Weihaiwei and Hong Kong's New Territories, France with Guangzhouwan, and the powers marked out zones for railways and mines; Chinese feared the country would be carved up like a melon. Meanwhile missionaries and converts were spreading through northern villages, disputes with their neighbours multiplied, and flood and drought left many peasants destitute.

The Boxers grew out of Shandong's village martial-arts societies, whose rituals were believed to make them invulnerable. They burned churches, killed missionaries and Chinese Christians and tore up railways and telegraph lines. In June 1900 they poured into Beijing and Tianjin; the German minister, Clemens von Ketteler, and a Japanese diplomat were killed, and Boxers and Qing troops besieged the Legation Quarter for nearly two months. On 21 June the court declared war, but Li Hongzhang, Zhang Zhidong and other south-eastern governors ignored the edict and kept their provinces out of the war. Across the north over two hundred foreign missionaries and their children and tens of thousands of Chinese Christians were killed.

In mid-June a relief column under Admiral Edward Seymour was turned back; the allies took the Dagu forts and, in July, Tianjin. In August a force of about 20,000 marched on Beijing, broke in on the 14th and relieved the legations; Cixi fled west with the emperor. Allied troops looted and killed across the region, and Russia occupied all of Manchuria, massacring thousands of Chinese at Blagoveshchensk and in the Sixty-Four Villages. The Boxer Protocol of 7 September 1901 with eleven powers imposed 450 million taels over 39 years, razed the Dagu forts and let foreign troops guard the legations and the railway to Shanhaiguan.
facts: 450 million taels; about 980 million with interest

steps: The 1911 Revolution

After 1900 the court tried reform, abolishing the examinations, training a New Army and preparing a constitution, but could not win back support. On 10 October 1911 troops rose at Wuchang, and within two months more than ten provinces broke away. On 1 January 1912 Sun Yat-sen became provisional president of the Republic of China in Nanjing; on 12 February the boy emperor Puyi abdicated, ending two millennia of imperial rule.

p: After the Boxer Protocol the court launched the New Policies. It trained a modern army, encouraged industry and in 1905 abolished the civil service examinations after some 1,300 years. In 1904–1905 Japan and Russia fought over Manchuria on Chinese soil, and Japan won the Liaodong lease and the railway south of Changchun. In 1908 the court promised a constitution after nine years of preparation, and provincial assemblies met in 1909. But the first cabinet, formed in May 1911, had only four Han Chinese among thirteen ministers, most of the rest Manchu nobles; the 'princes' cabinet' bitterly disappointed the constitutionalists.

The revolutionaries wanted to end the dynasty. In 1905 Sun Yat-sen united several groups in Tokyo as the Tongmenghui, the Revolutionary Alliance, pledged to 'expel the Manchus, restore China, found a republic, equalise land rights'. Rising after rising in the south failed, among them the Guangzhou uprising of April 1911. In May 1911 the court nationalised the trunk railways and signed a loan with a four-power banking consortium to build them; protest flared in Sichuan, and New Army troops were sent from Hubei to suppress it. On the evening of 10 October revolutionaries in the Wuchang garrison rose prematurely, took the city and made the brigade commander Li Yuanhong military governor of Hubei.

Province after province broke with the court. The Qing recalled Yuan Shikai as prime minister; once his Beiyang Army had retaken Hankou and Hanyang, he negotiated with the south. On 29 December delegates of 17 provinces elected Sun Yat-sen provisional president. Yuan traded the abdication for the presidency: on 12 February 1912 Empress Dowager Longyu issued the edict for the six-year-old Puyi, ending 268 years of Qing rule, and in March Yuan took office in Beijing. The atlas's last snapshot is from 1900, so the map still shows the Qing and the Korean Empire; Japan's annexation of Korea in 1910, Outer Mongolia's declaration of independence in late 1911 and Tibet's expulsion of the Qing garrison in 1912 are not drawn.

burning-books: Burning of books and burying of scholars

p: Borders start from the historical base maps of aourednik/historical-basemaps (GPL-3.0). That data is coarse for China, and all 53 snapshots are revised for this atlas: the extent of the Xia, Shang and Western Zhou, and the borders between the states of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States, the Northern and Southern dynasties, the Five Dynasties and other periods of division, are rough outlines after the standard historical atlases (chiefly the picture given by Tan Qixiang's Historical Atlas of China), not traced from them. Read them as sketches. In November 2026 an AI assistant also checked every snapshot against the histories, polity by polity, and corrected those the source puts in the wrong place, under the wrong name or far beyond their real extent (Nanzhao drawn in Burma, for one); the corrections too are rough outlines.

Where the histories put a border on the Huai, the Yangtze or the Yellow River between Shanxi and Shaanxi, it follows the river as drawn by Natural Earth (public domain). Rivers and coastlines are today's; their changes over time are not shown. Areas are approximate and cover only the map window.

Chinese history has an exact year-by-year chronology only from 841 BC, the first year of the Gonghe regency. Earlier dates follow the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project (published 2000) and are marked "c.". Whether the Xia existed, and whether Erlitou was its capital, is still debated. Later dates follow the standard chronology; there is no year 0.

The events and story chapters were written by an AI assistant (Anthropic's Claude) from the standard histories and scholarship, not copied from any one work. In November 2026 their dates, numbers, names, quotations and claims such as 'earliest' or 'largest' were checked one by one, mainly against the sources below: some 1,200 held, and 60 were wrong or stated too firmly; these have been corrected, or the text now notes the disagreement. The check, too, was done by AI with online sources; no historian has reviewed the texts.
Mistakes may remain: for any particular fact, rely on the primary sources and specialist works. Corrections are welcome on GitHub.
